div.p: Tottrp.

THE CLERK OF THE WEATHER. There once was a boy home from school, Who found rainy weather the rule; And though six weeks had passed, Yet still it rained fast, And the air was unpleasantly cool .• To this juvenile home from his school. Then the small boy began to look glum, And he said, "Will the sun never _come? I've but three days more: Then, with holidays o'er, I must go back to read, write, and sum! No wonder I look rather glum! "No woneler I feel it's a shame, For of cricket I've not had a game; And the beautiful fishing For which I've been wishing Has been angling, but only in name! No wonder I feel it's a shame!" Then the small boy was struck with a thought; For, day after day, he had sought The big old barometer, That, true as chronometer, The state of the weather had taught; And the sight of it gave him a thought. "This old thing is to blame, I can see! I'll smash it to pieces," said he. "Then for three days together In bright summer weather I'll have all the fun that can be: For this thing is to blame, I can see!" Then he knocked the barometer o'er, Into hundreds of pieces or more; Yet each day, I've heard— First, second, and third— The weather was worse than before, Was really much worse than before r —Little Folks.
G. W,

A Harmless Burglar.—One who breaks into a perspiration. Countess: "I told you expressly to paint the chamber bloed-colour, and you have made it blue." Painter I beg your pardon. I thought the gracious countess had blue blood:" A member of a club objected to the publication of the list of the meeting nights of the club, " because," said he, "if it's published, we married men will have to account for - the off nights." The motion to publish was lost. A CONJUGAL CONUNDRUM. ,Which is of the greater value, prithee say, The bride or bridegroom ?--Must the truth be told? Alas, it must? The bride is given away ; The bridegroom's often regularly sold. .13-‘4le a straw stack sat a tramp—a jolly tramp, and wise :10, while he patched his tattered coat, did thus solilo- qu',e —"lt seems so sad that my lone life doth ever down- ward tend, and drags me into wretchedness; but still I'm on the mend. And when I need a little cash, I make no loud laments, but by a straw stack sit me down, and gather in my rents." The teller of a bank in New York reports the following in.tiident :—A. German citizen approaching the window, re- qa,•sted that a cheque payable to the order of Schweitzer- case be cashed. "Ja, dot's me," he nodded reassuringly, in answer to the teller's look of inquiry. "But I don't know :that ;you are Mr. Schweitzercase. Irou must get yourself isle:Aided," said the teller. " How vas dot ?" asked the Geraian citizen, with a puzzled look. "You must get some one to identify you," repeated the bank officer •, "I don't know you." " Ah, ja!" cried Hans, much relieved. "Dot's al'. right. I don't know you neider." WHAT TIGER Dio.—l will tell you a story about a very clever dog, named Tiger. Tiger used to be sent every morning by "IRS -El-Air to the butcher's shop with a copper coin, to buy his breakfast; but one day his usual shop was, for some rea.son, closed, so the dog made his way to another butcher's. But no sooner had he put down the piece of money than the butcher took it, put into the till, and refused to give Tiger his meat. The dog did not, however, take much notice of this treatment at the time; but the next morning he went again to the cheating butcher, and put down his coin, with his paw upon it; and when the man had given him the meat, as he did this time, and as about to take the money, he suddenly swallowed his breakfast, and then sped off with the coin in his mouth as fast as ever he could.—' Be. for November. A BIT OF RocKv-MouNTAIN SCF.NERY.—It is a chari acteristic of the Utah portion of the Rocky-Mountain chain, and one that disappoints many a traveller, that there are here no imposing and ragged peaks' no sharp sum- mits, no snow-covered passes, and little that is wild anel rugqed. All that those who remember Switierland havq 4 been ,accustomed to connect in their minds with great groans of mountain-masses must be sought elsewhere. Thl Plains themselves rise; one does not leave them in order tq _

, climb. Over a vast, grass-covered, and almost unbroken, graiwal slope, covering hundreds of miles of country, the wayfarer has come imperceptibly to the great water-shed. It is scenery of prairie, not of hills and peaks, that has sur eounded his journey. For the last fifty miles, indeed, beforei the arrival at Sherman, the rise is td been barely appreciable but that is all. A new circumstance makes the descent from the great height much more perceptible and enjoyablei through a new sensation. It is then that the traveller over doer railways, who has flattered himself that the "lightning' expres,s" of his own region was the highest possible form of locomotive speed, first learns the real meaning of a "down: grade." The descent from Sherman to the Laramie-Plains is a new esperience to such people as have not slid down a 1 a3sian ice-hill, or fallen from a fourth-story window. Let the hardy individual 'who would enjoy it to the full betake h:onself to the last platform of the last car, or the foremost platform of the front one, and there hold hard to brake or railing, to watch the bewitched world spin and whirl.— " .Picturesque America" fae November. _ _
AN 01.15 DELUSION.—Oar forefathers were possessed of the idea that no nation could be rich which suffered money _ _

to go out of its custody. Hence the English monarchs appointed a great officer, called the King's Exchanger, who superintended, either in person or by deputy, all foreign commerce, in order to prevent money from leaving the kirg-lorn, or to assist the entrance of money into it. In. course of time, when it was found that certain kinds of trade could not be carried on unless permission to export money was given, precautions were taken that the goods which were bought with this money shoublbe sold for more money, and that the country should thus be indirectly enriched. With the same object of underselling othecountries, and thus of obtaininglmore of this coveted wealth, laws were enacted in order to keep down wages. To prevent any por- tion of the money which was held at home from leaving the country. Englishmen were not allowed to bay foreign goods, however cheap they might be. Laws were passed, giving, under the name of a bounty, premiums on those who could succeed in underselling their neighbours abroad; and other laws forbad the importation of food lest a portion of. the precious store of gold and silver should fall into the hands of foreigners. Trade was restricted, cartailed, ham- pered ; a thousand jealousies were engendered, and made bitter in order to effect that which could never be done, even if it were ever SO ranch wished, and never should have been done, Oen if it had been possible. The worst parts of the commercial system which fifty years ago prevailed in this country, sprang entirely from the notion that. money was wealth; and though we have slowly and with difficulty, got rid of the delusion, with its consequences, other nations have so familiarised themselves with the restrictions which "ach a policy imposed, that they-think their prosperity is hela together by the chains in which they have fettered their trade.—Cassell's " Popular Educator" for November. PRESTON AND THE CORONATION OF JAMES IL—The coronation of James IL at Westminster, took place OD the 23rd April, 1685, and notice given in the London Gazette of that date to the peers and peeresses te send in the name of the gentleman or page who is to wait upon them in the great Hall where their Majesties dine, in order to have tiokets given them; farther, all persons are warned that they do not presume to print or publish any account or rela- tion of the said coronation without the leave of the EAI Marshal. Thereafter we have an account of the ceremony, published by authority, as follows :—" Their Majesties, Juries 11. and Mary of Modena, being come to Westminster Hall about eleven of the clock in the morning, and being seated on the throne there the sword of state, the sword cuetana, and the two-pointed sword, together with the gol- den spurs, were presented to his Majesty, and laid on a table before him, and the crown and other regalia having been brolght by the Dean and Prebends of Westminster in pro- cession, and presented severally to his Majesty, were like- wise laid on the table, and then delivered to those who were to bear them in procession, in which his Majesty, walking unisir .a_ rich canopy, borne by 10 Barons of the Cinque Ports, proceeded on foot upon bleu cloth spread from the steps of the throne in Westminster Hall to the steps of the theatre in the quire of the Collegiate Church of St. Peter, Westminster, when the ceremony proceeded, and the crown being put on just at three o'clock in the afternoon all the people shouted, the drums and trumpets sounded, the guns In St. James's Park and the great guns at the Tower were discharged, and all the peers put on their crowns." In those • days faith in omens had not 'died out. The choice of St. George's Day for the coronation was doubtless in the hope qf its proving a fortunate one; but Burnet tells us that (owing probably to the breaking of one of the staves that supported it) the canopy over his Majesty fell down, and that the crown being too large for his head, came too far over his face; 'but, he adds, that which the London Gazette does not notice, that the" Queen, with the peeresses, made a more graceful figure." Subsequently the whole company, except the church (meaning, of course, the Churchmen) of Westminster, returned to the hall, and were conducted to their several tables to dinner, already furnished before they came in. The first course for their Majesties' table being served with the usual pomp and ceremony, the Lord High Steward between the Lord High Constable and be Bart Marshall, riding in before it on horseback, and before the second course Sir Charles Dymocke, the King's champion, in complete armour, accompanied by the Lord High Constable and Elrl Marshall, on horseback, performed the usual chal enge. The day was of course a public hon. day, and an occasion of riotous merriment to the Commons, whose rejoicing for the event seems to have reached the climax at Preston, in Lancashire, where we find the people drank their Majesties' health upon their knees, round a great bon fire.—Oddfellows' Magazine. Peon/ OF LANCASHIRE.—We understand that Mr. J. C. Melvin is collecting material for a Flora of Lancashire.— Science Monthly. M. Craponne, chief engineer to the Lyons Gas Company, utilisee coke dust for firing purposes by mixing it with pul- verised pitch, softening the mass, and compressing it into briquettes. The fuel is used along with coke, and is said to answer.—Science Monthly. A GIGANTIC REPTlLE.—Professor Marsh has " restored " the Brontosaurus, one of the most gigantic of the extinct animals of America, and published a description of it. The reptile seems to have been about 50 feet in length, weighed about 20 tons, had feet measuring about a square yard, possessed a very small head, and was not furnished with either offensive or defensive weapons. RSTA.I,NING THE COLOURS IN DRIED FLOWERS.—A simple method of preserving the original colours of flowers dried in the herbarium press is recommended in Science Gossip. It is to brush the petals with a weak solution of alum, the liquid being applied with a fine camel-hairbrush. Specimens so treated before preserving are said to retain their tints beautifully, the plan only failing in about one case out of ten. Dr. Grassi is said to have made the important discovery that flies are active agents in the propagation of disease. They take the ova of parasitical worms into their mouths and discharge them unchanged in convenient places, often upon substances to be used as human food. Dr. Grassi is so impressed with the magnitude and seriousness of the consequences that he hopes some effectual means may soon be found of destroying flies.—Science Monthly. DISCOVERIES IN LONDON.—WhiIe excavating for the ex- tension of the buildings known as New Courts Chambers in Chancery-lane into Southampton Buildings, the workmen came upon some chalk walls and glazed tiles. Mr. John Sachs, of the Middlesex Archreological Society, was at once communicated with, and careful investigations revealed two pertions of undoubted Roman walls of chalk and cement, with some tiles of red material, glazed with yellow, and be- neath a deposit of charcoal, doubtless a landmark, for which purpose such deposits have been frequently used, from their imperishable nature. The surmise that this is Ithe site of the first home of the Knights Tempters is borne out by the quantity of human remains that have also been found, it being well known that the Knights removed their most important monuments to the Temple, leasing less im- portant remains behind. Quantities of old Samon pottery, in fragments, also came to light. It is expected that more discoveries will follow. THE ELECTRIC LIGHT ON RATLWAYS.—SUCCESSFUL TRTAL.--On the Brighton Line the saloons of certain trains have been lit by electricity for some little time ; but other lines have been slow to follow the example in consequence of the difficulties connected with the storage of electricity. An invention has now been patented by which these will be obviated. Electricity is generated by a primary battery, which can be carried underneath a railway carriage, or in any convenient part of the train. The battery is composed of zinc and carbon plates, and is charged with a chemical for the absorption of hydrogen, which, the inventors affirm, will cost only one-eighth of the amount demanded for the chemicals hitherto used for that purpose. Among the merits claimed for tha inventian are the exceedingly low internal resistance of the battery, the facility with which it can be charged, and its freedom from noxious fumes. A trial of the system was made on the Great Northern Line on Thursday week when the Pullman dining-car of the 5 40 express to Leeds was lit by six Swan incandescent L lamps, supplied with electricity from one battery of 12 cells, the demensions of the battery being :—Length, 4ft., breadth Bin., and depth Bin. The lamps diffused a bright, warm, and perfectly steady light, which at no moment affected by tin oscilliation of the cacriage, made it not only possi- possible, but perfectly easy, to read a newspaper or book printed in small type. The result of other preliminary trials of the system has been that several railway companies, including the Great Eastern, the South-Eastern, and the London and South-Western have shown A desire to adopt it. The light can be turned on or off at pleasure, and it can therefore be used in the day when a train is passing through a tunnel. The inventors of the battery exprese a belief that they will be able to supply private dwellings with electric light for less than the estimate lately put forward by the Edison Company and the Crotilcher Company. The battery which was used on Thursday weighed under 1501 b., and one capable of supplying 13 lights for 18 continuous , hours would weigh about 3 cwt. The inventors of the , system are Mr. G. C. V. Holmes and Mr. F. E. Burke. Mr. F. Cheeqwright, who is connected ,with the Sykes Block system, has also taken an active Share in the introduction of the light, which was on Tharay under the manage- ment of Mr. E. Travers Zohrab, railway engineer.

Pride comes before a waterfall (when your friends have not seen it). There's many a slip 'twixt the cook and the trip. " Mayl have the honour to conduct your daughter to the supper table ?" asked a society gentleman of a lady from the country who is ataying with some friends whom she is visiting. "May you take her to supper ?" was the response. " Why, of course; and you can take me, too. That's what we cattle here for."

AFRICAN PUZZLE.S.—Africa is, indeed, a great ethno- graphic puzzlt. The maize, for example, is commonly said to be a New World plant, unknown in Europe until after the discovery of America, and hence the grains of Indian corn, which are sold to credulous travellers as contemporary with the mummies from the side of which they are said to be taken, must be bracketed with the Mexican Dahlia bulbs, and the Chinese scent-bottles, with mottoes quoted from poems which were not composed till two thousand years after the Theban tombs in which they are said to be found were made. But we are staggered to find maize cultivated as an ordinary crop everywhere, in the most remote parts of Central Africa, by people who have never seen white men, who have no tradition of the time when the corn was not grown as food and for making beer, and are absolutely ignorant, even in their legends, of any race from whom they could have obtained this all-important element in the economy of so many native American nationalities. What is more, there is scarcely any African tribe raised above the lowest grade of savagedom that does not own, or has not owned, for uncounted generations, droves of cattle and flocks of domestic fowls. When did they get them ? Throughout savage Africa there is no trace of any stone building, or indeed of any edifice which could have seen reared by a superior race, and yet it is hard to conceive whence came the maize, the fowls, and the cattle.—" The Peoples of the World" for Notember. THE EDUCATION OF A GREAT ENGINEER.—It would be difficult to find a more really helpful book to put into the hands of any earnest and sensible young man about to enter upon industrial occupation, and especially if it were a mechanical one, than the Autobiography of James Nasmyth, the inventor of the steam hammer, edited by Dr. Smiles. James Nasmyth himself was born on the 9th of August, 1808, and was the youngest in a family of six daughters and four eons. The sketch of the simple home life of this family is one of the most interesting features of the book— simple in its homely thrift and virtue, but full of useful and elevated industry. All the children were early instructed in the art of drawing, and out of the father's class for his children grew an art class, conducted by the daughters, to which many of the young ladies of the Edinburgh families —kept at home by the European war—resorted for the com- pletion of their accomplishments. When not drawing or painting in ail, the pupils were occupied in sketching from nature in the delightful outskirts of Edinburgh. James Nasmyth became agreat proficient in the use of his pencil, and he joins with others who are, or ought to be, authori- ties upon the subject of education, in the high value he sets upon this art. He calls it "graphic language" :—" A few strokes of the pencil can convey ideas which quires of writ- ing would fail to impart, This is one of the most valuable gifts which a man who has to do with practical subjects can possess. The language of the pencil' is truly a uni- versal one, especially in communicating ideas which have reference to material forms. And yet it is in a great measure neglected in'our modern system of so-called education." Again, and in another connection, he writes—" It formed the principal part of my own education. It gave me the power of recording observations with a few graphic strokes of the pencil ; and far surpassed in expression any number of mere words. . . . This accomplishment of accurate drawing, which I achieved for the most part in my father's workroom, served me many a good turn in future years with reference to the engineering work which became the business of my life." But his father's workehop.with its lathe, its fur- ance and its bench,was equally his delight. "I was constantly busy—mind, hands, and body were kept in a state of de- lightful and instructive activity." He became initiated into every variety'of mechanical and chemical manipula- tion, made his own tools, constructed his own chemical ap- paratus, as far as lay in his power, and went on to the preparation of all his own chemical agents. This was a true technical education for him, and for the companions, sometimes of humble birth, who shared many of his pur- suits. It was this that led him to write :—" The truth is thit the eyes and the fingers—the bare fingers—are the two principal inlets to sound practical instruction. They are the chief sources of trustworthy knowledge in all the ma- terials and operations which the engineer has to deal with. No book knowledge can avail for that purpose. The nature and properties of the materials must come in through the finger ends. Hence I have no faith in young engineers who are addicted to wearing kid gloves. Gloves, especially kid gloves, are perfect non-conductors of technical knowledge.' None the less did James Nasmyth avail himself of all the advantages of the scientific lectures which the University of Edinburgh offered for those who would search for know- ledge down to its foundations in law, and pursues it through all the fields of investigation and speculation. He was as earnest in these studies as in those of the more immediately practical kind, carryinginto all the spirit of these words of To encounter and overcome a difficulty is the most in- teresting of all things." No wonder, then, that at the age of 19, when the subject of steam carriages' to run upon common roads was occupying attention, he first produced, with his own hands, a small working model, for the Scottish Society of Arts, and then, by aid of a grant of £6O, which they collected for the purpose, constructed an engine and carriage in one, which ran with a load of eight passengers upon the Queensferry roed. COTTAGE GARDENING.

BEETROOT may be taken up any time now, and with as little injury to the roots as possible; if they are much broken the colouring matter runs out into the water they are boiled in, so that they are of a pale colour instead of a rich dark red. Any of the roots that may have greenish or yellowish tops should be discarded. They are what are termed "rogues," and when cooked are very coarse and stringy. A good Beetroot should be tender and crisp when sliced for use. To preserve them over the winter, it is necessary that they should be cool and not too dry. They may be stored in the ground similar to potatoes, but on no account must they be allowed to get frozen. The merits of the Beetroot are not sufficiently known, or their culture would be more general. CELERY.—Advantage must be taken of any dry time to close this up, as it suffers from the frost. On heavy land earthing up celery is a troublesome business, on account of the difficulty to get the soil sufficiently fine to place round them. When wet it is so adhesive that there is no separating it, and when dry it is so hard that it requires some force to break it; but, if it is caught in a medium condition, there is a chance of overcoming the difficulties. A writer in The Times, some two or three weeks back, has evidently had a visit in his locality (Cheltenham) from our old acquaintance, the celery fly " Tephritis onopordinis," which he designates as a new disease. We have been troubled with it very much this season, and we hear that it is equally bad in other localities. POTATOES STORED IN PITS should be examined. Hear- ing complaints of some keeping badly, we opened one con- taining an early kind, and found a great number affected with the murrain, though all appeared perfectly sound when stored. When potatoes are pitted and decay occurs to any extent, the whole are enclosed in a contaminated at- mosphere, and consequently demand immediate attention. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Rose cuttings may be put in now. We select shoots from a foot to 18 inches long, which we take hold of and draw downwards so as to cause them to

slip off without having to use the knife. This secures to each what gardeners term a "heel." No further manipula- tion is required beyond removing the leaves from the part , that will go in the ground, and shortening at the other end so as to reduce it to about nine inches in length; the cutting I is then ready for insertion. 'Where the soil is stiff, some of 1 , a lighter nature may be added. The cuttings can scarcely 1 be put in too firmly, and to do that effectually we cut a I cavity eight inches deep, having a line to guide us. In the bottom we place two inches of sand. The cuttings are then arranged six inches distant, with their base in the sand, adding about two inches of sandy soil along the row so as to cover the cuttings that much. On this some of the ordi- nary soil is placed, and the whole trodden by a side action of the foot, which gives more pressure against the bank the cuttings are laid against than a downward tread. The remainder of the soil may then be added, and more ground dug for another row, about a foot wide, patting it down with the back of the spade. The line is then stretched and another trench cut eight inches from the other. By beating the soil moderately firm a good back is secured for the cut- tings to lean against, and it resists the pressure of the foot when they are trodden in. The ground should be main- tained at the same level as started with ; if it is otherwise the rows will be uneven, and the water will flow into the lowest spaces, and most probably destroy the cuttings. The majority of the shoots put in in this way will form root, and will flower next season. TIM GRASS PLOT should be mown quite close, or cut with shears, as the case may be, and afterwards have a good beating down with the back of the spade. This is best done by commencing at one corner and stepping backwards; if a few boughs are placed upon it, footmarks will not be quite so numerous as they are usually seen. If the surface is allowed to set after being beaten and before it has been walked upon, impressions will not be so easily made after- wards. We should prefer a bed of ashes to the so-called grass plot we see in the front of some dwellings. Some are really more like a mud plot. For the sake of cleanliness and the additional comfort that would follow, we would at once abolish it, and, as we have hinted, substitute ashes or gravel; but it will require some rougher material under- neath to a depth of 6in, to act as drainage. The above ar- rangement, with a border for flowers all round, would prove far more enjoyable. THE WlNDOW.—Geraniams of the zonal section should be carefully looked over, especially those packed closely in boxes, and if there are any decayed portions they should be removed by cutting close or even into a living part of the shoot. The surface of the cuts should be dressed with fresh slacked lime in a powdered state, which in all probability will prevent further decay in that portion. Should the whole of the plants appear damp, they may be dried if placed on the floor in front of a declining-kitchen fire after the inmates have retired to rest. A little forethought of this nature may save scores of plants. We recollect plants that had been grown in boxes for several years without any accommodation better than the kitchen floor in winter. In summer they were placed in front of the cottage, and in autumn were put in the kitchen, the door of which had a few squares of glass in the upper part. The plants were kept as near the door as possible, but in frosty weather were moved near the fire. The thermometer to indicate the tem- perature of the air surrounding them was a small vessel containing water attached to the side of one of the boxes, and so long as the water was not frozen the owner of the plants considered them safe. A simple test of the coldness of the atmosphere is demonstrated to us by Nature as the season comes round, yet few think of turning it to any prac- tical use in the, absence of a thermometer.

ALLEHED Clll-LD MURDER.—At the West Bromwich Police Court, on Satuidav, Emma Ford, aged 16, a domestic ser- vant, was charged. with causing the death of her child on October 8. The girl gave birth to the child in her bed-room at the house where he was employed. The body of a newly-born female child was found concealed in her 'ex. The doctor certified that the child was fully developed, and had been born alive, but had subsequently died from suffo- cation through being placed under some articles of clothing in the box. The prisoner was committed to the assizes on the charge of wilful murder. PROSPECTS OF JEWISH COLONISNTION IN PALESTINE.--I have arrived at the following results regarding the present condition of Jewish agriculture in this one province of Palestine alone, which may do something to dispel the popular impression that no Jews are engaged at present in that country in agricultural pursuits—that the local con- ditions are unfavourable to agricultural enterprise on account of its insecurity—and that, even if they were not, the Jews as a race would never be induced to apply them- selves to it. Of native Jews, not recent emigrants, there are at least forty families—there may be more—who live by agriculture. Besides these, there are about a hundred able-bodied men among the population of Sated who work as farm labourers for hire. And there are over ninety families of Russian and Roumanian refugees who have established themselves in colonies within the last year, and are actively engaged in tilling the soil,—making a total of about a thousand souls who are supporting themselves by their labours on the soil, and this in spite of the Most strenuous opposition on the part of the Turkish Govern- ment and its officials. This is exclusive of all the rest of Palestine. The danger is not so much from Bedouin Arabs—who, so far as I know, have never yet dis- turbed any of these Jewish agriculturists—as from the native authorities, and a want, not of perseverance or agricultural aptitude, but of discipline and harmony among the Jews themselves. The colony of Summarin especially is a notable instance of an unnecessary waste of funds, all of which have been subscribed by Jews themselves, owing to mismanegement on the part of the central organising committee, and a want of harmony on the part of the colo- nists. Upwards of 200,000 francs have already been spent on this colony, which has in it every element of success, and upon which the colonists have been working indefatigably ; but a far greater number of families have been sent out than the amount of land purchased could support, and the money has been spent so injudiciously that the colonists must undergo privations before they have sold their first crop, which might have been avoided; and indeed, unless some charitable persons will come forward to purchase more land for the surplus families—and a good tract may be bought in the neighbourhood—it is difficult to see how the means of subsistence are to be provided. The experience of the colony near Sated tells a very different tale, and bids fair to afford an illustration of the fact, that in spite of all the difficulties with which they have had to contend, the problem of Jewish colonisation is by means insoluble; and that it needs only a wise and skilful direction, a firm hand, end the necessary protection against injustice and the in- fraction of treaty rights by the Turkish Government, to ensure success.—Blackicood's Magazine. THE MORAL TENDENCY OF LITERARY AND ARTISTIC CULTURE.—It is perftctly true that men's views of what is desirable depend upon their characters, and that the innate proclivities to which we give that name are not touched by any amount of instruction. But it does not follow that even mere intellectual education may not, to an indefinite extent, modify the practical manifestation of the characters of men in their actions, by supplying them with motives unknown to the ignorant. A pleasure-loving character will have pleasure of some sort; but, if you give him the choice,. he may prefer pleasures which do not degrade him to those which do. And this choice is offered to every man who possesses in literary or artistic culture a never-failing source of pleasure, which are neither withered by age, nor staled by custom, nor embittered in the recollection by the pangs of self-reproach.—Professor Huxley on Science and Culture. _

THE LUTHER ANNIVERSARY. THE REV: THOMAS RIPPON AND THE VATICAN. The Rev. Thomas Rippon, preaching at Bewsey-road Chapel, Warrington, on Sunday, from the text, "And many shall rejoice at his birth" (Luke i. 14), said it was fitting Methodists should remember gratefully Luther and his work. Being Evangelical Christians, their Evangelism was the outcome of the Reformation. He would not denounce the church out of which Luther came, and which he sought to reform. He had no sympathy with those controversialists who tried to prove that the Pope was "The Man of Sin," and the Roman Church a "Synagogue of Satan." He would like to believe that there were many in the Church of Rome marching on to heaven. He urged his hearers not to be jealous in admitting this, and to be open and honest adversaries. He spoke first of Romanism as it was, 400 years ago, with reference to Martin Luther and his work. 'The Church of Rome stood in need of reform; and the Reformation was a "return to truth and reality in opposi- tion to falsehood and semblance." Luther's •task was to bring it back to reality. In considering the second part of his subject, viz., " Romanism as it is," he asked, was there need for e Luther to-day? Were there evils in the Church of Rome now, of a-like character to those that existed four centuries ago? lied the church changed, and, if so, for better or for worse ? He desired to state, as if in the pre- sence of his Roman Catholic friends, with candour and respect, why he was a Protestant. He protested against the Church of Rome on theological grounds. He could not hold with the confessional, Mariolatry, the assump- tion of infallibility, nor sacramentarianism. And he protested against the Papal system on political grounds. It arrogated for itself absolute despotism. Its desire for supreme civil control was dominant. As Mr. Gladstone in his "Vatican Decrees" made plain, the theory of Rome was that every human being in things spiritual and things temporal must acknowledge the supreme sovereignty of the Roman Pontiff. That from the month of July, 1870, and onwards (when the decree of infallibility was passed) the Pope claimed with plenary authority from every convert and member of his church that he should "place his loyalty and civil duty at the mercy of another," , that other being himself, the Pope. And acting upon this claim we had, therefore, a divided allegiance on the part of those who were the Pope's followers, as the words often ex- pressed implied, "A Catholic first, an Englishman after- wards," which meant that in any case of conflict between the Queen and the Pops, the Roman Catholic would follow the Pope and let the Queen shift for herself. And on secular grounds he was a Protestant, because the tendency of Rome was to obstruct the social, intellectual, and spiritual ad- vancement of the people. Whatever advance had been made in knowledge, in freedom and wealth, and in the arts of life, had been made in spite ef her. Whoever passed in Germany from a Roman Catholic to a Protestant principality, in Switz,rland from a Roman Catholic to a Protestant canton, in Ireland from a Roman Catholic to Protestant county, found that he had passed from a lower to a higher grade of civilisation. And that was the natural result of a system that tended to obstruct the advancing march of intellect and human progress. The preacher addressed himself to those within the pale of the Roman Church. He could not hope to lead them over to his Church, or to lisp his shibboleth. Then he would say: try and reform your Church. that it might be in the coming time, as in the old past it had been, a safe fold for the sheep of God. And next he addressed those outside the Roman Church. Those of the Anglican Church who imitated the Roman, and those of the so-called Evan- gelical and Dissenting Churches who denounced wholesale and without reserve the Roman Church as regards faith and practice. The Catholic Ritualist should be true to the Church as by law established. To take pay from Anglican coffers to do so well the Roman part was not honest. Be- sides the werslaip of the beautiful' was not the worship of holiness. eMithetic amusements were not for the house of God. His evangelical and protesting friends should not de- claim against the Church of Rome without good warrant. They should be thankful for the good it had accomplished. , They were to recognise the good it was doing, and to believe that in spite of errors God might continue to use it and I make it a bleeding and salvation unto very many.

- - The death is announced of the Rev. Sir Henry Moncrieff, D.D., principal clerk of the Scotch Free Church Assembly. The Liberals of Newry have selected Mr. Thomas Darcy Hoey, J.P., as the candidate to contest the borough at the next general election. During a gale on Sunday the barque Ennomia, from Troon to Demerara, was mrecked on the island of Mull, and four of the crew were drowned. It is stated that James Cole the Thornton Heath mur- derer, has been reprieved, the Official inquiry having shown him to be of unsound mind. During a quarrel between two Irishmen, named Casey and Butler, at Ryhope, Sunderland, the latter stabbed Casey in he abdomen, infl:cting a dangerous wound. The Duke and Duchess of Connaught, accompanied by their suite, left Brindisi for Bombay on Monday morning by the Peninsular and Oriental Company's steamer Cathay. At the ManchPster Assizes on Tuesday, Justice Hawkins sentenced William Haslam to 15 years' penal servitude for attempting to murder his wife, at Bury, on the 16:h Sep-

tember. The anniversary of the battle of Inkerman was observed in the customary manner on Monday, the colours of the various regiments of the British army which took part in the engagement being decorated with laurel. THE GREAT FRAUDS AT PRESTON. - There is reason to think the frauds will not exceed £lO,OOO. The sub-manager, Tally, was last seen at Manchester, but it is believed that he has got out of the country. Dr. Swabey, for many years one of the leading advocates in the probate and Divorce Court, died on Friday night at his residence, Langley, near Slough. The deceased gentle- man was Chancellor of the dioceses of Oxford and Ripon. The statue of the late Alexander Dumas in the Place Malesherbes, Paris, was unveiled on Saturday. Several speeches were delivered expressing admiration of the de- ceased and of his son, who was present at ther ceremony. The latest incident in the chequered history of St. Jude's Church, Liverpool, consists in the filing of a petition for liquidation on behalf of the Curate-in-Charge, the Rev. J. W. Wasdale Watson, whose liabilities are put down at

£B2l. During a quarrel at Pontypridd, bqween two occupants of a lodging-hose, a woman struck her adversary on the bead with a poker, fracturing his skull. The man retaliated by stabbing her in the hip. Both parties are in a critical condition abd have been apprehended. The Marquis and Marchioness of Lorne arrived in Liver- pool on Monday from Canada. They were receiveny the Duke of Albany, and an address of welcame was presented at the Town Hall, where they were entertained at luncheon by the Mayor, and sasequently ',eft for London. At Sheffield, on Tuesday, Robert Glover, plate-roller, was fined £5 for ill-treating his wife. The case was a most heartless one. He struck the woman in the face, locked her in a bed-room, stripped her naked, and drenched her with dirty water. Finally she was rescued by the neighbours. A determined suicide has been committed at Hull Police Station. A marine-store dealer named Henry Bellefelt, 37 years of age, was arrested on Saturday afternoon on a charge of receiving stolen property. Shortly after he had been placed in the cell he hanged himself to a bolt in the door-

.• trap. lan Saturday morning several children were playing in West-street, Leek, with a quantity of gunpowder. A train ivas laid and fired, and by some means the packet ignited sad caused an explosion. Several of the lads were -scorched, and one named Mellor had the sigbt of both eyes

lestroyen. -A toll house at Banner Cross, near Sheffield, which was occupied by the tollkeeper only in the day time, was on • Tuesday morning found to have been wrecked, apparently by an explosion of gunpowder. The incident is regarded .As a "practical joke" in connection with the Gunpowder - Plot celebrations of the previous night. ALLEGED WIFE blunpza.—At Bury, on Monday, Peter Hilton, landlord of the Foresters' Arms, Whitefield, near -Manchester, was remanded, charged with-causing the death of his wife. It was alleged that prisoner, while drunk on Saturday, quarrelled with the deceased and knocked her down, she dying next morning. PLOT TO BLOW ta. THE COURTS OF JUSTICE.—The klianclard states that, prior to the re-opening of the Law Courts, information was received at the Home Office that an attempt would le made on the day of opening to damage the 'Royal Courts of Justice. A carefel examination of the building was consequently made, and the approaches care-

fully guarded. Tun POOR OF BIRMINGHAM —ln view of the terrible poverty found to exist among the poorer children attending the Board schools, a movement has been started in Bir- mingham for providing them with a good soup or meat dinner two or three times a week during the winter months. With this object Mr. Richard Tangye has contributed -SlOO, and other smaller donations are announced. At Hull Police Court, on Monday, a labourer named Wm. Joyce was charged with assaulting William Seger, a crane- driver. On Saturday night the two men, who were in a public-house, quarrelled, and went into the street to fight. Joyce struck Seger a blow in the face which felled him. _Seger was taken home, and seine hours after he was found dead on a couch. Prisoner was remanded. SALE OF MARWOOD'S EFFECTS.—The sale of Marwood's effects was concluded at Horncastle on Tuesday in the pre- sence of a large number of people. Amongst the lots were two old saucers, which fetched 10s 6d; a purse;29B; pair of 'spectacles, 15s; a Gladstene bag, £8; Marwoed's favour- ite rope, £4 10s; a dirty old carpet bag, 21s; a pair of old stockings, ss; and a dirty old necktie and cuffs, lie. ATTE2,II.I, TO WRECK i PASSENGER, TRAIN.—A passenger . train, due at Maidstone at 8-30 on Sunday night, on enter- ing the cutting at Little Brick-lane, about half a mile from the end of its journey, encountered two wooden sleepers which bad been maliciously placed on the rails. Fortuna- tely, the wheels of the engine cut through the obstruction, and although a violent shock was experienced none of the passengers were hurt. Exaectrricee.—flenry Powell. 24 years of age, bricklayer, . was executed at Wandsworth Gaol shortly before nine o'clock on Tuesday morning for the murder of John Dimery Bruton, son of his master, a builder at Balham. The culprit never attempted to palliate his offence, and, though listen- ing to the clergyman, remained an atheist to the end. He walked firmly to the scaffold, where Binna, the new execu- tioner; quickly completed the arrangements. Death appeared almost instantaneous. "Guy FAWKES " ACCIDENTS.—At Accrington, on Mon- day, Edmond Lord, aged 19, a glazier, fired a revolver, and, to the horror of the bystanders, a youth named Joseph Whittakerason of a weaver, fell shot in the cheat. He was removed home VI a precarious state. Lard was taken into custody.—A young man, living near Atherstone had his band blown away while engaged in the celebration. At Eastbourne the Fifth of November carnival was carried out . on a most elaborate scale. The town was brilliantly illumi- nated, and monster processions, with bands and banners, paraded the streets, which were crowded with spectators. Several effigies were burnt. THE CASE OF THE RUNAWAY LIVERPOOL PRIEST.—The Tablet has the following concerning the Rev. John Banks, late of the Church of our Lady of Reconciliation, Eldon- street, Liverpool.—" The sad clerical scandal which took place a few weeks ago, and was reported in many of the papers, has happily ended with a complete submission and repentance of the unhappy priest. Having.placel himself . entirely in the hands of his bishop, the ease was not Dressed for trial at the assizes, but was withdrawn on a technical point of law. A life of penance and retirement from the world is the atonement which is now voluntarily sought by one who is deeply penitent." THE OUTRAGES IN LONDON.—On Saturdev the inquiry commenced by the Home Office relative to the explosions on Tuesday night on the Metropolitan and Metropolitan Dis- trict Railways was continued by Colonel Majendie Captain Caudill, and Dr. Dupre, the Government analytical chemist. So far as was ascertained, nothing was discovered which would lead to any other conclusion than that previously arrived at, viz., that the destruc•ion was caused by dyna- mite, nitro-glycerine, or some subataneeof a nitro-compound and explosive nature. It was reported late on Saturday evening that the result of several inspections of the scene of the explosion at rraed•street station and examinations of the debris was the discovery of a fuse which, it is believed, was connected with the compound used in the perpetration , of the outrage. EXTRAORDINARY SHOOTING AFFAIR. A mysterious shooting affair has occurred at Castleton, Rochdale. Three young men, respectably dressed, walked up a lane, and one of the three, named Alfred Roberts, of Digby-terrace, Lon- don, painter, was shot in the face with a pistol. The names .of the other men are George Jackson, of York, tailor, and •'George Hall, of London, clerk. The pistol was charged with powder and small pellets, and Jackson was holding the weapon when it accidentally went off. Jackson was • terribly frightened by the occurrence; he made off, and has rot since been seen. Roberts was conveyed-to the Roch- dale Infirmary, and his friends have since been communi- cated with. His eye was shot, but no clear account has been given to show how the affair occurred,nor how the two young men fell in with Jaekeon. Ass result of communi- cations with the Metropolitan police, information was re- ceived in Rocladale that Hall was " wanted " on a serious charge. He was arrested, and on Monday a London detec- tive received him in charge. GREAT FIRES IN Lognox.—A great fire broke out in a timber yard at Haggerstone, on Saturday, and continued burning several days despite the efforts of Captain Shaw and a full staff of firemen. It is estimated that the damage p will amount to about £20,000. On Monday during the day nothing but immense voAtetnes of smoke could be seen, but after dark a lurid reflection was cait Over a large portion of East London, inducing many thousand people to throng to the scene. The traffic in the canal was partially suspended, in consequence of the constant falling of immense quanti- ties of burning wood, and the sappy of coal te! otee bowing gasworks had to be conveyed by another ronte.—A serious fire broke out on Monday' evening, on the premises of Messrs. Pewtreas and Company, general packers, London,' which comprise the greater part of the block a buildings between Lawrence POUlltlleV.hiGe and Lawrence Pountney Hill, having the main entrance in Canon-street. The basement of the part of the buildings facing Cannon-street is occupied by the Telegraph Works Company (Limited), who bare a large amount of india- rubber material in stock: but the fire brieade succeeded in preventing the fire from reaching the company's portion of the buildings, although it was much demeged by smoke and water. The premises of Messrs. Pewtrese, which are very extensive, were coinpietey gutted, and the damage is estimated at many thousands a pound', but they are be- tieved to be insured. • • 20' The Diamond Dyes for auntie uze havc no equals. POLITICAL The committee charged with the selection of a Liberal can- didate for the vacancy that will arise at the close of the pre- sent Parliament by the retirement of Mr. Morley, M.P., from the representation of Bristol, have resolved to recom- mend to the Liberal Association Mr. William Henry Wells, the present member for Coventry. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE ABOLITION OF SLAVERY.—A member of the Liberal party in Bournemouth having written to the Premier calling attention to a recent speech by a Couservative lecturer, Mr. Gladstone's secretary has replied saying:—" Mr. Gladstone observes .the lecturer states that the Tory party abolished slavery, which is grossly untrue, and that Mr. Gladstone apposed abolition of slavery, which is also absolutely untrue. The lecturer may find in the debate pn the bill a reference to Mr. Gladstone by the present Lord Derby, which he ought to have quoted if he chose to touch the subject." THE PROGRAMME OF NEXT SESSION. The following appears in the Pall Mall Gazette :—"We have reason to believe that although the Government cannot be said to have arrived at any definite decision as to the programme of next session, yet it is probable that it will introduce at the beginning of the session a measure of electoral reform, which will apply to all parts of Great Britain and Ireland, making household suffrage the uniform rule both in town and country. If so, this will entail a reduction of the Irish borough franchise, which at present is a DI rating franchise, but which in future will be the same as in England. This Household Suffrage Bill will have precedence of all other measures. Although temporarily disconnected from the Franchise Bill the question of redistribution of seats will probably be declared by the Government to be an integral part of the scheme of electoral reform which must be dealt with before an appeal is made to the country. The details of the scheme of redistribution are as yet unsettled, but it ' may be taken for granted that it will not embody the prin- ciple of minority representation, and that it will go on the same lines as those which have preceded it. An attempt will probably be made to make the settlement on .a self-re- adjusting basis after each census, so as to dispense with thh necessity for any further reform bills, but neither on that point, nor on any of the others on which definite statements have been sat forth, have Ministers arrived at any final de- cision."

On Wednesday morning, a serious fire broke out in the town of Oakengates, near Wellington, by which a public house and two other houses were completely destroyed. SHOCKING ACCIDENT.—A labourer named Bache, his wife, and three children were seriously burnt at their home, at Toll End, Tipton, on Tuesday night, by the overturning of some boiling tar. A Swaff ham correspondent says that, while but shooVng on Wednesday afternoon at Beecham Well, Lord De Clifford was severely wounded in the head, owing to one of the barrels of his gun bursting. The London correspondent of the Dublin Express of Thursday says :—lt is stated that influences are at work which will result in the sendiag of Lord Lorne as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. A'PRESTON MURDER CASE.—At the Manchester Assizes, on Thursday, Thomas Riley, 55, mason, was charged with the murder of a women named Elizabeth Alston, at Preston, on 27th September. He was sentenced to death. The Gown Prince of Portugal arrived in London on We 6 nesday. His Highness will occupy the Royal apartments at Claridge's Hotel until the Queen returns from Balmoral, when he will become the guest of Her Majesty at Windsor. FIFTEF.N VESSELS ASHORE.—A Ramsgate correspondent says the placing of a new light on the Long Sand has been attended by unfortunate results, no fewer than 15 vessels of various rigs having in consquence gone ashore on: the Knock. Joseph Wharton, constable in the Manchester police force, who waa found guilty at Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, of the manslaughter of Edmund Parkinson, on September 16, was, on Wednesday, sentenced to four months' impri- sonment. The revenue returns from the Ist April to 3rd November show—Receipts, £47,157,079; expenditure, £49,t'20,760; balances, £3,378,913. Corresponding period last year— Receipts, £46,416,739 ; expenditure, £52,007,731; balances, £1,699,945. On Tuesday evening, shortly after the arrival of the mail boat at Jersey, an elderly man named Venner. who had just arrived, walked into the eating-house belonging to Mr. Wright, drew a revolver, and shot him, the bullet entering Wright's lung. . A FEMALE BURGLAR —At Greenwich on Tuesday, Han- nah Dowell, 17, was sentenced to six we:lte' har 1 labour and four years in a reformatory for burglary. Upon hearing the sentence the prisoner screamed and clung to the dock and had to be carried from court. , At Devon and Cornwall Assizes, at Exeter, Abraham Boswell, travelling tinker, charged with the murder of Thomas Hugh Down, also an itinerent tinker, at Cubert, Cornwall, on the 2nd of October, was found guilty of man- slaughter, and sentenced to 20 yearg' penal servitude. , A WOULD BE LIA.NGMAN.—At a meeting of the Finance Committee of the Durham Town Council, an extreordinary letter was read from a person residing in Micklegate, York. who applied for the office of executioner of the condemned man in Durham Gaol. He said he would do it for £7 10s. A large block of buildings in Buchanan-street, Glasgow, occupied by a firm of upholsterers, took fire on Saturday evening, and were totally destroyed. The flames also ex- tended to adjoining buildings, and the premises of the Glas- gow Herald were with difficulty saved. A rough estimate of the damage places the amount at £300,000. 1 At the Manchester Assizes, Septimus Lockwood Lamb, a , telegraph clerk, and Heury Hulme, a compositor, were sen- tenced to twelve months' imprisonment, and John E. Gart- aide, also a-telegraph clerk, to six months' imprisonment, for conspiringto iutefcept arid disclose certain telegraph mes- sagesconveying the results of certain horseeaces. At the Yorkshire Assizes, on Thursday, George Pinder, described as respectable and well-to-do, was convicted of having set fire to some materials in a Hull warehouse on twe occasions in September. The prisoner appears to have made a number of attempts to burn down the warehouse, but his motive was not at all clear. He was sentenced to five years' penal servitude. SHOCKING FATALITY.—An inquest was held at Black- burn, on Tuesday morning, touching the death of Robert 'Parkinson, labourer, 19 years of age. He was engaged in pointing some chimney stacks in Elizabeth-street, Higher Andley, when he rolled off the roof and fell into the beck- yard of one of the houses. His skull was fractured, and he was killed on the spot. A verdict of accidental death was returned. SCOTCH Pro IRoN.—Since the breaking up of the agree- ment with the English iron masters the Scotch iron masters have acted independently of one another. They have all been obliged to grant the miners an advance of sixpence per day. Although this advance increases the cost of pro- duction of pig iron still the iron market has not been affected, the price now touched being the lowest for three years. . A letter carrier was on Wednesday indicted at the Not- tingham Assizes, and pleaded guilty to stealing two regis- tered letters containing sums of money in coin. It was re- marked by Mr. Justice Stephen that the usual punishment in these cases was penal servitude, but in view of the pri- soner's youth. previous good character, and the strong temptation offered by the insertion of coin in letters, he woul& only pass a sentence of twelve months' imprison- ment. On Thursday Sir Moses Montefiore entered upon his hundredth year, and at Ramsgate, where the venerable Baronet has a marine residence, the day was observed as a general holiday. Early in the morning Sir Moses received a telegram from the Queen congratulating him sincerely on his entering upon the hundredth year of a useful and hon- ourable life. Congratulations were also received from the Duke of Edinburgh. Addresses were presented, the town was gaily decorated, triumphal arches were erected in the main thoroughfares, business was entirely suspended, there was a procession nearly two miles long, and in the evening there was an illumination of the town. The woman Scott, who is charged with murdering her infant child whilst on a journey from Southport to Staly- bridge, was again before the Stalybridge justices on Wednes- day. The prisoner was tried at Chester Assizes, but as Lord Justice Baggallay was of opinion that the Court had no ' - - elin jurisdiction, the place of death not being fixed in Cheshire, , ALARMING ACCIDENT AT A DURHAM the jury was discharged, and Scott taken before magistrates having jurisdiction in Lancashire. _DISTRICT NEWS. ASHTON. ASHTON RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.—The members of this association held a meeting last evening (I.lu:sday ), at the Robin Hood Hotel, Ashton. There was a fair attend- ance, and Mr. J. Miteaell (president of the association) occupied the chair. The matters which came up for discus- sion related to the cemetery question and the forthcoming electioa of members of the Local Board. UNLAWFULLY REMOVING SWlNE.—William Mather was surnmaned at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, for causing three pigs to be removed from the borough of St. Helens into the township of Ashton, contrary to the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, and Wm. John- son was summoned for removing the same.—P.C. Ratcliff proved seeing Johnson driving the pigs from St. Helens to Ashton, on the 25th ultirno.—Mather W4S fined 5s and costs, and Johnson was ordered to pay the costs. THE LUTHER COMMEMORATION: LECTURE AT ASIITOI.T. —The 400th anniversary of the Luther's birth will be com- memorated at Ashton on Monday evening next by a lecturer in the Cave-Browne Protestant Institute, Heath- lane. The title is " Was Luther the first Protestant ? " and the subject will be treated by the popular and esteemed Rev. W. Preston, MA, vicar of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn. Fuller particulars will be found in our announce- ment columns. We hope there will be a crowded atten- dance. SPECIAL SEltOiOiS ON LUTHER.—The present year being the 400th anniversary of the birth of Luther, the great Reformer, the Rev. H. Wilson, of the Ashton Congregational Church, commenced a course of sermons on Luther and his work on Sunday morning last. The second sermon on the same subject was given in the evening of the same day, and we understand that the third and fourth will be given on Sunday next. Last Sunday there were large congregations. and the greatest interest was taken in the remarks of the rev. gentleman. THE ASHTON CHURCH ASSOCIATION BRASS AND REED BAND.—The rirst practice of the members of the newly- formed brass and reed hand in connection with the Cave- Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, was held on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. Singleton, bandmaster of the North Ashton Brass Band, has been appointed master of the new band, and we may add he is a gentleman well quali- fied for the post. The committee have acted wisely in thus honouring a local musician, whose abilities are well known. There are 20 members at present, and the practice nights for the future will be Wednesday and Saturday in each week.

A Lima dcspalch of Monday's date states that the Peru- vian garrison of Arequipa murdered two of the aides-de• camp of Admiral Mentero, because that offic,..r had refused to continue the defence against the Cbi ' The New York correspondent of the Standard says there is a general agreement among the critics that Mr. Irving's Louis Xf. is the best part lie has presented. Although some previous audiences were larger, none has been more enthusiastic. Sons disorder has beal caused in certain districts of Servia by the gendarmes attempting to enforce orders issued by the prefects that all arms in the hands of civilians should be given lip to the authorities. General Nikelic, former Minister of War, has proceeded to the disaffected districts with a battalion of troops to put down the rising. SUPPOSED NIHILIST INCENDIAILISM.—A telezram received from Warsaw stales that a lire has occurred at the Marie Institute iu that city, by which the building has been com- pletely gutted. The fire is believed to be due to incendiar- ism committed with the object of preventing the discovery of some Nihilist documents which were coacealed on the premises, THE OCCUPATION OF EGYPP.—It is understood that arrangements are being made by the Government for shortly reducing the force in Egypt to, it is believed, about 3,000 men. The Admiralty have advertised for transports to bring away the mounted troops, and her Majesty's troopships will carry the infantry battalions to be moved to En,;laud and the Midlterranr an. .

TERRIBLE FIRE IN A COTTON FACTORY.—An followed by a fire, occurred in a cotton factory at Roubaix, near Lisle, on Tuesday morning. Most of the operatives, who were almost all women, eEcaped with trifling injuries; but eleven were killed in throwing themselves from the windows, and six, whose eselpe was from the first cut off, were literally roasted alive. THE FRENCH IN MADAGASCAR.-1 semi-official contra- diction is given in Paris to the intelligence Published by a L-mdon morning paper that the French authorities, profiting by the discontent prevailing in the licint camp, had de- manded a large war indemnity in addition to their previous conditions. It is declared that no modification has been made ir}, the French ultimatum already presented to the 1 nova Government. _

KING VICTOR EMMANUEL.—The Capitan Fracasset says: I We have good authority for stating that a Papal Ball has been prepared for placing the Pantheon under an interdict, and that it will be promulgated should the projected monu- ment to the late King Victor Emmanuel be placed. in the centre of the church, or should Protestant or evengelicil associations enter the edifice to attend the commemorative funeral ceremony. DYNAMITE OUTRAGE IN LYONE.—The revival of the dynamite policy in England has been followed soon by the renewed activity of the anarchists at Lyons, who favour the employment of similar means for carrying out their objects. Early on Monday morning an iafernal machine, which had been placed in front of the mansion of a wealthy Lyons merchant, was exploded, and caused immense damage to the building, bat fortunately no one was wounded. The acceptmce of the resignation by King Alfonso of the Duc de Fernan None; as Spanish Ambassador to France, is officially announced. It is understood that Marshal Ser- rano will be his successor. In receiving the newly-appointed provincial governors on Tuesday the Spanish Minister of the Interior urged them to do their utmost to put an end to the petty tyranny of the landed proprietors, and also to spare no efforts in their respective provinces to support the policy which the CY overnment intended to pursue of con- cord and conciliation between all the sections of the Liberal

• _ ODDFELLOWS' MEETING AT ASHTON. - Tile monthly meeting of the members of the Loyal Triumphant lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, 1%1.1J., was held at the G-erard's Arms, Ashton, on Saturday evening last. There was a very good attendance, and Prov. C: S. John Hodgkinson presided as N. G. Discussions took place re- lative to lodge business, and three new members were initiated, one candidate being proposed. Nominations for the various offices for the ensuing year were then received; the offices that will be contested being those of trustee to the lodge, lodge surgeon, and secretary. One of the new mem- bers, Brother Alker, gave a sang in a capital manner, after which the lodge closed in the usual form.

A despatch brought by mail from Capetown reports that on the 3rd ultiino Usibepu made a night march and fell on the Abayulusini adherents of the king, belongisg to the Usutu party. Before dawn he completely routed then, killing half of the mete of the irapi. Usibepu was said to be holding sanguinary carnival in Cetewayo's territory, killing all the king's people that fall into his hands. Inter-tribal fighting is reported from Pon- doland. The Begarnanas and 51avutes have been engaged in strife several days past, ri suiting in coins ef their num- ber being killed and many wounded. Siyoyo and Vallello were also preparing for war.

PLOT TO ASSASSINATE PRINCE BISMARCK —lntelligeßCe from Derschau states that a person named Piotrowski has been arrested at that place, charged on his own confesiion, with having bet!' despatched by the Nihilists to •carry out an attempt upon the life of Prince Bismarck. At the judicial examination tiotrowski said he was a Russian actor. He had been provided by the Nihilists with means for his journey, and he had travelled by way of Riga to Dantsic. At the latter place his Blaney had been s!olen tram him. An instrument for injecting morphia and a Nihilist poem were found on the prisoner when he was arrested. Several of the papers, referring to the arrest, regard the prisoner either as an impostor or lunatic. THE EGYPTIAN GOVERNMENT AND THE SUEZ CANAL There is no foundation for the statement published by a London weekly paper that MM. Keller and Cavalli, acting as legal advisers of the Egyptian Government, bad been requested to reconsider the question of how far the various conventions between the Government and M. de Lesseps conferred upon the latter any kind of monopoly, and that these gentlemen bad repotted that no such monopoly ex- isted. MM. Keller and Cavalli have not been asked to sub- mit a report upon any question concerning the Suez Canal. M. Cavalli, moreover, has not entered upon his duties as legal adviser. The construction of a second Suez Canal is not regarded as an urgent question by the Egyptian Govern- ment.

THREATENING THE LIFE OF THE MARQUIS or LANDS* DOWNE.—The Toronto Globe publishes the fallowing des- patch from Ottawa :—Since taking up his residence at Rid- eau Hall. the Marquis of Lansdowne has received a number of anonymous letters threatening his life. The matter is now being investigated, although h;s Excellency feels no alarm on the subject. The letters are believed to have been sent by some mischievous person from a desire to annoy him, or possibly by individuals anxious to obtain employ- ment as.extta detectives. It will be remembered that the Marquis of Lorne received a number of threatening letters last winter, and it can scarcely be thought tbat the scoun- drels who would contemplate injuring the Governor-General would take the precaution te warn him beforehand.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

The rioting in Londonderry has abated. Several persons charged with stone-throwing were fined on Monday. The strike of factory girls continues. A report from the Galway county states that at a place called Woodlawn, near Athenry, a bailiff on the property of Castleblakeney was shot dead in his own house. THE PRISONER OTONNELL.—Owing to last week's Fenian outrages in Lond,n, the authorities have since taken extraordinary precautions to ensure the safe custody of the prisoner O'Donnell, who will shortly be tried for shooting the informer Carey A SEOCKING STABBING CASE.—A young man named John , Lydon was charged at the Galway Petty Sessions, on Mon- days with having, on Saturday night, stabbed Patrick Con- nor. The men quarrelled in a lodging-house, and during the dispute the prisoner thrust a shoemaker's knife into Ce.nnor's chest, over the heart. The prisoner was committed fer trial. Peter Wade, labourer,. was charged bsfore the Rathfarn- 'ham magistrates on Saturday with the murder of Patrick 'Quinn, of Beech Park. The principal witness was Mrs. Mary Quinn, widow of the murdered man, who deposed that she heard cries on the evening named, and ran out of her house. She found her husband lying in the avenue. The prisoner had been at the deceased's house the same evening. The prisoner was remanded. Senor Castelar, who aspires to be regarded as a statesman, has published 'chat amounts to a defence ef the assassina- tion of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke. He asserts that "all the might of England failed to protect Carey from the execution of the verdict of the Irish nation." It has escaped his observation that the man who shot Carey is extremely anxious to disclaim having received any " mandate" of the kind; and that perhaps is the only comment which it is worth while to make on Senor Castelar's effusion. ; THE CHIEF SECRETARY AND THE ULSTER LIBERALS.— The secretary of the Ulster Liberal Society has received the following letter from Mr. Trevelyan :—" I have received with great interest the series of resolutions passed by the Ulster Liberal Society. Pray convey to Lord Waveney and the members of the society my warm appreciation of their expressions of confidence in the Government, and the re- spect and interest which I feel for their recommenda- tions of the policy which should be pursued with regard to Ireland." A Facetote Fleire.—A Limerick correspondent telegraphs that a very seriousriot occurred at Rathkeale Fair on Tuesday between two factions from the neighbourhood of Askeaton, in the course of which forty persons were seriously wounded. The town was in the hands of the rioters for several hours, during which business was suspended. A small body of police, who on the scene, were kept at bay by the rioters until the arrival of reinforcements, when the streets were cleared and a large number of persons art ested. Some of the prisoners were rescued from custody, but the police retained 23. THE PREMED AND nix ULSTER LIBERALS. Dr. Wylie the secretary of the Ulster Liberal Society has re- ceiyed the following communication from the Prime Minister :—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, November 3. Sir,—l acknowledge the receipt of the resolutions enclosed in your letter of the Ist instant. upon grounds much higher than the support of any Ministry or party, I bail the expression of views which combine attachment to the em- pire with the principal of equal rights for the three king- doms and loyalty to the Throne, with a stout obedience to law and order on the part of those who praclaim it as their watchword.—' have the honour to be your faithful servant, ; V. E. GLADSTONE."

div.head: CONNOLLY'S TICKETS AND THEIR
div.p: CONNOLLY'S TICKETS AND THEIR
VENDORS. MAGISTERIAL STRICTURES.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, before Mr. W. W. Pilkington and Alderman Cook, James Gornall, grocer, College-street; Sarah Banks, publican; J. Wilkinson, tobac- conist, Baldwin-street; and W. Pemberton, tobacconist, Shaw- street; were each charged with unlawfully and knowingly suffering to be kept open in their houses a certain lottery called the " Cesarewitch Stakes," not authorised by Parlia- ment, in which said lottery prizes of money were awarded to certain subscribers thereto, by or fer whom certain prizes should be drawn contrary to the statute in such cases made seed provided. Mr. H. L. Riley prosecuted on behalf of the county authorities; and the defendants were represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, with the exception of Mrs. Banks, for whom Mr. Peck, of Wigan, appeared. The evidence in these cases was identical with that given a fortnight previously in a similar case heard in the same court, namely, that on the oth October, two police officers, P.C's Caunce and Brooks, went disguised as plasterer's labourers to the shops of the defendant's and bought what are known as Connolly's tickets, for which if they possessed a winning number they were to receive prizes of money. On the Tuesday following they again went to the same shops and were supplied with lists which showed the winning numbers.—ln mitigation of the charge it was pointed out that the business of selling these tickets had been carried on open.y in the town fer years,flo that the polite must have been cognisant of it., yet these proceedings had been taken without any previous warning as to the illegaiity of the business such as had been given in other towns.—Mr. Pilkington said the Bench had decided to convict in each case, but they took into consideration the fact that there had not been very much warning. But at the same titne they had no doubt whatever that everyone selling those tickets knew and had known all along that it was illegal, and beyond that it was one of the most mis- chievous things going on in the town. It was taking the earnings of a number of workingmen, and especially younger people, and be had known of cases in which nearly the whole of the wages had been taken to buy these things. It had caused a great deal of misery and a great deal of poverty. If there bad been more warning given than there had been they (the Bench) would have been inclined to put on the full penalty. In these cases, however, they would only put on a fine of XS and costs each.

The Dean of Manchester, the Very Rev. Dr. Cowie, has been appointed to the Deanery of Exeter. The house and shop of a draper at Batley Carr were destroyed by fire early on Tuesday morning, in conse- quence, it is stated, of a firework having been thrown into the shop. M. DE LESSEES' VISIT TO ENGLAND.—The Paris corres- pondent of the Central News telegraphs :—I have just had a conversation with M. de Lesseps. He assured me that he had no deplomatic object in going to England, nor had be been charged with any mission. While there he should visit Liverpool, Manchester, and other large places, and he hoped to convince English shipowners that their grievances were mostly imaginary. It had not yetbeen decided whether ' a second canal should be constructed or the present one enlarged. A very pretty little military job, intended for the benefit of H.R.U. the Duke ef Connaught, has been nipped in the bud in rather an amusing way. When it was at first an- nounced, people wondered why a Royal Prince should have been sent to command at Meerut—qa fever-stricken spot, so often stigmatised as the white man's grave. But it was never intended that the Duke should stay at Meerut. Within four months from the present date the post of Commander- in-Chief in Bombay will fall vacant by the retirement of Sir Arthur Hardinge. It was all arranged that the Duke of Connaught, as next in seniority on the spot, should succeed to the command. Just at the eleventh hour, however, an unfortunate discovery was made. This was the existence of a certain Major-General Phayre, also on the spot, and commauding a division at Mhow. General Phayre is a long way senior to the Duke of Connaught, and by no possible means could he be passed ove..-. When the Bombay com- mand falls vacant, therefore, it must go to Phayre, if it is to be given locally; if not, someone must be sent out from England. In no case, however, could the Duke of Con- naught succeed; and thus this very clever scheme is alto- gether dinhed.

div.p: CADISEEAD.
The body of a man, supposed to be a navvy, has been dragged out of the river at Cadisbead.
