div.p: PROD SHAM.

FREEMASONEY.—The Ctrolmondeley Lodge, No. 1908, which was started two years ago, has fully justified the reasons given for its consecration, as it now ajoys a pros- perous existence, and holds a position with regard to mem- bership quite equal to any in the province of Chester, so ad- mirable governed by Bro. Lord de Tabley, P.G.M. All con- nected with the lodge are earnest masons, and there is little doubt its future career will sill further evidence the true spirit of Freema.sonry. The annual installation in connec- tion with the " Claolmondeley " took place on Tuesday afternoon at the Commercial Hotel, Frodsham, where the lodge was opened by Bro. G. H. Danby, the retiring W.M., who was supported by Bros. J. K. Digges, P.P.G.A D.C.; J. J. Yapp‘ S.W.; H. E. Heywood, J.W. ; J. J. Radford, secretary; John Ashton, S.D. ; T. Hitcher', J.D. ; C. H. Lewin, J.G.; J. Roberts, tyler; Bros. J. Humphreys, J. R. Tomlinson, P.M. 368 ; J. Salmon, P.P.G.S.D. ; W. Garnett, i and J. Brandreth, The visitors present included Bros. F. Thomas, P.M., 721; 'F. Knowles, S.W., 721; H. Ellis, W.M., 721 ; J. Lockwood, 758 ; A. Parker, 425.; R. Edwards, 753 ; J. B. Mackenzie, P.M., treasurer, 1,609; J. C. Robinson, P.M., 249; C. W. Dun- can, W.M., 425; and S. NV. Ramsden, S.W., 425. After the transaction of some preliminary business, Bro. John Yapp was presented for installation, and the first portion of the ceremony was performed by the retiring master. Bro. G. H. Danby. The chair was subsequently taken by Bro. J. Sal- mon, who, in an effective manner, concluded the duties of installing master. The following orethren were eubsequently invested :—Bros. G. H. Danby, I.P.M. and treasurer; H. E. Heywood, S.W.; J. J. Radford, J. W.; J. Ashton, secretary; T. H. Hitchen, S.D.; C. H. Lewin, J.D. ; J. Humphreys, organist; J. Acton,l.G. ; and J. Roberts, tyler. After busi- ness the brethren adjourned to the restaurant of Miss Bibby, Frodsham, where an excellent banquet was served by Messrs. Biker and Sons, of Chester. Bro. J. Yapp, the wor- shipful master, gave the usual loyal and Masonic toasts in brief and pointed terms, and during the evening a highly en- joyable musical programme was given by Bros. Humphreys, Knowles, Ormer, and Robinson.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLBORNE CII,JRCR Cnota FUND.—A special sermon in aid of the cbeir fnnl was preached in the Golborne Parish Church, on Sunday evening last, by the Rev. J. Carson, curate of Winwick. There was a good atte.dancei and the sum of £3 es. 7d. was collected MAGIC LANTERN EirrEarsirwurcr.—A magic lantern entertainment of a pleasing character was given in Mr. Brewis's school-room, Golborne, on Wednesday evening. The views represented scenery in London, Paris, Rome. and other places on the Continent, China, and other coun- tries. At the close a number of comic slides were shown ( n the canvas; the juveniles manifesting great interest in

them. FORMATION OF A CHURCH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—The movement for the establishment of a local branch of the Church of England Temperance Society has been brought to a successful issue; and the first business meeting of the new organisation was held in the church school on Monday evening last. There was a very good attendance; and in the absence of the Rector (the Rev. C. T. Quirk) through indisposition, the chair was occupied by the Rev. W. Thorpe, curate. An address on the principles and working of the society was given by the Rev. J. Hurst, of Liverpool, organising secretary of the Church of England Temperance Society for the diocese of Liverpool, after the enrolment of members took place. Fifty persons gave in their names, 48 of whom pledged themselves as total abstainers, and eight as "temperate" members. Mr. T. Gregory was sub- sequently elected secretary, and Mr. A. Caunce treasurer. It is intended that a meeting of the Golborne branch shall be held each month, and we wish the new society a success- ful career. _

------- HALTON. HALTON PAROCHIAL CLOTHING SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of this society, which was instituted by Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., in May, 1634, was held on Friday. Lady Brooke, as treasurer, announced that the number enrolled on the books for the past year W. 19 163; whilst the weekly subscriptions, together with the bonuses, amounted to £l7B 18s. 2d. The bundles of clothing. were distributed. HALTON 'WESLEY/1N BAND OF HOPE.—The second meet- ing of this society wis held on Thursday evening, Nov. Ist. in the Wesleyan schoolroom. Mr. A. White (of Helsby), occupied the chair, and opened the proceedings with a very interesting and amusing address. Suitable readings, recita- tions &c., were given 437 the members in a very satisfactory manner, which were heartily appreciated by a large and at- tentive audience. At the close, 21 pledges were taken, making the total number of members 100. HAYDOCK.

THE HARVEST FESTIVAL SERVICES AT ST. JAMES'S CHURCH, HAYDOCE.—The special harvest thanksgiving ser- vices were continued in St. James's Church, Haydock, on Sunday last, when sermons were preached by the Rev. H. Sherlock, vicar, the Rev. F. Firman, vicar of St. James the Less, Liverpool, and the Rev. W. F. Lovell, Houghton Regis. There were large congregations, and the offertories realised the sum of LW. TH.E HAYDOCK COLLIERY SCHOOL. A goodly number of persons assembled in this school on Monday evening last, when a pleasing magic lantern entertainment was given. The first part censisted of the exhibition of about 50 celoured views illustrating Livingstone's and Stanley's travels; the second part, views of "A trip to the Mediter- ranean;" and the third part was headed "Picture gallery of local -luminaries—a series of well-known happy Hay- dockers, prepared specialty for the occasion." The various slides were clearly shown on the canvas and the entertain- ment was greatly appreciated. Mr. John White sang one or two selections in a capital style, Mr. Charles Forshaw played on his cornet, and Mr. A L. Evans presided at the pianoforte and hartnonium. FRAUDULENTLY REMOVING GOODS AT BILLINGE.—Peter Gasket' was summoned for fraudulently removing goods from a house at Biilinge Higher End, of which he was tenant, with flee intention of evading payment of rent.— Mary Ann Rigby said that she was daughter of John Rigby, and owner of the house which defendant had occupied at Billinge Higher End at a rental of is. 3d. a week. On the 24th ult. he left the house, and was then owing Ds. in rent. On the 24th Octooer witness went to the place and defend- ant paid her is. 61. towards the arrears he was owing. Going again at a later date she found that defendant hat 4 gone away without giving notice and had taken the furni- ture with him, which was worth 58.—The bench made an I order for double the value of the furniture. IMYTON. A VIGOROUS MOTHER-IN-LAW.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Martha Anders, of Huyton, was charged wiqi hying assaulted Mary Ann Critchley.—lt seemed that the defendant was the mother-in-law of the complainant, and they all lived together in the same house. On the 31st ult. a quarrel arose between them, and the de- fendant put her d tughter-in-law oat of the house, and ac- cording to the latter struck her on the head.—The deftn- dant, however, denkd having struck the complainantewho, she said, called her an "old witch."—The Bench considered it was a family quarrel, which ought never to have come before them. They would therefore dismiss it. HUY TON QUARRY. The Huyton Quarry branch of the Church of Et:elan:l Temperance Sojety, cn Merida,- 1141 their forenigOtly meeting, the Rev. W. 'T. Southward, MA., presided, and with Mears. Wilkinson and **itidiehurst, contriWted readings ;
Mr. W. Lunt. songs, and Mr. Nickson, of Waterloo, gave an address. Four persons joined the society.
6 VER.

. --- On Monday, a foreigner, employed at Mr. Falk's Meadow Bank Salt Works, named Standrush, was brought before Mr. Slater, Mayor of Over, for being drunk and incapable in New-road, over, on the previous Stturday night. Prislner had imbibed so freely, that he thought of lancing, his bed in the road ; but the police officers had him conveyed to the lockups in a wheelbrrrow.—lt appeared that no ono could make the prisoner understand the nature of the charge, and the Mayor therefore discharged him on his paying 25., the Cost of his "coach" and his fare in the lockups. PENKE TH.

Guy FANVES' DAY AT PENKETH.—The custom of keep- ing the 11th of November was kept up with great vigour at Penketh. Bonfires, torchlights, ate., were freely indulged in. There was a large bonfire on the recreation, and this was seen for a great distance. Mr. R. Ockleshaw kindly con- tributed one pound's worth of fireworks for the amusement of the juveniles of Penketh, besides providing the fuel for the bonfire. All passed oti without injury to anyone. On Tuesday the annual meeting of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Penketh Elementary School. The Rey. a Sandys Jackson, vicar of Sankey, was in the chair. The Rev. Jellinger E. Symons attended as a depu- tation, and gave some excellent and interesting infOrmation on the work of the Society at home and abroad. Mr. R. Garnett read the report. There was a moderate attendance, and the meeting concluded Tr ith the Benediction. A col- lection was made at the close. PENKETH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—LISt Wednesday the members of the above association met for their weekly session, when the night was devoted to two papers, one on "Free Trade," by Mr. C. Spensely, Silver- street schools, Warrington, and the other lay Mr. 13. Hobson on " Reciprocity." Both papers were excellent composi- tions, and reflected great credit on the ability displayed by the above gentlemen. At the close a little discussion took place, but it was eventually adjourned till the following week. Mr. James Watson was in the chair. . SANDBACH. THE DEFAULT OF THE SANDBACH LOCAL BOARD.—At a meeting of the Sandbach Local Board, held on Monday night, a letter was read from the Local Government Board, intimating the result of the late inquiry relative to the com- plaint made by certain of the inhabitants that the Board had made default in providing a water supply and sewage works. The Local Government Board had decided that the ease against the Local Board had been proved, but in considera- tion of their having admitted some allegations, three weeks' time would be allowed them to decide what to do. Dr. Fox, the medical officer, alluding to some remarks which he had •made before the inspector at the inquiry, said that his testi- , mony was to the effect that in 1873 all the infantile popu• lation susceptible to scarlet fever had been cleared away. • A long discussion took place as to whether the Board should proceed first with the sewage works or water works. It was decided that the Board, in deference to the pressure of • the Local Government Board, determine to obtain a water 'supply in the most economical manner possible. and also deal with the sewage of those portions of the district which re- quire it. Negotiations for the purchase of the gasworks from the present owners net haying come to a satisfactory conclusion, the Board decided to apply to the Lucid Govern- ment Board for permission to borrow money to erect gas- works of their own.

div.p: WHITLEY.

PROLIf IC DUCES AT WHITLEY.—We have been shown SiX duck eggs weighing 111 bs., laid within the past ten days by fowls belonging to Mr. Barber, Merryfall Farm, Whitley. This is unusual at this season of the year. WINSFORD. CHRIST CHUFICH.—On Wednesday evening the anniver- sary services in commemoration of the re-opening of the above church was held. There was a full choral service with an anthem. The Rev. A. J. Blencowe, M.A., vicar of Witton, Northwich, preached an excellent sermon to a good congregation, though the church was not full. The offer- tory was devoted to the purchase of books and tracts from the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge. PRESENTATION.—Miss Chritnes, the mistress of the infant department of the Weaver Navigation School, Winsford, has been presented (on the occasion of her leaving for a school near Brighton) with two volumes of " Howe's Corn- mentary on the New Testament," as a token of affection from the school children; also with a beautiful electro- plated teapot, as a mark of esteem from the teachers and elder scholars of the Sunday school. Miss L. Picksteck, her pupil teacher, presented her at the same time with a beauti- ful workbox and writing desk combined. The Rev. E. Nixon, manager of the school, also gave her "Farrar's Life of Christ," in appreciation of her ten years' service at the scho.l. Miss Chrimes carries with her the respect and good wishes of parents, scholars and all connected with the school. ' SALT TRADE.— A very full demand for November has kept stocks completely at Zero. Total from Mersey WOOLTON, DILUTED MILK AT WAYERTREE.—Stephen Brunt, a milk dealer, at Woolton, was on Tuesday charged at the Pros- cot Police Court with having sold diluted mik.—The charge was proved by Superintendent Barker and Inspector Keigh- ley. and a fine of 10s. and costs imposed. The %Veolton Temperance Association, on Saturday even- ing past, commenced a series of free weekly entertainments in the Congregational Schoel-room. The chair was taken by J. R. McDonald, M R.C. (secretary of the Liverpeol Young Mens' Christian Association), who gave an able ad- dress on the temperance question. The programme comprised glees, sengs and recitations by the Congregational glee patty; and Mr. %V. D. Stoba (of Huyton), gave four of his popular " Lancashire sketches; " the room was well tilled with aa appreciative audience, and the entertainment closed with the usual votes of thanks. • ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. RAILWAY DEVELOPMENT IN CHESIIIRE.—The heshire Lines Railway Company, worked in connection with the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln and the Midland Com- panies, contemplate making considerable extensions of their existing systems running from Manchester through North- wich to Chester. One portion of their scheme will, it is uederstood, be to cut a new line right across Cheshire from their station near Cuddington joining the Cambrian line at Greddington, near Whitchurch, thus tapping the North Wales mineral traffic. ALLEGED WHOLESALE SWINDLING.—At Crewe, on 'Tues- day, Percy Morris, a respectably-dressed young man, was ! committed for trial on three charges of obtaining money by false pretences. The prisoner had been going about the country representing that he was connected with Morris and Co., publishers, of Nottingham, and canvassing for adver- tisements for a Cheshire directory. The receipts in his book showed that he had obtained over £lBO from 500 persons in Cheshi7e.—John Stafford, printer, Nottingham, said that three years ago he printed a directory for the prisoner's father. He had not yet been paid for it. He had had a sign over his premises painted "Morris and Co," but that had long since been removed, anl there .was no such firm now in Nottingham.—Mr. Johnson, of Crewe who had given prisoner money for an advertisement, said that he gays an address at Nottingham and also at Chester.—Detective Murphy said that thb address at Chester was a fictitious one.—"l'wo hotel-keepers, one at Macclesfield and the other at Chester, were called to prove that the priscner had stayed at their respective houses for several weeks and had lert without paving his accounte.—Mr. Seller, of Chester, for the defence, argued that the prosecution had failed to show that the prisoner did not intend to publish a directory. if he did not do that the remedy was by civil action for the recovery of the money.—The prisoner's father said het gave his son permission to republish the book.—The prisoner was committed for trial on each charge. WHISTON.

A CANDID FOWL STEALER.—At the Preocot Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, a young man, belonging to Parr was charged with haying stolen four ducks, vat Ued at 1.15., the property of Mr. litnrner, farmer, Whiston.—The prisoner, it seemed, had been seen by a police officer at 1 o'clock on the morning of the 2nd inst. going towards his home carry- ing the four ducks, and when asked where be had got theft he replied, "I have stolen them and in try a dozen more. It was afterwards ascertained that -the ducks had .been stolen from the prosecutor's.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for one month.

Swift, of Parr, who had contracted to run 100 yards level for 15 side. Tom Potter was ret lin, (1 as starter. Greenough quickly took up the running, and breasted the tape an ;easy winner by fully three yards. , r, •

( PRESCOL LIBERAL CLUB.—The members of this elate have, it is stated, taken on lease the house and premises in the Market-place, lately occupied by Dr. Green : where they intend to carry out such necessary alterations and improve- ments as will conduce to the amusement and pleasure of it Imembers. ! THE ST. HELENS THF.ATRE.—On Friday, Mr. J. 0. Swift I applied to the St. Helens magistrates on behalf of Mr. G. F. Charles, the lessee, for a renewal of the license of the ITheatre Royal, St. Helens.—Mr. Charles was called, and said that the means of egress from the building had re- cently been much improved. In case of fire it could now be emptied in less than five minutes.--Mr. Hart, the boroagh surveyor, said he was quite satisfied with the arrangements th it had been made for emptying the theatre.—The renewal of license was granted. ASSAULTING A POLICEMAN AT Sc. HELENS.—A reennt- able-looking man, aimed Peter Harding. was, on Monday, charged, at the Sr. Helens Police Court, with having been drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Police- constable Verde-, on Saturday night.—Vardv stated Veen in consequence of his disorderly behaviour in-Westfield-At-set, he took the prisoner into custody, about half-past six en Saturday evening. Hardin.; thereupon turned round. knocked the officer down, and kicked him on the head and legs.—A fine of 53. and costs was imposed for the drunkefl. ness, and 7s. 6d. and costs for the assault. TILE ASSAULT WITH A POKER.—An elderly man netend John Kelly was charged, at the St. Helens Police C ~,t, on Monday, with having assaulted Michael Buree.—Barke stated that about half-past nine, on the p-se' • :4 Saturday night, he had been crossing the coi d h .ee \V aen he heard a woman screaming 'murder: He ran down to the canal bank, and there saw the prisoner beating a woman. He re- monstrated with him, upon which Kelly turned round am] beat him on the head twice with a poker. In consequence of the loss of blood he was afterwards compelled to go to Dr. Gaskell and have the wounds stitched.—The prismer was committed to the Sessions. A Too ZEALOUS FOOTBALL PLAYER. Solomon Simp- kins, a young man, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, with having assaulted a lal named Wm. Ashley, on the 27th ult.—Mr. H. L. Riley defended.—it ap- peared that on the day in question a football match had been going on in a field in Rebins-lane, as the complainant and his father were teeming.. They both went into the field, and the ball happening tor come near the complainant he kicked it. This irritated the defendant so Much that he gave Ashley a kick with his foot. It was aleo stated by the boy's father that his son had in consequence of the injury from the kick been laid up for more than a week.—A time of is. and costs was imposed. .. FORAGING FOR A DINNER. A collier, named Janes Marsh, who did not appear, was on Monday, charged at the St. • Helens Police Court, with having had in his possession a rabbit, and a net used in taking game, on the 29th ult.— Sergeant Sherriff said that about 10 o'cleck on the night of the day in question he saw the defendant csming out of Elms Grove, near Sherdley Park, with something lea:kr under his coat. He stopped and swelled him, and foen-el the net produced, and a rabbit, in his possession.—ln answer to a question, the defendant said he "thought he ' would have a rabbit for his dinner," aud consequently went ' into Sherdley Park in search of one.—Defendant had•been previously convicted of theft.—He was fined £2 and Costs or 28 days. DISHONEST WORKMEN.—It the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, Joseph Welsh, a tarter, recently employed made the Corporation, was charged on remand with having stonn a quantity of -corn and soft soap, the property of the C r- poration.—The prisoner, it seemed, had been employed AI the Corporation's Sutton stables as temporaryhorse-keeper, and had on one occasion been seen by PC. Carter taking smoothing away from the stables. The officer stopped ledna and the.corn and soft soap was found in his possession, which be, admitted that he was Carrying away withint authority.—A fine of 20s. was imposed.---A chemical worker, named Thomas Woods, was also fined 20s. fcr ha.ying.stolen six begs, the property of Messrs. Marsh-ell and Sons, chemical manufacturers, Pocket-Nook. FEMALE PILFERERS AT ST. HELEN'S.—Three reaps ctab;Fe dressed women, named Sarah Millington, Mary Barker, and Alice Evans, were, on Monday, charged, at the St. Helens Police Court, with having stolen a quantity of coal from the premises of the Phcenix colliery, Sutton, the property of Messrs. B. B. Glover and Co.—Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted,. and from his statement it appeared that a good deal of annoyance had been caused at the Plwenix colliery by women carrying away coal from a coal heap. A watch was consequently set, and the defendants caught in the act of carrying coal away.—The defendants attempted to excuse themselves by saying they did not know they were doing wrong, as they only took away what they considered to be rubbish.—A lite of Se. was inflicted in each case. BRUTAL ATTACK ON A LANDLIID.—On Saturday, at the St. Helens Police Court, James Millighan was charged with having unlawfully wounded an old man named Jas. An- ders.—Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—The prisoner it scentede lodged with the prosecutor at 36, Water-street. On the Saturday night previous Anders had been lying on a sofa in his house, when IMillighan carne in and pulled him off, and then brutally kicked him on the head with his clogs, inflicting a deep wound, about two inches long, and also cut his nose to the bone.—ln defence it was urged that a struggle had taken place between the two men, in :he course of which the wounds were inflicted. The prisoner, it was stated, had been attacked by his landlord, and only de— fended himself.—A fine of £2 and costs was inflicted. lIREISING INTO A HOUSE AT BROAD GREEN. A man named George Morton was, on Wednesday, charged at Prescot Police Court with having broken into a house at Brod Green, in the early part of Octobsr, and stolen there- &nen a quantity of clothing, Sic., the whole valued at £7 10s. The owner of the house, it appeared, had been from home at the time of the robbery, and the prisoner, taking advantage 94. f this absencn broke into the house by way of the cellar window. He succeeded in getting away with the stolen articles and afterwards attempted to p iwn one of the suits with Mr. Greaves pawnbroker, Church-street, War— rington. Mr. Greaves, however, suspected the prisoner and sent for a policeman, who took bins into custody. Morton then confessed to the robbery.—He was sent to the assizes for trial. • PITCIi AND Toss AT PRESCOT : HEAVY PENALTIES.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, three young men, named John Woodwerd, John Suggerstone, and George Jervis, were charged with having played at pitch and toss in Niolyneux-lane, Prescot. on the 21st October. Superin- tendent Barker said that a great deal of complaint was nude owing to people playing at this game at Prescot on Sundays.—The Bench said Suggeistone, who did not appear, and seemed to be a ringleader, would have to go to gaol for one month ; Woodward, who had been convicted seven times before, would be fined 1 and costs, or one month's imprisonment; and Jervis would be fined 103. and costs. or 14 days' imprisonment. Five other youths, named Robert Woods, Robert Atherton, George Byrom, John Critchley, and William Bradley, were each tined 23. GI. and costs for a like offence at the same place. A CRUEL STETMOTHER.—At the St. Helens Peli,pe Court, on Thursday, a lad named Robert Traylor, aged 14 years, was charged with having stolen 17s, the property of Iris father, who lives at Gerard's Bridge.—Superintendent Johnson said lie would not ask the Bench to deal severely with the lad considering the circumstances of the c,s3. He had been much abused by his step-mother, wlao on one occasion was sent to gaol for three months for tieing him to a bed and cruelly beating him. After taking the money the prisoner had run away to It ainhill, where he received employment, and appeared to be very comfortable. The employer there was willing to take him back again.—The boy's father then came forward and said he did not wish him to be punished as it had been the ill-usage of his stepmother which led him to take the money.—The Chairman (Alderman Harri- son) said under the circumstances the boy would be dis- charged. A MASTER CARTER SENT TO GAOL FOR CRUELTY TO HORSES.—John Robinsen, a muter carter belonging to Liverpool, was charged at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, with haying caused three horses to be used whilst in an unfit condition, and two lads named William Gossage and John Gossage were charged with: driving the same horses at Wavertree on the 22nd ult.—Mr. T. Swift defended. —lt was stated in evidence that the first-named defendant kept nearly a score of horses, and had been convicted no less than twenty-nine times for cruelty to animals —The Chair- man said it was a nice list, and the Bench considered it was one of the worst cases of the kind they had ever dealt with. Fines did not seem to have any effect on the defen- dant, and they would therefore send him to gaol for one month's hard labour in respect of each case. The two lads wlep were only servants of Rebiason would be fined 10, and costs each. . WORKING MEN'S ENTERTAINMENT AT PRESCOT.—The fifth entertainment was held in the Town hall, on Monday evening, last, when a good company was present. F. Smith, Esq., presided, and addressed a few words to the meeting previous to the carrying out of the programme, which con- sisted of readings, recitations, solos, and duets. The reci- tations and readings were given by Mr. W. Brown and Mr. J. Sephton ; the solos were sung by Miss Lea Miss Keefe, and Mr. Philips; and Mr. T. Makin introduced a new fea- ture in the entertainment, by playing a solo on the cornet, and was warmly atrtilauded. The Misses Keefe sang A doer and received a well merited encore. The humorous sang of Miss Keefe, given in corresponding attire, deliebted the company, who recalled her. Selections on the piano by Miss Hatton and Miss Cook were very nicely given. Tee singing of the National Anthem closed the programme. The committee spare no pains in bringing out good talent, and it is hoped their efforts will be acknowledged and appreciated by the inhabitants of Prescot. NUTOROYE NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL In connection with the opening services of the above chapel a tea party and meeting were held on Monday. The tea, which was given by Mr. John Foulkes, Nutgrove, was served in the schoolroom beneath the old chapel, and was partaken of by nearly 400 persons. About 80 complimentary tickets had been sent to friends and those who assisted at the bazaar. The tables were presided over by Mesdames W. Foulkes, E. Ashton, W. Smith, J. Roscoe, W. liitchen, J. Pennington, Prince, Aspinall, Lyon. Lewis, anti Misses F. Gaskell. M. llopton, E. A. Stanley, M. A. Brown, H. Pen- nington, and S. Singleton. After tire tea a meeting, attended by nearly 500 persons. was held in the new chapel. Mr. John Spence, of Sutton, occupied the chair, and there were also present the Revs. J. M. Warnsley, G. Smith (of St. Helens), and J. M. Fairbourn (of Earlestown), Dr. McNicoll and Messrs Joseph Saxon (Southport), and J. T. Anderton. The collection taken at the meetine amounted to ,£lO 14s 2d, the totet rceip's ill c.mnection with 11)0 opening s,rvices being e:211, anti thus leaving about £OO to clear 110 new chapel of;debt. . . ,

TUE LANCASHIRE 11201.1-. AND COAL TRADE.—A dull tone continues generally throughout the iron trade of the Man- chester district. Fair iniuiries are reported for forge pig iron for delivery over the first half of next year at about dci under the prices asked by makers. One or two sellers of district iron are open to take orders at about 44s 4d, less 41, for forge Lincolnshire, delivered equal to Manchester. Most of the makers, Irewever, hold for 44s 10d for forge and 453 63 to 45s 10d for foundry, which in a few special cases is being obtained, but no large business is done on this basis. Local makers of pig iron still quote 45s 6d, less nel for forge and foundry, delivered equal to Maahester, and a few small orders are booked at this figure. The bulk of the offers are at about 63 less, but these are declined. In the finished iron trade the tone generally is scarcely so healthy as it has been. Most of the makers are still kept going with orders for present delivery, but with the possibility of an easing down in prices with the lull following the close of the shipping szason there is very little buying going on for forward delivery, and in some cases makers show rather more anxiety to secure orders. Prices remain at about .£6 2s Gd to £6 53 for bars, £6 lOs to £9 12s 6d for hoops, and £8 for sheets, delivered into the Manchester district.— Although the wages agitation in the coal trade causes a somee hat uneasy feeling with regard to the future, the pos- sibilities of a strike de not seem to be regarded with any great anxiety by consumers, and the chance of the pits being stooped ha certainly not yet proved a basis upon which sellers can get any higher prices. For the time of the year the demand for all classes of coal continues only moderate, and prices do not more than maintain a steady tone at about late rates. In a few cases where prices were ' on a low ba3is there has been a little stiffening up in house fire coal since the commencement of the month, but there has been no general actual unward movement, and the ad- vance of 53 per ton put on common furnace coal, burgy, and lack by one of the Manchester firms has not been fol- lowed elsewhere. The general demand, both for house fire and manufacturing purposes, is about sufficient to take away the present output, but there is no pressure. Engine classes of fuel continue bad to sell, and although slack is not quite se great a drug as it has been, supplies in the market are still excessive. Shipping has been rather quieter, with good steam coal delivered at Liverpool or Garstun not averaging more than about 7s 91 per ton At the pit mouth pi-4;0 are about as under :—Best coal 98 63 to 10s. seconds 7s 6d to Bs, common house fire coal 63 Oct to 7s, steam and forge coals 5s 6d to 6s, burgy 43 63 to ss, good slack 3s ad to 4; and counnou about 3a per ton.

Since the publication in the National Review of Lord SALISBURY'S article on artizans and labourers dwellings, frequent reference has been made both on the plat- form and in the press to the importance of the question the noble 'Marquis thus raised, but whether mooted from a philanthropic motive, or from a desire to cunningly divert public attention from political matters of more pressing moment, we will not stay to inquire. It is sufficient for our purpose at present to point out that various remedies have been suggested for the serious evils which, it is admitted on all hands, are inti- mately associated with overcrowding ; it has been shown that the subject is one fraught with many and grave difficulties; and it will therefore have to be dealt with cautiously and gradually as opportunity arises. Our Con- servative friends do not appear to be agreed as to their policy on this question. We note that en Saturday, the Home Secretary of the late Government, Sir RICHARD CROSS, made reference to the subject in his speech at Aberdeen when being presented with the freedom of the city, and if there is one Statesman more able than another to speak with authority on overcrowding it must, we should say, be Sir RICHARD CROSS, for he is the author of the Artizans Dwellings Act," passed in 1875—a bill which was destined to work quite a revolution in a sanitary point of view, as well as to provide better homes for the working people in our large centres.- So far, however, from the sanguine antici- pations formed being justified by experience, we all know that the bill, by reason of its permissive character no less than by the large amounts which it has been found necessary to pay in compensation for pro- perty demolished, has been, almost, if not entirely, a dead letter. In the passing of tie Act through Parliament, Sir RICHARD was careful, as all Conservative: a7e, to guard the landlord's interest; but it would seem that in this instance, at any rate, the worthy baronet has had occasion to change his mind. He went to the one extreme in defending the landlords, and now he goes to the other in condemning them. He now believe 3 it to be a mistake to give com- pensation to the owners of the "miser- able houses" which disgraced London, and he expresses a hope that compensation to the landlords will for ever be put an end to, because he says he looks upon the owners of much of the property in London "as people who are worth very little con- sideration." Sir RICHARD would now give to landlords the actual value -of their property prior to demolition, having regard only tp the rental which ought to be paid, not to the extortionate rents now being charged. In other words, he would insist upon the "duties of property" being re- spected; and if landlords did not regard the comfort and health of the tenants of their property, he would take care that, ii its demolition, they should not derive any pecu- niary benefit for their neglect of sanitary requirements, though such a ber.fit they practically have derived. We hail with satis- faction this changed attitude of the late HOME SECRETARY, and we can quite under- stand that had he another similar bill to draft he would-deal with the question in an entirely different manner. "He knows," says a writer on this subject, "why his own measure failed. It failed because the cost of buying rotten houses, according to the profit made upon them by grasping and unscrupulous landlords, made it impossible to get a fair profit out of new dwellings for the same class erected with sanitary improvements. To get rid of that blot, Sir RICHARD has now de- livered his soul. He will have no mercy on the merciless landlord. He will pay him, not upon his immoral profits, but on his moral ones, and make it unprofitable, therefore, for a landlord to create fever dens." We only wish Sir RICHARD were able to imbue some of his colleagues with similar sentiments to those which, he himself now entertains on this question. Then it would not be difficult for the present Government to introduce a bill for the development of Sir RICHARD'S Artizans' Dwellings Act, excellent in many respects, and to carry it. We are afraid, however, that Sir RICHARD is much in ad- vance of many of the members of the late Government, and certainly he is more pro- nounced than Lord SALISBURY, who, true to his antecedents, is not disposed to make- landlords pay for making their property clean, healthy, and habitable. Yet this is only what a tenant has a right to expect, and what a landlord ought to be compelled to attend to. It is noticeable also that Sir RICHARD and Lord SALISBURY are at issue with reference to the authority who ought to be entru-,ted with the carrying out of any scheme for the provision of better dwellings for cur working people. Sir RICHARD, being a commoner, has, naturally enough, faith in our represen- taAve institutions, and w4.-:uld have no hesita- tion in committing to our Town Councils the spending of any money which might be voted for the purpose of improving the exist- ing or providing news dwellings. other hand, Lord SALISBURY, a peer, has, of course, no faith in our representative in- stitutions, and would be opposed to the expenditure of money so voted being handed over to "municipal bodies," his reason being that in these bodies there is an absence of economy. This statement is not consistent with fact. It is not difficult to point to Town Councils which look after gas, water, and other corporate undertakings and work ;hem at a c6nsiderable profit; and why they should not also be trusted to spend ' money on improved sanitary dwellings we are at a loss to understand. The reason given by the noble Marquis is to us, as it must be to most people, an exceedingly flimsy and un- tenable one. His Lordship, it seems, would rather trust the money with private bodies, in which we regret to think there is often much jobbery and corruption practised; or he would spend it in giving encouragement to "specu- lative builders," an instance of whose economy is this week presented to us by a case from Birmingham. There a "speculative builder" named HUMPAGE has just stopped payment, and no wonder when we find him buying diamonds and jewellery to the extent of £3,000, furniture and pictures to the valne of £5,750, Dresden figures amounting to ro,ooo, and investing in other equally ex- travagant luxuries. This "speculative builder" boasted that his -house equalled that of Baron GRANT, and we should not wonder that its grandeur surpassed that of the Mar- quis of SALISBURY'S mansion at Hatfield. Surely his lordship cannot be in earnest in suggesting that the "speculative builders" should be summoned to our aid in dealing with the over-crowding in our large towns; ' but, if in earnest, it only proves that his lord- I ship will not trust the representative bodies elected by ,the working classes, whose in- terests he professes to be so desirous to pro- mote. His lordship is given to dilate upon the want of harmony in the Liberal Cabinet 1 on important points of policy. The speech of; Sir RICHARD CROSS on Saturday bristles with uncontrovertible evidence that on some vital j questions affecting the policy—as shadowed , forth by Lord SALISBURY —of the future Con- servative Cabinet, there are at least two likely members of that Cabinet directly at variance. That being so, we think we ought to hear , much less of Liberal disunion—from Lord SALISBURY at any rate.
RUNCORN'S NEW TOWN HALL.
The ban? of the Commissioners' lives for the past

eight years has been removed. Waterloo House, typical of dissension in the Council Chamber and a disasterous compromise in the law courts, has under - gone many changes. Originally the residence of a gentleman, then for a short period a hospital for infectious diseases, and again a private residence, it has now assumed a character which bids fair to be permanent. Transformed into Runcorn Town Hall, it is not probable that the present generation will see it adapted to any uses different to those to which it was formally dedicated on Wednesday. For the multifarious offices of a Town Hall the building is extremely well arranged, and the money that has been expended upon it—purchase, cost of law suit, and fittings—does not exceed the intrinsic value of he property ; and we congratulate the ratepayers upon being in possession of such a structure for the transaction of public business. There is ample ac- eomodation for .the four most important public authorities in the town—the Board of Commissioners) the School Board, the Free Library, and the Over- Seers—and we trust that there will be no impediment to the School Board taking up its quarters Within the Town Hall. The admirable way in which Waterloo House Committee,

presided ever by Mr. Shaw, has conducted the trrangement hitherto, would preclude such a con• tingency arising, for we are convinced they will be ready and willing to do all in their power to meet the wishes of the School Board. The advantages of con centrating the public offices in one building situated lita a o9ntral position are palpable, and the conveni- ences of the New Town Hall cannot be over.

estimated. Mr. Meadoweroft's name will be in- separably linked with the building. As Chairman of the Board he was the central figure in the modest Ceremony that marked the formal opening of the Premises on Wednesday, and the able speech which he then delivered was full of reminiscences interest- ing to the natives and residents of the ancient town. Meadowcroft, whose wise and impartial control of the Board is deserving of the warmest praise, is worthy of the honour of opening the New Town Hell; and we wonld conclude our brief remarks by expressing the hope that within the walls of the hindsome Counoil Chumber will never occur those stormy scenes in which personal feeling and prejudice has played so prominent a part in die past.

GUNPOWDER PLOT AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.—In neither of the twin towns of the Mersey was the memory of Guy Fawkes extensively observed. A few bonfires threw a Lurid glare against the dark clouds, the air resounded at in- tervals with the detonations of toy cannons, while fireworks occasionally flashed across the sky. H fppily no accidents were reported. A MIDNIGHT ROBBERY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Eliza Ann Davies, a tramp, waq charged With stealing 83 from an engine driver named John Parr.— Complainant stated that abut midnight on Saturday he Met the Prisoner in Victoria-road, and after having some conversation with her gave her fici, and accoinpanied her to Bridge-street. Prisoner was the " worse for drink," and a constable took her into custody. Afterwards, the witness found that Se had been abstracted from his trousers pockets. Re saw the prisoner place some money on the form at the Police station, and sitting upon it.—Prisoner pl :Med guilty, and she was sentenced to a month's hard labcur.

EXPERT YOUNG THIEVES AT RENCOL N WAKES.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas John Oliver ,and Owen McDonald, boys, both aged ten, were brought up la custody charged with stealing a florin, the property of Mary Dowdell. on Saturday night the prosecutrix had a stall on the fair ground, and placed a florin, with other Money, in a box on the stall. Immediately McDonald snatched it up. passed it to Oliver, an(t then both ran away. Subsequently they were arrested by P.S. Whalley, to whom they accused each other of the theft.—The magistrates ordered Oliver to receive six strokes with the birch rod, but McDonald, who had recently been charged with felony, was Sent to gaol for 14 days, afterwards to be confined in a reformatory for a period of five years. The Bench severely r eprimanded the woman for exposing her money. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—The members of the Band of Hope Society in connection with this Church gave an enterZainment to a good audience in Zion , Chapel, on Monday evening. In the absence of Mrs. Valise, the wife of the paLtor, Mr. Joseph Betney presided, and delivered an address, in which he dwelt upon the import- ance of parents signing the pledge, and thus giving their Children a good example. An excellent programme of songs flci recitations was gone through in good style, the follow- ing taking part :—Harry Wilcock, Walter Mellor, Lilian Waight, Mary Wilcock;Ruth Worthington, Archibald Gray, Eliza Waight. Jane Summerbell, Bertha Price, Margaret A. Ashton, Mr. Bustwell. Ellen Ferber, Jessie Betney. Hill, anl E. Barges. The choir and children rendered several rtongs and hymns under the conductorship of Mr. D. Price. DEPRAUDING THE RAILWAY COMPANY AT RUNCORN.— Before Mr. John Brundritt and Mr. James Handley, at Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, Michael Hilditeh, who stated he was a potter from Burslem, but who had every appearance of being a tramp, was charged with attempting to defraud the London and North-Western Railway Com- Pany by travelling from Liverpool to Runcorn without having previously paid his faro.—Mr. Ferrand, of the solici- tors' department. Lime-street, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the company.—From the evidence of Mr. Apple- ton, stationmaster, Runcorn, it appeared that on the six o'clock train from Lime-street arriving in Runcorn on Tues- day evening, the tickets of the passmgers were examined. „, the prisoner was found in a third-class compartment, but he was unable to produce any ticket. He excusld himself by Saving th it he intended Co go on to Longport, where he Would obtain the amount of the fare from his friends, and Pay the railway company. He gave Mr. Appleton a wrong name.—The Bench fined him 10s. and costs Os. 4d., or 14 41:vs' imprisinmenf. The prisoner went to gaol.

THE ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT FROM A RUNCORN PUBLICAN.—At Runcorn Ponca Court, on Thursday, Mr. James Handley on the Bench, John Needham, afl dman hailing from Winsford, was brought up on remand, charged with embezzling £7 6s. and £3 6s. Bd. respectively, the monies of his employer Wm Chadwick.—The prisoner was undefended.—Mr. Chadwick, who is the landlord of the Greenway Vaults, is the owner of a river flit named Agnes, of which the prisoner has been captain for a period of 14 months. The arrangement between the parties was that known as "thirds/' viz., that the prisoner was to appropriate two-thirds of the profits for his labour, and at stated intervals hand over the remaining third to his master. This arrangement was pretty regularly kept until March last, when the last settle- ment between the parties took place. About six weeks ago Mr. Chadwick received a letter from H. Hall, the mate of the flat, informing him that the prisoner had deserted her at Birkenhead. Mr. Chadwick went to that place, and dis- covered that the prisoner had embezzled the sum of about £29.—Witnesses were called who proved that the prisoner had received freights from merchants at Lancaster and Birkenhead for which he had not accounted.—lnspector Hollingworth deposed to apprehending the prisoner on the Ist of November at Winsford. He was in bed at the time. The inspector informed him why he was arrested, and the prisoner replied that it had taken all the money to keep himself and his wife and family on account of the bad weather.—The prisoner was committed to Knutsford sessions for trial.

The Pope with the cares of Roman Catholic christendom on his shoulders living prisoner in a palace in a southern city, turns his mind to a grievance of the Irish priesthood, and seeks to redress it. Pio Nono seems to have thought that a parish priest should have something else to do than to be seen with his parishioners riding after the hounds, and so that Pontiff issued his veto and forbade the practice. The hunts went on as usual, but the clergy stayed at home. On a chongi tonhca, Leo XIII. takes a wider view, and gives the Irish priesthood the benefit of his latitude. It is well the House is not sitting, or poor Mr. Eriington might be badgered about one of the objects of his mission to Rome.

We have had a bad week wich fires, and their occurrence and the disasters resulting from them have made others think seriously on possible consequences besides poor owners who have lost their property and poor shareholders who will lose some ot their dividend. There can be no doubt but that the diaggerston's was an honest fire ; still we live in days when, with the comoiittal of Walters fresh in the public mind, we have reason to suspect much fraud, and, with the underground explosions still un- discovered, much nefarious outrage. There are plenty of tradesmen who want fires very badly, and ruffians who would blow up a train would not hesitate to set fire to a timber store. Captain Shaw and his brigade deserved all sorts of praise for the speed with which the engines and the men were on the spot. And still we know—or rather we don't yet know—the damage that was done. It seems, moreover, that that fire absorbed half the brigade and half the engines of the capital—l believe, in- deed, more than half. If we had had another of equal magnitude at the same time, the loss of property might have been enormous.

UNITED CHESHIRE AND LANCASHIRE BUILDING SOCIETY, RUNCORN—.The annual meeting was held in Holy Trinity Schools, on Thursday evening. Mr. Timothy Simister pre- sided, and there was a large attendance of members. The report and balance sheet was read by Mr. J. W. Lightburn, the secretary. The committee state that in presenting their twentieth annual report they have to repeat what was stated last year, viz., that nntil the withdrawal notices are either satisfied or withdrawn they can neither pay dividends nor advance moneys on mortgage. The total profits of the society for the past year amount to £1,601 7s 41, out of which £929 8s 2d has been spent on improvement and special repairs to properties in the possession of the society, with the result that these properties are now almost fully tenanted, and promise to yield a considerably increased revenue in the ensuing year. The nett profits of last year not having been paid in dividends, have been added to the reserve fund, which amounts to £4,703 14s, and as the nett balance of this year's profits amounting to £459 5s 3d will be dealt with in a Apailar manner, the total balance in favour of the society to meet any loss that may occur, or to assist in pay- ing future dividends, amounts to £5,162 19s 3d. The com• mittee will continue to use every effort to realise the society's securities when opportunities present themselves. —The report and balance sheet were adopted. After numerous inquiries had been answered, apparently to the satisfaction of the members, a vote of thanks was passed to tha p”e.ie,nr, treesurer. committee. and secretary for th.ir cervices uuring Lae past year. Tile retiring members of the committee, Messrs. Johnson, Rhodes, and Pritchard, were re-elected, and all the officers were re-appointed.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT _FROM A RUNCORN PUBLIC-HOUSE.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT _FROM A RUNCORN PUBLIC-HOUSE.

Yesterday morning, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. James Handley, an elderly men, named JameS Mdlington, was brought up, in custody, charged with stealing 2s. Bd., the money of Edward Banks, landlord of the Gram Inn. —About twenty minutes to eleven on Thursday night, the prisoner went into the Grapes Inn, where the landlord sup- plied him with a glass of beer. Banks then went into the kitchen, and in a short time he heard the sound of money falling to the ground, and going into the bar dis- covered that about 3s, had been abstracted from a tin box placed tlkere for the convenience of the servant girl. A. penny was also found near the box. Subsequently the pri- soner was apprehended by P.C. Kelly, who found 4s. 6d. in his pocket.—The prisoner was remanded until to-day to Permit further inquiries to be made.

The monthly meeting wax held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday afternoon. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present Dr. Steele, Messrs. John Simpson, F. A. Lake, W. Handley, P. Briscoe, 'l'. Riley, W. Brookes (secretary), and J. D. Jones (librarian). —The Librarian reported that during October 1,147 volumes were borrowed from the landing library as follows : Theology, 18; philosophy, political economy, &c., 14; his- tory, travels, biography, 139; science and art, 48; poetry, 9; prose, fiction, 849; miscellaneous, 70;—a decrease of 524 compared with the corresponding month last year.—lt was decided to ensure the library at tha maximum sum of £1 per volume.—lt was also decided, on the Illation of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. LAZE, to have a reading-roots on the nights that the library was now open for reading books and such reviews and periodicals as the committee might decide to take.—The Book Selection Committee recom- mended the purchase of volumes to the value of £2o.—The recommendation was agreed to.
MASONIC CELEBRATION AT RUNCORN.

The Provincial Grand Chapter of Cheshire was held in Runcorn Public Hill on Wednesday. It was opened in due and solemn form by E. C. Buller, senior P.H. of Cheshire, acting in the absence of the Right Hon. Lord de Tabley, the M.E. grand superintendent. E. Corn. Marwood, P,P.G.H., acted as H.E. Corn., J.P. Platt, P.P.G.H., acted as J. The acting Grand Superintendent then called upon Bro. G. W. Latham, P.G.S.E , to read the minutes of the last Grand Chapter meeting, which he did. He also called the roll of chapters. The following brethren were invested as pro- vineial grand officers for the ensuing year :—W. Marquis, P.G.H.; F. A. Dickson, P.G.J.; G. W. Latham, ; W. Mellor, P.G.P. Sog.; J. P. Bardsley, first assistant P.G. Sog.; W. R. Was., 2nd assistant, P G. Sog.; P. Wadsworth, P.G. treasurer R. C. Edwards, P.G. Sd. B.; C. Booth, P.G. St. B. • H. Lord de Tabley, the Most Excellent Provincial Grand Superintendent, stat- ing his inability t& attend the Provincial Grand Chapter through illness, and expressing the sentiment that although he was not present, his heart was with them. Briscoe, J. Prit- chard, W. Fisher, S. Taylor, H. White, F. Fairhurst, F. A. Lake, J. W. Lightburn, Dr. Mouritz,(medical officer), W. H. Linaker (law-clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), M. Barker. (surveyor).

THE TOWN FREE FROM SMALL-PDX. Dr. MOURITZ presented the following report :—The num- ber of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 29. Of the above deaths, nine were due to chest affections, six to abdominal affections five to nervous Affections, four to senile decay, and two to Phthisis. Croup, premature birth, ulceration, and typhoid fever, account for one each; representing a death-rate of 23 per 1,000 per annum. Three inquests were held. Total deaths, 32. Six- teen deaths occurred among children five years and under, and of these 14 were below one year. Dr. .I.EELE said it ought to be made known to the public that whilst Widnes was seriously suffering from small-pox, Runcorn was entirely free from the disease.
THE SAFETY OF THE THEATRE: THE CAMDEN LEANING

CHIMNEY. Mr. BARKER reported to the Highway Committee that be visited the Theatre Royal on the 11th 0;;tolItr, but there being no light he could not make a proper inspection Nevertheless the whole structure is slight, and from the first was understood to be only temporary, although it had been there now more than twenty years. The structure had never had the sanction oi the Board, and he certainly could lot certify it as a properly built place for a public audience. He may also state that his.attention had been called to the leaning chimaey of the Camden Works. Some people thought that it was going worse, but be could not perceive tuy difference in its position for the last ten years, but he had enly tested it in one way. The Surveyor was instructed to make further exlmina- tions of the theatre and chimney.

ETJILDING OPERATIONS. The Highway Cotnmittee recomtnended for approval plans of six houses in Collier-street, for Mr. H. White ; church in Greenway-road, for Canon Barclay and others ; house and shop at the bottom of Percival-lane, for Mr. John Roberts; alteration to house in Albert-street for Mr. Samuel Dobson ; six houses in Thomas-street, for Mr. H. White. SAThe minutes of the committee were passed, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Dr. STEELE. The former gentleman observed that he considered it a great honour to be chairman of the Highway and Sanitary Committee at the present time. when the Board had removed to a new habitation. He trusted everyone of them would have one aim in that room, and that was te get through the business with efficiency and despatch. He remembered the estab- lishment of the Board 31 years ago very well. That period seemed to have flashed rapidly away, and the men who used to sit round the old table at the old Town Hall were gone. He hoped they would have some happy times in that loom, and be possessed with a desire to increase the public good.

div.head: VACANCY ON THE FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE VACANCY ON THE FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

Mr. FAIRHURST proposed that Mr. J. R. Frith be ap- pointed a member of the Free Library Committee in place of Dr. MacDougall. He believed Mr. Frith worked very hard for the formation of the library, and he was a well- known gentleman in the town. They could, he was core, appoint no one better to fill the place..
. Mr. PRIICIIARD seconded the motion. Mr. Frith was a most suitable person indeed to hold the position. Mr. SHAW: I beg to support the motion.
Carried unanimously. THIL OLD OFFICE CLOCK.

The seal of the Board was affixed to the agreement with the county authorities for the sale of the public offices in Bridge-street. A short discussion took place as to the dis- posal of the clock, and the suggestion that a tower be erected upon the Market Hall, and the clock so placed that one dial could be seen from Delph Bridge and the other from the lower part of the town met with general favour. It was .greed that it would be no use at Waterloo House. lhe consideration of the matter was referred to the Highway Committee. The meeting then terminated.

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Nev. 80) Very few features of general interest present theltselves for repart on the business of the pest week A rather firmer tone has prevailed for the leading securities induced by more pro- mising trade returns, and some Press comments calculated to engender confidence as re;ards the near future, and the heavy railway secut Ries have in most cases responded favourably. Business, too, has been rather more an' ive generally. the aggre- gate of transactions being in exce 41 of that reported for several recent weeks. For foreign stocks quotations have moved some- what irregularly, Egyptians of all issues and Mexicans 3 per cent. being quoted higher, whilst Argentine and -hard dollar bonds.Turko (both registered and stamped), Spanish., and Italian are all lower, the decline, however, is fractional except in the cases of Argentine and Turkish registered Stock, both of which quote 1 down. Mexican Railway Stock has been freely sold. and mark a very severe fall on the week. Quotations last marked when we wrote a week ago were 88 S, and they now stand 72i 73 or a fall of about 15 per cent. in a week's time. Then traffic announcement was anticipated in some degree, but after publication further decline took place, followed by another fall on the announcement of a 4 per cent, dividend on the half- year, this being considerably below expectation. Miscellaneous shares have had a fair amount of attention, and the total of ceilings reported is comparatively good. Quotations have undergone numerous changes, and taken altogether, numeri- cally, a slight adverse balance is to be noted.

div.head: Tettero to the editor.
div.p: Tettero to the editor.
FOOTBALL NOTES BY “LEATHER HUNTER."

_ Sir,—W ill you kindly allow ma space in your columns to I correct a statement by "Leather Hunter" in his notes of Saturday last. He says that the Temperance team are addicted to ranch charging, and that they very often go in for playing the man, instead of the ball. Such is not the case, and 1 think that before he published such a statement he ought to have been sure of its truth, as he does not know what harm he might do the Temperance club, even if It were true, which it is not. Considering the position 'Mr. " Leather Hunter" holds in the Earlestown club, I think his talk is ridiculous. I have had the honour to watch all the matches the Temperance team have played at home, and I am sure pleaPanter and quieter games need not be played, excepting the Cup-tie match with Stacksteads, which I admit was rather wet and rough, but I am given to under- stand they were severely handled when they went to Stack- steads. Hoping that in future "Leather Hunter" will hold to the truth in his notes, and that he will not deprecate other clubs and extoll his own all he can, I remain yours, etc., FAIRPLAY.

div.head: " TIIE BITTER CRY OF OUTCAST LONDON."
div.p: " TIIE BITTER CRY OF OUTCAST LONDON."

Sir,—l have no doubt the harrowing details given in my last from the pamphlet bearing the above heading may lead some who desire to benefit England's toiliog, vet poverty- stricken sons, to think a little as to the remedy. Charles Kingsley, writing nearly twenty years ago, says :—" That social evils, like dust and dirt, have a tendency to re-accu- mulate perpetually; so that however well this generation may have swept their house, the rising generation will have assuredly in twenty years time to sweep it over again." The time given has elapsed, and here we are with the broom again. Shall it be said that all sweeping is ineffectual; that as Francis acon wrote in 1650, so we may write now id man, that he is "Curet from his cradle, and brought up to years with cares and fears? " Were we not well assured that our present social system is bad and artificial, despon- dency would take told of us, and no attempt would be made to remove the curse. But the poor man is becoming a poli- tician; an aggressive one. Blankets for the poor, coals for the poor, music for the poor, will no longer suffice to keep them in order. What they want and what they mean to have is work for every man and pay for every man. Ac- cording to the Daily News, he maintains "that it is to a great extent due to the religious bodies that things are not radically reformed. They inculcate patient submission where there should be self-assertion, and a demand for fair play." This is true, and until workingmen throw aside such drivelling teachings, and assert their right to the earth and the fulness thereof, so long will their homes remain the abodes of misery. In the section devoted to poverty, the writer of the " Bitter Cry" gives a few instances that are becoming tolerably familiar to newspaper readers. A child seven years old is known easily to earn 108 6d a week by thieving; if he is honest he can earn by match-box making 2&-d a gross, and have the privilege of finding his own paste and string. Before he can gain as much as the young thief he must make 56 gross of match- boxes a week, or 1,296 a day. Half that amount is as much as an adult can accomplish, Women for finishing trousers _ _

- . recinve 24d. a pair, and find their own thread, work seven- teen hours and no meal time, and receive the splendid sum of one shilling. For making men's shirts 10d. a dozen, lawn tennis aprons 3d. a dozen. Women and children employed in sack-making receive a farthing each, paliasses lid. each. Says one man,—" My master gets a pound for what he gives me 35. for making." For making fishing boots soli at three guineas the workman receives ss. 3d. if to order, if for stock 45. 6d. Sir, the list is enough to mike a man's blood boil. _ _ _ . _ . . .
These are not sketches derived from the abodes of crime, but

relate to people who are trying to gain an honest livelihood. Making articles of dress for young ladies at 3d. a dozen, in- stead of the curse resting on the poor surely it ought to fol- low the wearers of these garments into their splendid man- sions. We read of the Glasgow bank thieves and their religious cant, of the Preston-bank and the forger leaving his family at church, of the Liverpool corner man, and his im- mense transactions in the swindling line. What can the workingman think when he reads of those in high places preying upon one azother Why, nothing but that the means for it all is extracted out of bie flesh and blood. Em- ployers have so completed the system of competition that one perpetual effort is being made to screw the workman's wages out of him. No man can bring up a family on the small sums that are usually received by labourers, indeed the sum received by the poorer paid artisan is quite inadequate. The life of a married man Le One long Continued struggle with the wolf at the door. And this will continue so long as we fail to boldly grasp the question. Merely to keep on applying artificial remedies is only staving off the evil day. Lord Salisbury says he has no fear of revolution. I am not so sanguine about that. Revolution ef one kind is fast shaping itself in the minds of the people, and it will I much denend upon the class to whom his lordship belongs whether another and less peaceable upheaval does not do something towards reversing the positions we now hold.l Lord Salliutt earliest ancestor was David Cecil. who iYbe- queathed his danght'et suniof 5.,20 at 'his death. To-day the man ValM Writes articles respecting labourere' dwellings, and is anxious about the preservation of our glorious constitution, has a rent roll of £33,294 witheut counting his London property. His property on the south side of the Thames within the last few years has risen 50 per cent. This worthy upholder of things as they are now holds land in London of which he has no title deeds, and of which a few generations ago a yearly rental of a few shil- lings was paid to the parish, but the minute book of the parish vanished mysteriously and the rent ceased to be paid. We have this valiant champion of the poor man giving his opinion as to the means of improving the labourer's dwel- ling, and like Prince Bismarck he would call in the aid of Parliament. A cottage of a healthy description will cost £l5O. This sum must yield 6 per cent.-4 per cent. for the landlord and 2 per cent. for the repairs—but this means 3s. 6d. per week rent; and labotirers, say on the Ha•field estate, could not afford this. So if these cottages are to be built at all it must be done by charitable persons, unless, says his lordship, wages rise considerably higher. Aye, tbere is thesrub. If the wages of farm labourers rise the farmer cries out that he cannot pay his rent, so to meet the dilemma cottages are being cleared off the estates as being in the first place unprofitable, and in the next place to keep hovels about the place means harbouring poachers. His lordship tells us that a million acres have been withdrawn from the plough within ten years. This means, I beg to tell him, that the Scotch clearance system is being adopted in England with but one result, viz,, that of driving a large agricultural population into the towns, and 30 increasing the difficulties of our town resident population. Here we have the chief cause of the " bitter cry." A wealthy landlord system, that instead of finding employ- ment for the peasant drives him and his family to compete with his brother labourer in the town. The land question contains the whole panacea for all our evils, but its ramifi- cations are so intricate, it contains so many side issues, that the ordinary workman fails to comprehend it, or he would at once insist upon the revolution Lord Salisbury has no fear of. Nearly the whole of the wealth upon which our English gentry yearly revel is extracted directly or indi- rectly from trade and commerce, and no return is made for it. While they sleep their banking account grows. For every acre of ground withdrawn from the plough a human )Ite is blasted. I may here state that in Manchester there are slop factories, where country girls seek, and too often find work, in which the great majority employed have to eke, out their earnings by walking Oxford-street and Peter-street. To this are cur sisters and daughters forced in consequence of the overcrowding of our towns. Ask the managers of any of our large firms how many applications they receive for any vacancy that may ()may; how many applications for lads to be placed as apprentices. Ask the shopkeepers how many applicants they refuse during th, year. These are all people whe are willing to work and yet find none to do, who, as I have said, are forced to compete with their brothers of the town for means whereby to live. No wonder at the poverty and misery. Lord Salisbury tells us to build the workingman's house a few storeys higher. He refers to the population question in quite a respectable fashion—"ln France the domestic arrangements are so superior to ours ' that the labouring man is seldom troubled with a large family, in consequence the competition is less keen amongst them than with us." To build houses lofty is no remedy. To talk of the population question in such a mincing style gives no information. Lord Sherbrooke, writing on the county franchise, bewails placing the supreme power of the State in the hands of the poor and ignorant, as being likely to destroy it." I say, in return, that you cannot-destroy the State by elevating the people, and you do this when you give them an interest in the State. Allow me to point out another feature—the People are being educated. As intelligent men, they will refuse to enlist, not having any particular interest at stake. Why should bright youths, fresh from school, as I hope they all will be presently, volunteer to defend Lord Sher- brooke's estates, or any one else's? Allow our rural popu- lation td- Plant themselves firmly in the land, to surround themseftee with their happy families, to cease adding to the population of towns, and then the struggle will be less keep, and some reason may be found for the patriotic feeng so much talked of by Orangemen. Following the land ques-

tion, as an important factor in the "bitter cry," is the drink question. Whatever may be ultimately decided upon as to the course to be adopted with public-houses, no doubt can remain as to their being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the community. The moderate drinker, even, feels that he is conniving at a traffic second only in its evils to the slave trade. It has been suggested that they be closed at noon on Saturdays, or at latest at nine o'clock. This might be tried. Also, to prohibit publicans from selling beer to children under 14 years of age. The fami- liarity bred in children for the common dram shop is one of the methods whereby drunkards are made. The next im- portant feature is the habitations of workmen. You may build good houses either in long barrack-looking rows, or in the direction where land costs nothing. It ivill all avail nothing. Out of the dismal court the outcast will carry his load of misery—but he will not lose it-in the new house; the old associations will cling to him. Aspirations for a higher and a brighter life must he planted, the circum- stances of life must be made more favourable, before it is worth living. It has taken the Radicals years of preaching before even Sir R. Cross would acknowledge the rights of jworking men. And now we mean to have them, however , (property may fare. CLIFFORD DIX. Warrington, Nov., 1883.
ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION. - FIRST

AID TO THE INJURED. Sir,—The remarks of the Deputy Coroner in reference to the sad end of the young man Ashley, who bled to death, and the case of the boy Cunningham, who was rescued from drowning in the Dukes Canal, at Runcorn, again clearly and fully demonstrate the necessity of instructing the work- ing-classes as to the mode of procedure in case of accident. There is not the slightest doubt that Ashley's life might have been saved had any person who had attended St. John's Ambulance classes been present, but unfortunately no such person was at hand, and a valuable life was lost. The boy Cunningham would certainly have died had it not hap- pened that two police officers, who were acquainted with the proper means of restoring the apparently drowned, were at hand and promptly took the necessary steps, thereby sav- ing a life—doing one of the noblest acts that man can per- form. In London, Liverpool, and many other cities and large and small towns, numbers of ladies, clergymen, vol- unteers, constables, dock labourers, and in fact persons of almost all ages and positions have joined classes and passed examinations under the above-named Association, which 1 has for it head a no less important a personage than His Grace the Duke of Manchester, the Earl , of Derby being the head of the Liverpool centre." Up- wards of 20,000 persons have successfully passed the ex- aminations, and now hold certificates of proficiency. An attempt was made by the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Associati•at to form a class last year, but the desired success did not attend the effort. The expense of a class is about £3, and of two classes about £5. Not more than 30 persons from each class may present themselves to the surgeon- examiner, but any number can attend a class and receive instruction—mixed classes of males and females prohibited. The course of instruction consists of five lectures, and a medical gentleman in the town was liberal enough to volun- teer his services to the Young Men's Cnristian Association. My object in writing this letter is to try and form a class in Runcorn. Sufficient members could easily be obtained, but who will find the "sinews of war ?" Surely some of our philanthropic townsmen will come forward and assist in a 1 cause which has but one equal for the amount of good work it performs, an that one the Missionary Societies.—Yours , truly, T. CLWYDFRO WILLIAMS. 34, Rutland-street, Runcorn. let November, 1883.
