div.head: EXAMINET SATURDAN, NOVEMBER 10, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINET SATURDAN, NOVEMBER 10, 1883.

out of the two htmlred and eighty-nine recruits, who had reached the same point as Stephen. Nothing from this time was talked of in the hut among the recruits but this prize, and the men who were thought the likeliest to win.

Day by d.iy, as they returned from the rifle range, new men who had done well in the day were pitted against those who had been conspicuous before; but presently one man who had uot been at first conspicuously successful was found to be rising fast. The excitement was increased' when Stephen's own cap- tain, Etheredge, added a new prize to the former one._

Hotter than ever waxed the contest between some four cr five competitors who had gradually distanced all the rest. But the one nun before•mentioned who had silently crept on till he was ahead, now kept ahead, and eventually was declared the winner of both the prizes. Need it be said who that man was ?—Stephen. No winner at the antique Olympian games felt more proud than he; nor could have been more enthusiastically honoured at the close by the assembled multitude of red coats. One happy day had come at last to compensate for all he had suffered.

And then came the congratulations of the officers; Captain Etheredge the first, who shook him warmly by the hand. Then the mussetry instructor and the non-commissioned officers who had drilled him, and amongst the rest Sergeant O'Shaughnessy At the sight of him Stephen's proud humility, his elo- quently modest silence, was broken through; and while shaking hands with him he found it barely possible to keep from a hearty laugh. "Well, my boy," said the Drill Sergeant, "you see I did the job for you!' And Stephen could rf,t but leave the flattering unction in his soul undisturbed.

Our young soldier mow joined the ranks of his comparry. The next day he was warned for garrison guard, and then fulfill eel, for the first time, the duty of garrison sentry. To that succeeded regimental guard. The men composing this are very strictly inspected, and the smartest man•i,.:long them is selected as the Colonel's orderly. This is considered a great honour, and brings with it important privileges. It is amusing to see the nal of the men in the extra cleaning of their belts and general brightening up of every part of their uniform before the parade, when the business of selection is about to take place. The disengaged men— those who may be said to have dropped out of the running —will gather round to try if they guess beforehand the lucky soldier. Stephen was again to the front in the estimation of these . _
critics, but not alone. Another man was considered to stand just as good a chance. And great was the excitement among their cornrwies of the regiment as to which would be chosen.

The question was settled—by Stephen's being ordered to the front as Colonel's Orderly. While so acting his duties finished about four o'clock; and as he had no sentry duty to perform, he spent his nights quietly in bed. But to Stephen the great charm of his new post was that it broup,,lit him into continual contact with men of his own social order and education; and who mostly took pleasure in saying a few words to him—out of the usual routine—whenever he came to them at the business of his post. CHAPTER XXXIX.—GLortv IN Two AspEcTs _

Many weeks have passed since the incidents recorded in the last chapter. It is the afternoon of a day in October, but one of those extraordinary days which October oc- casionally gives when all the heat as well as all the glory of summer seems to revive. The whole camp is out enjoying the fervent warmth, the fresh a:r, and the delicious sunshine from wbfch, however, many have sought shelter wherever they can at the shady sides of the dwelling places for the sake of their games. The scene near a particular group of huts, where a larger space than usual happens to be somewhat protected from the direct sunrays, is extremely animated. Many sold e:s are scattered about; some lying on the ground engaged in cardigatnes, others playing at quoits amid frequent shouts and laughter at the hits of the missiles, a few are asleep, and one or two in corners, or wherever they could find a spot a little apart, are reading—and these are the men who will be soon rising to be non-commissioned officers, with possibly even still higher rank in the distant future.

At one part of the scene a sentinel appears and disappears at intervals on guard of a tent, a little way off. Languid is his step, and sow; heavy to-day the weapon he carries, and which he frequently rests upon the ground, to seek rest from that which so oppresses him, but again lifts, to pursue the same weary eternal track. He has one consalation. He will soon be "off duty," like those he sees enjoying them- selves all around. And so he paces, and paces, backwards and forwards, resigned to discomfort—obedient to discipline, but hating the petty routine which makes up so much of his daily life. Through this scene moves occasionally a laughter mov- ing person and figure—Biddy, a seller of cakes, brandy balls, and soldiers' money begs; and who is suspected of dealing surreptitiously in drops of whiskey in answer to a timely hint. She wears a decayed pilot's coat over her ample nether garments--a coat patched all over, in wintry weather to keep it warm, in summer time to hide its rents and stains. About her neck is a thick comforter, while her head-dress is indescribable—something between a bonnet and a wide- awake—which she makes gay in its dilapidation by a bunch of artificial flowers that she once picked up, and so admired that she cleaves to them evermore. "Brandy balls, cakes, and soldiers' money bags !" Such is her unvarying cry, but which she adapts to the occasion, and to her liking or disliking for the man or men she is moving past, by the tones of her voice—now stentorian, now dropping to a lower pitch, but by no means to the soft and low, that "excellent thing in woman" of which Shakspeare speaks; for Biddy's voice, though expressive, is rougher than the roughest of the soldiers around her. In passing Tommy Atkins, who is not one of her favourites, she stops. to bawl in his ear " Cakes, brandy balls, and soldiers' money bags," and so produces an explosion from that not very amiable person: "May the devil take you for kicking up such a row. I've played a wrong card, he's down upon me, and I've lost the trick !' "If the devil does take me," retorts Biddy, nothing loth, "he'll let me go again when I tell him what a fine catch he'll get in you!" A roar of laughter from the listening soldiers who know Biddy's ways and the force of her tongue sets Biddy off again in triumph. "Cakes, brandy balls, and soldiers' money bags !" " Oh, Biddy, darling," says languishingly another soldier. " how much loiaAer am I to sigh all day, and dream all night about your beautiful self, and you won't even give me a kiss ?" "Won't I ?'' says Biddy. " Just you try me." And again the laughter is on Biddy's side. " Cakes, brandy balls, and soldiers' money bags !" "Boys, it's no use," now joins in yet a fresh voice, "you can't touch Biddy's heart. She's keeping all her favours for the young swell." "Shall I write him a love letter for you, Biddy ?"calls out Tommy Atkins, recovering from his former failure. Im- mediate was his punishment: " Ye'd best be thinking o' the love letter that will be written on your back with the cat-o'-nine-tails," shoats Biddy, amid universal mirth; and then repeating once more her c:v, which sounded like a triumphant war-whoop,as she looked round, she moved away in search of profitable busi- ness elsewhere. "Cakes, brandy Palls, and soldiers' money bags !" Among the card players sit a couple of men playing at dominoes, one of the pair, being no other than Gentleman Jack, a recent recruit; who after enlisting into and desert- ing from half a dozen regiments in succession, has found his way here, in his constant search for Stephen, but who does not yet know if he is to be here successful, for Stephen is away on special duty. The alteration in his appearance is extraordinary. The shabby, bloated, dirty-looki-ng civilian, in his dress suit of a former day, is now a healthy-looking, robust soldier, upon whom the red coat seems to confer quite a mew dignity and splendour from the contrast. Scarcely had the sounds of Biddy's voice ceased, ' before Gentleman Jack's was heard, as Ile placed in the distance his last piece, crying, "And there's game— Domino!" He rose, stretched himself, and began to pace about, look- ing at the hands of the soldiers who were card playing, and getting now and then a rough hint to move on, which he took with a smile, and did as requested. Suddenly broke out, upon the sultry and still air, the ex- hilarating sounds of a band in the distance. " What's the music for ?" he asked the nearest soldier, who happened to be Tommy Atkins. That persenage looked as though he thought the recruit had no right to ask him questions, or if be had, that he wasn't obliged to answer, but at last said briefly and "Riot of last night spreading. out."

More troops ordered The martial music Areiv every 'minute nearer, and pre- sently the band came in view, with a body of soldiers, whose march seemed to be taught by the music so grandly did they move in unison; and who were arrayt;cl in all the glittering and gorgeous panoply of war which the sun won- derfully magnified. This was the going oat. How different might be the coming in was shortly to be illustrated in equally impres- sive fashion. "Is the young swell, your comrade spoke of, among them ?" asked Gentleman Jack, benevolently unmindful of Tommy Atkins' c‘ia/lish manner. "No. He's with them as went out late last night, and are getting rough usage, I expect." " What's he called ? " "Stephen Sham]." "C—h—a—n ? " "No. S—h—a—n? " "Has he been long here ? " "Nearly three months." "Acd lcng enough," interjected a friendly voice, "to make him a / ight down smart soldier." "And the crack shot of the regiment," joined in another rd coat. "I hate the fellow!" shouted Tommy Atkins, as if to stop these testimonials to character on behalf of the swell. The soldiers laughed; and one of them did more, 193, remarking, " He threw you in the wrestling! " "And I'll throw him yet. But I hate the fellow for his humbag—pretending to take pride in roughing it with ,the roughest; and to like the hardships we all know very Well —we have only to grin and bear." , • A murmur of applause for once followed these words ,

div.head: ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL.
div.p: ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL.
BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of " HIRELL ; on, LOVE BORN OF STRIFE," "ABEL DRAKE'S WIFE," "ISRAEL MORT, OVERMAN," &C., &C.
CHAPTER XXXVII-SERGEANT O'SHArGITNESS

Stephen had accepted his advance to another squad as a sort of intimation that fortune had not quite forgotten him ; but he found the value of her bounty considerably impaired by the conditions that accompanied it. Sergeant O'Shaughnessy was the drill-master—a bad-tem- pered man naturally—but who could be mollified and made amiable by certain little attentions, such as the price of a pint ol porter after drill, or a timely gift of something else if money ran abort. But that to him, pleasant ctitom neglected, you had bet- I ter look to yourself when the next drill time came. Oaths would fly about you in every attempt to right what he directed, and if this violence did not set you in the way he wanted, or did not want you to go or to hold yourself, he would, before he had done with you, make you a fool or a guy for the great laughter ef all the others. Stephen had heard something of this but did not believe it. It seemed too shocking, too unjust, and above all too injurious to the service, for any man, however greedy, to venture on. On the first day under O'Shaughnessy things looked so well that Stephen was pleased. He was paid special atten- tion to; his half-intentional faults quite kindly pointed out, and the grizzled, weaxle-faced old soldier quite warmed to find all he said was so carefully attended to, and so promisingly carried into effect. "Shand, you'll do," he said at the close. And Shand was so pleased that be felt it impossible to degrade the charac- ter of the pleasure—for both of them—by anything so mean as a bribe—or aught that might be taken for a bribe. Next day Stephen found a great change. He did not get on half so well, the Sergeant's directions -seemed often con- tradictory, be get bothered, and then O'Shaughnessy came down upon him in a volley of the choicest abuse that can be found".even in a drill-sergeant's vocabulary. After this he seemed to grow milder, and Stephen im- proved in consequence. While he was trying whenever he dared, even for a mo- ment, to take his eye or his thought from O'Shanghnessy to think of his behaviour, he found the latter, not content with directing him how to hold himself, used his hand somewhat roughly to carry conviction more Promptly home to his person ;—and once more he clapped his hand upon his pockets in a manner that told Stepen he was inquiricg as to their contents. _

Now as that could hardly be for the purposes of the drill, Stephen had no alternative but to conclude he was trying whether there was anything to bribe with. It must be here explained that Stephen had drawn com- fort after the loss of his money in the barrack-room, from the remembrance that he had then his bounty money still to receive. Perhaps O'Shaughnessy had learned of his loss, and was now seeking to discover whether the bounty money was in hand. At all events he heard something, possibly keys, when he tapped; and very soon afterwards he came again to Stephen, and looking him suntinizingly in the face' said, to his unutterable surprise, "Shand, you are getting on the best in the squad to-day. I shall recommend you soon to a higher squad. But I see our discipline has been a little rough to you. You do not look well." Stephen was about to answer he was perfectly well, but O'Shaughnessy took him up hastily, saying, "That'll do. I can see. Never mind thanking me. Fall

out Of course Stephen fell out, very much perplexed, but waited about. Wheh the drill was over, and the men were dispersing, the Sergeant came to him and said, "Are you going canteen wav "I am going any way," replied Stephen, beginning to feel uncomfortable. "I heard of your loss, and I thought, Well, now, what greedy rascals there are in this world!' Take care you are not caught twice. Look sharp after your bounty money. And always keep enough by you for a pint of porter for Yourself, and for a friend. So mind your bounty money !" The words about the friend were so emphasied, it was impossible to mistake their meaning So there was an anxious moment while Stephen considered what to say, for he had already received the bounty money, and expended it, partly in charges for stoppages that he had no notion he would have to pay, bat chiefly in treating the men, which he was told was an invariable custom, and who got his last sixpence. " Unfortunately, sergeant," he said, "the bounty money has been taken too gpod care of." And he explained how. " What ! All gone?" asked O'Shaughnessy, with a smile that reminded Stephen, who delighted in Chaucer's Canterbury Talee, of "The smiler with the knife under the cloak."

"I have not even left myself enough for a pint of beer; or to ask you, sergeant, as I intended, if you would allow me the honour of presenting you with a little tobacco." "AU right, my boy; good eight!" As they separated, Stephen said to himself— Pity he bad suclian ugly smile, for I think, after all, he means well enough, but has such a devil of a temper. Possibly, when he has been las Ling out at me, its because of the stupidity of half-a-dozen others, which he fears to make worse by confusing them. Ah, well, when I get away frpm him, and into a still better class, I go to fresh woods and pastures new." O'Shaughnessy at the nest drill didn't care to conceal from the men he was for once in very bad temper. Now, the consequences fell upon this unfortunate, now upon that, and Stephen NM half inc:ined to think he was to be speci- ally favoured in being the only man in the squad to escape the Sergeant's amiabilities of word and manner. But O'Shaughnessy was a consummate artist in his voca- tion. The poor wretches who were shivering un ler his treatment of their dulness and awkwardness, might have been L, omowhat comforted could they have known the truth ; that he was not even thinking of them but of the Swell; for whom he was carefully preparing—tirst, by seeming not to be doing so; and, secondly, by enhancing Stephen's anticipations of his own particular good fortune, and then

lie came to Stephen, and struck him on the back to make i his chest stand out. Then on the stomach, to make that retire in. Saluting him with such remarks as, "Can't you just manage to do one thing right? Try, you counter jumper! I am wondering what. brought you here' among soldiers. Your place is the hawkward squad of the Kildare militia. Will you keep your hands back? They are flying about like the sails of a cracked old wind-, mill."

Here he gave Stephen a smart cut with his cane first on one hand, and then on the other, causing Stephen to utter an exclamation partly of pain, partly of anger. "There' now, you have run your ugly hand against my pace stick. Now mind! If you open your mouth I'll jump down your throat, stick and all.' As it happened tbe Adjutant was near, and noticing some- thing amiss from the attitude of the two men, 1243 came up and made inquiry. The Sergeant reported the statement he had taken care to prepare beforehand in case of need (knowing this kind of thing was not permitted), that Stephen had thrown his hand against the pace stick, Stephen was about to speak, but was stopped by the Ser- geant's " Silence ! No talking in the ranks." The Adjutant pretty well understood O'Shaughnessy's character; but he was found useful in drilling the rough recruits, so left very much to take his own way. The drill proceeded, the Adjutant looking on apparently quite satis- fied with O'Shaughnessy's explanation; and Stephen for- getting everything but the presence of the Adjutant, held himself—and moved—so weli in all the exercises, that as the drill ended, the Adjutant addressing Stephen, said, rather severely— " Whatever you may think, I can see you have had a good drill-master in Sergeant O'Shaughnessy ;" and saying no more he went away. . .

The very next morning be cinsed Stephen to be removed from the Sergeant's tender mercies, and advanced to a higher class, which entitled him to receive his rifle. CHAPTER XXXVII.I.—TRE WINNER OF THE PRIZE.

To have escaped the mercenary and brutal tyranny of O'Shaughnessy, and at the same time to have risen a very decided step in his drill were facts pleasant to reflect on. But even more full of hope and promise did the Adjutant's kindly, but wise interference seem to Stephen. He began from this moment to enter with zest into his duties, which primarily consisted of mastering the bayonet and firing exercises. These he accomplished in an un- usually short period; when on the recommendation of Ser- geant-Major Cross, who had kept his eye on Stephen all along, he, was moved on to the first, or final drilling-class. But taught by painful experience to expect some reverse after every success, he disciplined his mind, while others were disciplining the body; and kept himself prepared for disagreeables, sometimes wondering what they would be. Cooking was one of them. But he managed to get through without actual disgrace. But the worse deep he had to plunge into, the greatest shock to his taste, the most revolting to his sense of per- sonal dignity, was the coal carrying. Imagine a number of men with boxes beside a great heap of coal that has been shot down, for them to dispose of. Black grimy figures, and faces smeared with the coal dust, and sweat from the labour, carrying the loaded baskets to varying distances, amounting at times to as much as a quarter of a mile, and this continued fora considerable time.

It was not simply that Stephen thought how easily there might be contrivances found to lessen alike the labour and the foulness of the occupation but he wondered how the authorities could bear to see the practical standing of the soldier as an important member of the Commonwealth so lowered. To put an ideal flag of glory into one hand, and an actual coal box into the other in which to drag coals about hour after hour, struck him as a ludicrous, but also a painful and degrading inconsistency. However, he bent his b ick to that burden as well as to all the others, and with it accomplished a still Larder task, he held his tongue the while. The last steps of his drill were now begun. Company skirmishing; battalion drill ; the recruits course of mul- ketry ; the eight day position drill; and then the firing in large numbers. , _ While practice in these matters were going on \au inter- eating incident occurred. - The Musketry Inspector made it known that he would give a valuable prize to the best shot
of the "grumbler," as Tommy Atkins was called by his comrades.
"But who is he? Where did he come from ?" enquired Cientletnan Jack.

" Nohody knows," said Tommy's antagonist at cards. "Ay, and you may take your davit he had good reasens why nobody should know !'' retorted Tommy. "I'll bet," said the previous speaker. " he -never did a hard day's work afore he cime here. Why his hands were as white and delicate as a woman's."

" l'in sick of the swell, said Tommy Atkins, as he threw down the cards in his hand with a gesture implying he was equally sick of them, and, indeed, he had lost the game. "Let Jack, the recruit, give us a scng to take the taste of the swell out of our mouths."

Tommy had again succeeded in pleasing the auditory ; there was a general cry Of "Hear, bear, hear.' But before Gentlemin Jack could begin, a soldier came running in hot haste, bathed with sweat, who shouted out,

"News, boys! The riot is over. There has been a bloody fight—many of our lads badly hurt. A lot of 'em are just here. We must all lend a-hand. They are in a hawful plight." All the soldiers bounded instantly to their feet, and watched in dead silence the approach of their troops that had been announced, and ainoeg shom Gentleman Jack hoped to find Stephen.
(To be continued.)
MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT ST. HELENS.
SUSPECTED FOUL PLAY.

A great deal of excitement was caused at That° Heath on Senday afternoon by the announcement that the dead body of a man had been found in the disused stone delf near the railway station. 'I his delf is on private property, and lies just to the left of the road leading past the station. As the property on which it is situated is very inade- quately fenced, and is intersected by several footpaths con- tinually used by the people of the neighbourhood and others as " short cuts" in various directions, the dell has often been regarded as a source of danger. On Sunday afternoon a young man named Lewis was passing the deli when, on looking down, he saw the body of a maa lying at the bottom, having apparently fallen down at a point where the side is almost perpendicular and deepest. He at once gave information to Police-Sergeant Montgomery, who lives a short distance away, and that officer caused the body to be removed to the British Lion public-house, where it was identified as being that of Robert Davies, a collier, who had lodged at 43, Elephant-lane. On Monday afternoon an inquest was held by Mr. Barker, county coroner.—The brother of the deceased,a young man named Joseph Davies, was called, and spoke to having identified the body as that of his brother. Deceased was 26 years of age, and was steady and in good health, not being subject to tits or any- thing of that kind.—Thomas Williams, with whom the de- ceased had lodged, was also called.. He said deceased left the house at twenty minutes to eight on Saturday night to catch the quarter to eight train for St. Helens. Having only five minutes to get to the station, he commenced running as soon as he got out of the house. He was perfectly sober when he went out, and he knew the road to the station well, having often gone over it before. Witness had never known the deceased to take the road past the delf before. In answer to the ceroner, witness said he was of opinion that deceased had been watched from St. Helens, and then subjected to foul play. When he left home he had 245. in his possession and a silver watch guard, but only three half-pence was found upon him when dis- covered lying in the delf. Witness and his wife had, on Saturday night, sat up till a few minutes past 12 waiting for deceased's return, but at length cime to the conclusion that he had stayed at his brother's, and went to bed. He had scarcely got into bed when he heard a knock at the door, and thinking it was deceased he went down to let him in. Before opening the door, however, he called out de- ceased's name, and asked if it were him at the door, but no answer was returned. Witness therefore set down y the fire a few minutes, and at length as there was no further knock went to bed again. He did net know of any quarrel that deceased had with anybedy.—A youth, named James Lewis, then spoke to having first seen the body lying in the deli, and to having given information to the police.--4n answer to the Coroner, Sergeant Montgomery said he had caused inquiries to be made, but could not hear of defen- dant's having been in St. Helens on Saturday night. The station master also said he had not seen deceased there on Saturday night, but the train for St. Helens did not go till after eight o'clock, and not at a quarter to eight.—Sergeant Montgomery then spoke as to the state of the body when first found. The skull was completely fractured, one side being crushed in, and the neck apparently broken. There were found three half-pence la his pockets, some private letters and one or two other articles, one of which was a stud-case which the witness Williams said deceased had not possessed when he left home on Saturday night. There was no watch-guard in his pocket, nor was either the watch-guard or any money lying about where deceased had fallen. His clothes were but- toned, and did not seem to have been disarranged by a struggle. On the top of the deli, at the place from whence deceased had fallen, there were no marks of a struggle dis- covered, but if there had been marks they might have been obliterated by the large number of people who gathered at the spot on its being known that the body had been dis- covered.—Tha Coroner said the delf seemed be be a very dangerous place.—A Juryman said it was no good to anyone and ought to be filled up.—The Coroner: Filling it up will be too much expense, I surpese, but it is a very dangerous place—ln addressing the jury the Coroner said the death was a shocking and mysterieus one. It might be that the unfortunate man had simply fallen down the parapet in his attempt to take a short cut to St. Helens, and if it had not been for the difficulty as to what had become of his money he would have been much inclined to come to that con- clusion. It was really a mysterious affair, and he thought considering the whole facts it would be better to return an open verdict. It would then be left to the police to take proceedings against anybody if they could find any clue as to its having been the result of foul play.—An open verdict was consequently returned, and the jury also unanimously agreed that there should be a presentment to the owners of the delf to the effect that it should beeither properly fenced in or filled up for the protection of the public. After the inquest the body was removed to the house at which deceased had lodged. There his clothes were again searched, and a sovereign was foued hr inc of the pockets. As the fact that no money had been found on the person of deceased was what raised suspicions as to the mode of his death, there can noel be little doubt of its being accidental.

div.head: SF- HELENS COUNTY COURT.. WEDNEMAY.—Before Mr T. P. Thompson, judge.
div.p: SF- HELENS COUNTY COURT.. WEDNEMAY.—Before Mr T. P. Thompson, judge.

Mr. Husband, solicitor, who appeared on behalf of the Haiewood Brewery Company, asked that an order be made against Michael Ryan, a pensioner, belonging to Widnes, for the payment of £45 odd. The case, it seemed, had come down from the High Court, and the debt, which was for beer and rent, bad been contracted while the defendant was landlord of the Angel Inn, Runcorn. He at present worked at a Widnes caustic works, and also received a pen- Sian of Is 2d a day, and was conductor of a brass band at Widnes.—Mrs. Ryan said her husband was an invalid, and quite unable to work. He had nothing to do with any band, his only source of income being his pension. He could not possibly pay more than 25 per month.—Mr. Husband cha- racterised this offer as absurd; defendant ought to pay LI a month.—His Honour ordered the debt to be paid by in- stalments of 49 per month, with leave for the plaintiffs to apply for increased order if they thought fit.

HEAVY CLAIM BY A WIDNES WORKMAN. Thomas Carroll, a labourer, living at 4, Pool-street, Widnes, made a &altar for £2OO, as damages for bodily injuries sustained from the Widnes Colliery Cornpany.—A jury was em- pannelled.—Mr. Petersip Widifs, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pickford, barrister, Liverpool, for the defendants.— In opening the case, Mr. Peters slid he ought to explain that although the Widnes Colliery Company were the nominal defendants in this case, he was able to say, from his own knowledge, that the Employers' Liability Assurance Corporation of Liverpool had the conduct of the case 'entirely in their hands. From his further statement it ap- peared that the plaintiff, at the time of the accident, had been engaged as a labourer by the defendants at the Widnes foundry. On the morning of the day of the accident he was ordered by hisforeman, a man named Nixon, to go and unload "burner fronts," which are big pieces of iron weighing something like 15 or 16 hundredweights. This" burner front" was lying on a lurry placed in position near to the jib of a crane by which it had to be unloaded. In the act of unloading, however, the crane broke, and tippling over struck the defendant and inflicted serious injuries. His head was cut open, three of his ribs were broken, and he re- ceived other internal injuries. One of his legs were broken in several places, and his whole body severely crushed. The accident happened on the 2nd April, and since that time he had been completely laid up. He had been at death's door, and it was very doubtful whether he would again recover. At any rate the medical evidence would show that the in- jured leg would continue to be two inches shorter than the other, and that the plaintiff, who was but a young man, would be permanently maimed.—Dr. O'Keeffe was one of the witnesses for the plaintiff, and said that it would pro- bably be twelve months before plaintiff would be able to use his leg if it went on favourably.—For the defence Mr. Pickford called the foreman, William Nixon, who stated the lurry was nine feet further away from the crane than it ought to have been. Instead of plaintiff going to witness and asking for a horse to lime the lurry nearer he fastened the chain to it, and when the handles were turned, instead of the casting moving the jib of the crane heeled over and fell on plaintiff. • It was further contended that the wood was not rotten, but that the jerk snapped the sleepers.— In a lengthy summing up of the evidence his Honour said any man of ordinary sense would have known he was trying to lift the casting at a disadvantage when he had it nine feet out of plumb of the chain. If the jury thought the injury was brought about by the impro- per use of the crane by Carroll, who was the." boss " of the gang of labourers, then defendants were entitled to the ver- dict. But, on the other hand, if they thought Carroll did not bring it about by such improper use, and that there were faults in the wood which might haVe been discovered by reasonable examination, they would find a verdict for the plaintiff.—The jury retired, and after ten minutes ab- sence returned into Court with a verdict for the defendants.

IMPORTANT ACTION UNDER THE
EMPLOYERS' A.CT AT WARRINGTON.

DEFECTIVE MACHINERY AND ITS RESULTS. Oa Thursday, at the Warrington County Court, before W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Esq., judge, and a special jury, an action was heard in which the plaintiff, William Burgess, of 123, Knutsford-road, Warrington sawyer, claimed £250 from R. A. Naylor, of Howley Warrington, Mills, Warrington, timber merchant, as damages for personal injuries sus- tained whilst in the employ of the defendant, on the Bth June last, and that such accident was caused by the defec- tive condition of the saw and fence at the bench where he was engaged in cutting timber at the time of such accident. The action was under the Employers' Liability Act, and excited some interest.—Mr. Hamilton, barrister, Manchester (instructed by Robert Davies and Co.), appeared for plain- tiff, and Mr. Sutton, barrister, Manchester (instructed by Mr. W.. 11. Brook), for defendant. •

Mr. Hamilton opened the case by explaining the sections of the Act which related to the matter before the Court, and proceeded to state that plaintiff for a considerable time had worked as a sawyer, and was enc.:aged some time ago by the defendant's firm. He left them, but returned in March last and took charge of a circular saw machine on the defendant's premises. That portion of the machinery before the Court (produced) represented the part of the machine which was behind the saw. Now the duty of the plaintiff was this. He had to cut into small pieces baulks of timber and planks by means of the circular saw, and he had to attach the piece of wood to be cut to the drag (the drag being a piece of bent iron) on the timber attached to the pulley at the other end, which would draw the baulk of timber to the sew. Having done that he was at liberty, the baulk of timber having passed to the saw, merely to watch the mac!linery. When the baulk of timber was got near to the saw he had to sloop down and throw off the drag motion, which at once put the timber further through the saw, and having taken off the drag which had been propel- ling the timber he placed his left hand upon the baulk of timber at the side and pushed it through, so as to cut the saw through the whole length of the timber. That was the nature of plaintiff's work On resuming his employ- ment with defendant, plaintiff at once pointed out to the foreman and to the manager of the works that there was a very great defect in the piece of machinery, that ' defect being this. The upright board or fence was joined to two long screws called worms, and which passed through the scope at the back. These two worms were joined to the fence by means of bolts, but the fence, when the machine was properly constructed, worked upon a swivel through two lugs. The machine in question, however, had a serious defect in having only only one lug instead of two aud that in itself rendered it more difficult to keep the fence in a perfectly steady position. But then they submitted that in addition to such a defect in the fence, there was also at the time the accident happened a defect in the worm, which had been remedied since the occurrence. Then the third fault was, that at one end a bolt was put through which came out close to the nearest part of the fence, and that at the time of the accident there was a bolt, but not the same as it was at present. It was of a smaller size, and less adapted to keep the fence upright in its proper position. He had now described the nature of the rhachine that plaintiff was working. The defects had been repeatedly pointed out by the plaintiff, before the accident happened, to the manager and foreman, but whom he supposed did not find it a convenient- season to attend to them, as they told plaintiff to continue his work until they were slack enough to do the repairs. The circular saw was not as he would have supposed if it had not been ex- plained to him, a perfectly hard and unbending piece of metal; it was loose centred, The outside of the saw was perfectly steady, but the inner part nearer the middle was beaten in like a saucer .when the circular saw was in motion, the rim outside mast get heated, and the loose centre was to allow for the expansion of the outside rim, and then the machine worked truly. That was the reason they were made loose centred. there was a time when it could be found out that a saw was too loose centred, and in that case 4 required to be taken out and hammered so that it could have a right degree of looseness in the centre. If not the saw, instead of working straight, would lean one side or the other according to where the defect was, and re- quired a good deal more pressure upon the weight which was being sawn to keep it straight against the fence. Before ( the accident happened plaintiff had called attention to the I state of the saw with which he was set to work. On one occasion he drew the manager's attention to it and told him he could not work with a saw so loose in the centre as it was. Upon that two other men were called in, who tried their hands at packing the saw, but they failed in working the machine satisfactorily. Thereupon the foreman of the works, Mr. Hunt, ordered plaintiff to take out the loose centre saw and put in another. This was done, and the new work went or for some time until the manager found that the saw was a thick one, and thick saws were objected to by masters because more timber was wasted thereby. The manager said, "Put the old saw in again." There .was some demur at this, but ultimately the old saw was put in with the defects described. There were defects in the fence, worm, and bolt, and that was the state of affairs at the time of the accident. The accident happened in this way. Plain- tiff was guiding the wood along with his left hand, and bent down to throw off the drag motion. As he was doing that he had exercised some side pressure upon the baulk of timber. Partly owing to the saw being loose centred and not working truly, the fence, instead of being stationary, tilted up, and instead of the hand being down by the side of the timber was thrown up towards the top side, and in that way was taken into the saw and three of his fingers cut off. Plaintiff claimed compensation ac- cordingly. As to the extent the damages should be as- sessed, the Act stated that compensation should no given to ' workmen not exceeding the average earnings for three years of workmen engaged in the same class of employment as the injured man, the average being taken three years next before the accident. This man and others working in his capacity three years prior to the accident were earning £250 for the three years. Mr. Hamilton pointed out that through the loss of three fingers plaintiff would be utterly incapable of following the same class of work again. The following evidence was then adduced : —The plaintiff on being called, said : I have been a sawyer 10 years. Before September, 1881, I was in defendant's employ, and left him to go into that of the Cheshire Linea Committee. I went back to the defendant's in March of this year. When I re- turned to the defendant's service I was put to mind a circular saw. It was my duty as sawyer to attach the baulk to the
drag and then fix the position of the fence according to the thickness we want to cut the boards. I have then to set the

drag in motion. When the timber has gone past a roller I have to put my left hand up to steady it, and with the other hand put the drag out of motion. The rest of the baulk then requires pushing with a stick with the rigbt hand. When I went back into the defendant's employ in March I noticed defects in the fence. The worm on the right hand aide was worn, and had too much play, while the screw was hard worn in the threads. The lug was broken. I noticed the condition of the bolt near the

lug, and its threads were broken. The result of the long screw being hard worn was that the fence had of an inch play. The bolt only held on by one side instead of both, and it was not possible to fix the fence in a perfectly perpendicular position in con- sequence. The kind of work I was doing on the day of the accident required the fence to be perfectly upright. I could put the fence upright, but it would not remain firm owing to the screw being worn. I called the attention of Thomas Hunt, the foreman, to the condition of the fence on the 2nd April. He said, "Davies has worked it in that condition, and you must do the same, or we shall get someone else." I also called his attention to the condition of the saw, that it was too slack in the centre, and would not work right. He complained of my work, and I told him I could not make the saw work in the condition it was in. Two other sawyers in the employ of the defendant were then brought to the machine, and they tried to work it, but were not able to marage it satisfaOtorily. While I was try- ing it with these, men the manager (Shakeshaft) came past, and he asked me what was the matter with the aaw, and I said it was too slack in the centre and would not work properly. He told me to take the saw oat and take it to :he sharpening shop. After that I used a smaller saw Of the same guage, and then a thicker one. While I was working with the thicker saw, Mr. Shakeshaft came to me and said it took too much timber off, and he told me to put in the slack centred one. I did not obey his order but put in another one and went on working until about the sth of May, when Shakeshaft came te me and said that the fence was not right. He told me to fetch a screwdriver, and , he unscrewed the screw that divides the block of wood and the plate of iron. He told me to get a chip, and he put it between the block of wood and the plate of iron to bring it so that the fence would be upright. It had leaned back- wards before then. At that time I called his attention. to the condition of the fence, getting hold of it, and shaking it to show its shaky condition. He said "It is all right, Burgess, go on to your work." I next put in the loose centred saw about a week after' to do some other work that cottld only be done by that. I was working on the machine on the Bth June with the loose centred saw. Hunt came to me and said, "I want you to do this order "—a 12 plank, 15 feet ion!, 14 to 15 inches in. depth, and 3 inches thick, to cut into one-inch boards. I had instructions to use the loose centred saw for that particular order. He told ins to put the saw in, and get the order out quick, as the cart was waiting for it. The SAW did not work right, and I could not make it work right; it was too slack. In order to cut straight I had to put a pressure'against the plank with the left hand. With difficulty I sawed nine of these planks. While I was doing so I tried to make the saw w3rk true, by pulling the pack- logs out dnd repacking it. I also stoned" the teeth of the'saw to make them all level. While I was sawing the tenth plank I put the drag in motion, and when it had passed the roller I had my left hand on the plank, and I found that I had to put a deal of pressure against the plank to hold it up, because the drag was pulling towar& me, and the SAW was running from inc because it was too slack. I was putting the drag out of motion, bending down and still pressing the plank, when the4ence gave way, throwing my left hand right on to the saw. My second, , third, and fourth fingers of my left band were thereby cut ' off. The fence would not have given way if tke defects I pointed out had net existed. Both Hunt and Shake- shaft knew of the defects, and the latter had control over the machinery In the busiaess, and it was his duty to see that the machinery was in proper condition. After the ac- cident I was taken to the Infirmary, from which place I re- ceived.medical attentiop for fonr , months. I am not as capable now,. of. . managing. i-simiir achine the one . I was looking after. I cannot do the same work in consequence of losing my fingers.

I have since the accident tried to get employment, but waif refused owing to my three fingers being off. I Went to the defendant's yard on the 2nd July, with Mr. Jones, a fitter, and the fence was not in its place. I went for the saw to the defendant's fitters' shop, and the fitter, as soon as he 2aer us, put out his light. There has been an alteration in the fence since the accident; a new screw has been put through the riglit hand lug in place of the old one, that was veto out; a new washer has been put On to Cie screw attached to the worm.—Cross-sxamined by Mr. Sutton : The teeth are so placed that they come within 3-8:h of an inch from the fence. The saw is always in the saroe position after being fixed. It was my duty a° sawyer to fix the fence according to the thickness of a°3 boards wanted. If the fence is not true I adjust it by no" screwing some screws at the back and screwing it up again' If we have to do fine work we have to use a slack-centred saw, or if not a slick-centred one we must use a thicket one, which wastes more timber. I did this work, but the saws were out of order. There are -lu4 holes to th,Le bench, but there are tie plugs, and I did nut use any. .11 working the machine I have to put my right liana on the front of the timber and follow the timber as the drag drags it along. The drag carries the piece of timber Pot the roller, when ais my duty to take the drag off. Whet' with my right hand I took hold of the bar that stops the motion of the timber my face was not turntd away from the saw. It is not the custom of a careful siwyer to stop th! drag with his left band. Hunt was standing near at tell time of the accident, and I went to him immediately, an' then to the Infirmary. I did not then look at the fence, be I saw it give way. The top teeth of the saw were about ail inch or two above the timber. In " stoning " the sari h would be made duller, but it would not thereby require rne to put more presgare on the timber with my hand. It 13 Mr. Brown's duty to repair the machinery at 'the defell- dant's works. Mr. Brown has never asked me how the machine was working, and I never told him it wag. first class. I never pointed out the specific defects I hay' mentioned to-day to Mr. Hunt, but I believe I mentioned something of the screws to Mr. Shakeshaft on the sth Mai' —Re-examined by Mr. Hamilton: I had complained of more than one saw. It is not the practice now to use ploOt Hunt, Brown, and myself had to obey the manager P orders. I had also to obey Hunt's orders, but I think Bro Val has not.

John Joseph Watson, Brick-street, said he was a filecutter and a 'nob-stick" sawyer. (Laughter.) He was working at the defenda.it's at the time of the accident, but wasnonc out of employment. He saw the plaintiff show Shakeshaft the saw and shake it, and Shakeshaft said it was all right. Thomas Quinn. labourer, Old-road, Latchford, said he via° working for the defendants at the time the accident deur red.. Before the accident he heard the plaintiff say ttO Hunt that the saw was not fir to work, that it was too slaelc in the centre. Hunt cold plaintiff to get on with his work. as the cart was waiting. Plaintiff said he could not.de with that saw. Witness 54,W the accident. The fence "gal'e way, and the plaintiff's left hand was dragged on to the saw.

Joseph Davies, John-street, Northwich, said he was a sawyer. He had worked at the bench where the defendant worked. The screws and worm were very much worn, tbno allowing 3 Bths of an inch or more. He had frequentlY called the attention of Hunt and Shakeshaft to the Wsra screw and worm, and to the broken lug. He told them 00 it was in a dangerous condition. He had anticipateciwnst had happened to the plaintiff. He had had 18 or 19"Yss° experience as a sawyer. It was usu -1 to use a saw after it was "stoned" down, and there was no more risk in'doig so than when it was otherwise.

George t•ixamith, blacksmith, Howley-lane, said he 1 "backing up" for the plaintiff until the end of May, all he had also backed up for Davies. He had heard the cool: plaints made to Hunt and Shakeshaft. A man parte° Clarke worked at the machine A fortnight before the pla tiff went there, and witness had heard Clarke complaw' to Hunt and Shakesbaft reipecting the condition of the fence.

Edward Jones, fitter, Warrington, said he knew the fencer and he believed it was 15 or 20 years old. The plugs wer° never used now as they could get packing broader thaa tba plugs.—Cross-examined by Mr. Sutton: He could not re bow the accident could have taken place unless the mathote gave way in the manner he had described, or unless 13,2 placed his hand on the top of the timber. There was ow/ one bolt to hold the fence, the place at one end of the ma" chine where another bolt ought to be was broken off. As it was now half-past five, and there were still allullY ber of witnesses to be heard, the case was adjourned to to; day. One of the juryruen protested against the adjourn hearing being ran a Saturday, as it was inconvenient to al the jury. He was, he said, only what they might call. 16_ working man, and he had been brought there at great Or convenience to himself, and he thought for Saturday to ale° be taken away from him, when it was his busiest day! The Judge here interrupted, saying he was sorry that be could not avoid it. The counsel could net be present 00 any other day as they had to attend the Liverpoel Assize°' —The case was then adjourned toto-day (Saturday).

A CHILD FATALLY_ BURNT AT PRESCOT. On Saturday, an inquest was held at the Royal Oalff, Prescot, by F. Smith, Esq., coroner, touching the death 0' Adam Woods, who, as mentioned in our last, was frightfolli, burnt on Thursday last, and after enduring great agorni diet the next morning.—The first witness called was Bridge.: Woods, who deposed: I am the wife of John Woods,: an' am the mother of the deceased child. I live in Houghton" street. About 10 minutes to 12 on Thursday Morning / went out to Mrs. Leggett's shop. Before going I sent de ceased to a neighbour's house, expecting to return home air self before hirn. I was returning, but had not reached boron when I learnt that the child had been burnt. My husband, went for Dr. Green, who arrived in a very short time, ano, Dr. Hall came in the afternoon. The child died aht,nt o'clock the following day.—The Coroner: You don't how he got burnt ?—Witness: No, sir.—A Juror: How long were you out ?—Witness: Not more than 10 miuutes.*--10W far had von to go? To the middle of Houghton-street! The Coroner: You expected to get back before the child ?'":J Witness: Yes, sir.—The Corow-r : Was your husbali', working at home ?—Witness: Not then, sir.—The Coroneri I Do you think that was a proper thing to do ?—WitnesS; expected my husband, who had gone for some work to rdr; Beasley's, would have returned home before the Juror: Had the child been given to play with fire ?-7--W",„ ,- ness : Yes, if he could have got near the fire he woula ; was very fond of playing with fire.—The Coroner: Wbn'. kind of dress did the child wear it the time P—Witneae: Velveteen.—The Coroner: What was he doing ?—Witnes' Reaching a pot ito out of the pin which was on the fire! The Coroner: Did he tell you that ?—Witriess: Yes, he told me in the afternoon.—Mary Hute said: I live at 23, Houghton-street. OnTWIT; day about ten minutes to twelve I saw the 41)4: in the street. Its clothes were on fire, and I ran with roi_ shawl to put round it. A gentleman came up at the filo° and said give me the child. 1e wrapt the child in his colt which put out the flames. I then cut away its dress, t.,„°° off its clothes, and look the child to its home..." /I Coroner: Was there anybody is the house when yen g° there ?—Witness, No, •sir. Mrs. Sixsmith, a neighbstu.: Went with me. I then wont home and did not return 0, more. By this time there were many people in the house' —The Coroner: What clothes was the child wearing ?"; Witness: Velveteen.—The Coroner: Did you notice whethe: the child had a fork or anything in its, hand 7—Witnes3 : think it had, but could not be certain.—A Juror: Hove 100 g were you there altogether ?—Witness : About ten minute' Mr. Wood, the child's father, had gone by five minutes Prro vious.—The Coroner: Did you see the child go home beiclrot it was burnt ?—Witness : No, sir, it had been out before 0, another child. I met the father coming from Mr. Beastei and told him that his child had got very badly bunat, I did not think it wonld get better.—Mary Thompson 11: called as the next witness, and gave similar evidence.-1 Coroner,lll addressing the jury, said it had been clear made out that the cause of -death was purely acciden'al.':o The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," tm,„ for( min of the jury (Mr. Pratt) remarking that no 1310'; could in any way be attee.' ed to Mrs. Wood, the mother co. the deceased

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 1883.

, TRIAL iron MURDER. —On Thursday, at Nottingham Assizes, George Spurr, 33, collier, was charged with having murdered Miss Hannah Hunt, with whom he cohabited at Mansfield. On Sunday afternoon, September 2nd, the pri- soner took a gun and, it was alleged, shot Hunt in tne left arm. She died on the following Tuesday from the shock and loss of blood. A verdict of manslaughter was returned, and the prisoner was returned, and the prisoner Wll.B sen- tenced to 20 years' penal servitude. THE CHARGE AGAINST A Doc ron.—At the Hammersmith Police Court, on uesday, Mrs. Julian Deam Hardie, of , Goldhawk-road, Shepherd's Bush, married, was charged with ' being concerned with the late Dr. Haffenden in procuring abortion. The only witness examined was Mrs. Clark, a neighbourlof the prisoner, who deposed to Dr. II iffenden hav- ing attended the prisoner and written a prescription. The prisoner had told witness she expected to have a miscarriage. The magistrate committed the prisoner for trial, accepting bail as before. QUARTERLY MEETING OF EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLARS. —A quarterly meeting of the members of the Hope of Earles- town Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. There was a full attend- ance, and Brother H. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. After the routine business two members were "restored," and several candidates proposed. Brother John Warburton, L.D., read circulars from the Grand Lodge Executive con- taining valuable suggestions for the successful working of the lodge. The reports of the officers for the past quarter were then given, that of the W.S. (Brother E. Newman) stating that the number of members in good standing at the end of the previous quarter was 63, initiated last quarter 38, total 101. Of these 11 had been suspended or withdrawn, leaving a tot s4l of 90 good members, or an increase of 23. He thought that fact should encourage them to go on striving for the right, and continue the good work they were engaged upon. The report alluded to the meetings, coffee suppers, dm, held during the quarter. and in conclusion hoped by God's hell) the members would all overcome the great temptation they would be subjected to during the forthcoming festive season of Christmastide. The Juvenile Temple was in an encouraging position, the number of members at present being 38, an increase of 13 over the previous quarter. The financial reports were given by Bro. John Taylor, W.F.S., and Bro. George Warburton, W. Treasurer. They showed a good balance in hand after a quarter's heavy expenditure. All the reports were adopted, after which the officers for the ensuing quarter were installed as follows, by Bro. John Warburton, L.D., assisted by Bro. George Clarke, D.M. : Bro. John Taylor W.C.T.; Sister P. Walker, W.V.T.; Bro. E. Newman, W.gec.; Sister J. E. Warburton, W.F.Sec..; Bro. George Warburton, W.Treaa.; Bro. J. Torrance, W. Chaplain; Bro. Joseph James, W.M.; Sister J. Clarke, W.A. Sec.; Bro. John Bassett, W.D.M. ; Bro. H. Warburton, P.W.C.T.; Bro. George Warburton, sen., Bro. John Taylor, Sister Harriman, and Sister Walker were appointed as sick committee; Bro. George Warburton, jun., Bro. J. Gee, and Bro. E. Newman were elected absentee visitors committee ; and Bro. George Clarke and Bre. John Taylor were ap- pointed as a finance committee. One or two other items of lodge business were considered, and the meeting finished about 9-50. The backs and goal-keeper repelled the attack, but Bimm again sent in a splendid shot, by which Duabury headed the leather straight in the goal. Jenkinson caught it and threw it back, but another determined assault was made on the home goal. During the repeated scrlinmages which ensued in close proxi- mity to the Golborne uprights tne spectators literally crowded round them. The visitors continued to have the best of the game, and throughout the second half made one continual attack on the home goal. The excitement greatly increased as time drew to a close, the capital play of the Earlestonians and the god defence of the Golbornites being loudly cheered by their respective supporters. A few minutes before time a long :crimmage ensued in front of the Golborne goal, and two ot tne home players seized Dagnall and threw him to the ground. A scasne of the wildest excitement kllowed. The spectators rushed all over the field, and it seemed exceedingly likely that a free fight would take place. Strong words were spoken, and menacing threats were used; but the EarlesVcvn captain wisely drew his men from the ground, which they left amid the hissing of the home suppor- tete. The Earlestown spectators and players responded with hearty cheers and the match thus elosed, with the score at one goal to none in favour of Eariestown". RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Qua Rev. Canon Barclay. Present: The Rev. Father Fenneay, Messrs. J. Simpson, T. Norman, J. Prit- chard, R. Lea, P. Briscoe, F. Rigby (clerk). TIE BOARD AND TILE RIM W. Puusroer. After the minntes of the last meeting had been read, the question of the Rev. W. Preston's tenancy of Mill Brow school arose, arid, at the wish of the Chairman, the CLERK read the various agreements that had been made. On the 4th March, ISSO, the Clerk wrote to Mr. Preston informing him that the Beaed were willing to allow him the use of the school on Sundays at a rent of 305. per quarter, which had to be prepai.d, the caretaker to be paid by Mr. Preston for her extra labour. Subsequently Mr. Preston applied for the use of the class-room in which to hold a cottage meet- ing one night during the week ; and the Clerk replied that the Board agreed to do so on his agreeing to pay an annual rent of 153, and to compensate the caretaker for the extra labour which she would of necessity incur.—The CHAIR- MAN : That makes it very clear that the caretaker had to be paid extra remuneration by Mr. Preston.—The CLERK said Mr. Preston undertook not to use the school- room or the furniture on week days, and both the school-room and furniture had been used on week days. The Board had not been asked for the use of the large room on week days.—Mr. PRITCHARD said they had really deviated from the Board's arrangement. He thought they had acted somewhat indiscreetly in introdu- cing a strange person to do their cleaning and ignoring the Board's keeper.—Mr. LEA seid they did net want to bring the caretaker to clean after tea meetings.—The CLERK: But that is a condition of the letting. Mr. PRITCHARD con- sidered they had scarcely dealt fairly with the Board.—Mr. LEA said they certainly ought to have asked the Board to remove from the class-room into the larger room. This was no excuse for them in that respect.—The CLERK read the letter he had forwarded to Mr. Preston at the conclusion of last meeting. •After referring to matters then reported, it intimated that it would be necessary to terminate the tenancy unless the rent was paid with due regularity. Mr. Preston had replied as follows Trinity Parsonage. October 3J, 1283. —Mr and Gentlemen,— It has ctused me much pain that one of your members should tax me with a want of courtesy towards you. Nothing could be farther from my intention since I entertain a deep respect for you- honmarable body. The letter referring to the penny bank came as I was on the eve of going abroad. We regarded it as a license to opeu it the extra rent were paid, and intend- ing to pay we opened, and have been in operation tor some time which fact might have demonstrated that we were satis- fied with your terms. As to unpunctuatity in paying the rent, it is not the first time by many I have been behindhaad ; not from indifference but because I cannot always get in subscrip- tions in time. lam resp9nsible for much in this parish, and have been as much as £33 out of pocket. I now advance the amount doe, lie 8,/, in the hope I may have it repaid me some day. As to damage te eiteprope, ty I have inve,tigated the charge and And it has u u ndation whatever. We will be glad if some of your members will look in unawares at the services or bank and they will see that damage is net possible while we have the school in charge. lam satisfied that if my workers did any damage, they would be the first to reptir It. —I am. yours faithfully, Wm. PRESTON. —The CHAIRMAN: He accepts our terms.—The Cueng : Now he does. The CHAIRMAN: Ha did virtually by using the school for a bank. Tne beet assurance is paying the money.—Mr. SIMPSON : The payment of our rent must not be dependent upon Mr. Preston getting in his subscriptions.— The CHAIRMAN: No, no. That is merely an apology for delay.—The CLARE explained that when the desks were patin the classroom they were screwed down; but at the request of the Rev. W. Preston they were loosened. That gentleman promised to make good any defect which might aeise. One of the desks was now broken, and the difficulty would be to get a new one. Miss Wilton reported that she and the pupik teechers had to remove nine or a dozen heavy desks nearly every Monday muening.—The CHAIR- MAN: Mr. Preston says the young men more them to their proper places.—The CLEsti said he thought there would be a conflict of evidence, and be had asked Miss Wilton to write her report.—lt was poimted out that two locks and two keys had been broken, bat Mr. Liu said the young men denied breakibg the key on more thaakne occasion wken they got it repaired, and totally denied breaking the Jocks.—After some further discussion it was decided that the clerk should write and inform Mr. Preston that it was quite clear that dantage had been done to the furniture of the Board, and that the Board would expect Mr. Preston to make good all damage in the future, and that if the Association could not in future work amicably with the Board's representatives it would be necessaay to terminate the tenancy.—The CHAIRMAN That is a straight tip anyhow.—Mr. NORMAN was sure tke Board did not want to do anything which would hinder the young men from doing good at that end of the town if it was possible for them to do it. He should be the last man to do it at any rate.

Mr. BOWYER reported that returns from the public elemen- tary school for October, 1833, certified Government accom- modation,_2,7l6 ; total number on the rolls, 3,002; number on the Tolls corresponding period of last year, 2,843; in- crease in the number on the rolls, 159 ; total average attend- ance, 2,23911; average attendance corresponding period of last year, .1733; increase in average attendance, 536 1; per centage of attendanse,.7s.6,; average attendance for the year 1874. 1,252; increase in average attend..nce as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation ef the Boaro, 1,017.1; accommodation in excuse of average attendance, 446.9; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 236; number attending adventure schools under 9d per week, 49. At the Attendance Committee, held on the 17th October, 1883, I wuramoued 33 cases for contravention of the Educa- tion Acts; 26 parents appeared before the committee to explain the reasons why their children had not attended school regularly. Fens were remitted in two cases at the Mill-brow school to December 24th. One case was allowed half time, four parents were ordered to be summoned under the bee-laws, and the remaining cases the parents were ordered to se that their children attended better in future, or proceedings wunld be takan against them to compel their regular attendance at school. I have also to report a further list of irregulars and non-attenders. These cases have been dealt with previously, and the school fees in several cases are paid by RA Guardians. This list I lay before you, showing their attendance for the past four months. MORE CROW. ACCOMMODATION WANTED.—MR. PRITCHARD WI TYE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT.

About eight women appeared before the Board to com- plain tbat their children—girls in each instance—had been refused adrnianion into the schools in the town on the ground that there was no room for them, and asking what they should do. It was stated that the Wesleyan school had places for over 30 scholars, but the fees charged were in excess of the other sehoole, and the parents *ected to pay them. The deputation were requested to retire, and the Board's decision would be communicated to them through Mr. Bowyer.—The CLERK, in a speech of some length, ad- verted to a paragraph which had appeared in the local newspapers some two months ago, with respect to the School Board of Runcorn, being an extract from a Blue Book issued from the Education Department. It conveyed the impression that there had been a disagreement between the Runcorn Board and their teachers, while the Blue Book report from the inspector was referring to his district in Cheshire as a whole, and not to Runcorn.—Mr. PRITCHARD said the report sta:ed that the Runcorn School Board had twice proposed to build either one or more schools in the town, but that ic each instance they found on inquiry the existing aceommodation was safficient. The first portion of this statement WAS quite accurate, but to say that on en- quiry the Board found the accommodation sufficient was the opposite of fact. On each occasion before making pro- posals to erect schools, the Board had by taking a census satisfied themselves that their existed a deficiency of accommodation. it would be interesting to review the position of the Board with regard to this ques- tion. Since 1.875 the Board had greatly felt the need of more school aceornmodation ; se mach so that on two occa- sions they pror vied to erect a sehoel. In 1877 they proposed ta provide accommodation for £4OO children; in IEII for SOO children, and it was a well-known fact that in recent years there had been by no means sufficient accommodation for the number of children requiring education. Not only had this been the opinion of the Beard. As far back as 1877 the inspector reported thus There is no question aboat a want of additional accommodation. The schools are full." The Board having decided to build one school, the inspector thought two schools would be best—one in Newtown and the other one on Mill-brow. This deficiency was allowed by two inspectors, the present one and his predecessor. This opinion Was again confirmed by the Board in 1881, when a census revealed that there was a deficiency of 818 places. In spite of this fact the Education Department in May, 1881, wrote that they did not see any necessity for an additional school, and by some manipulation of figures, which caused much amusement at the Board at the time, they showed that there WAS a surplus of 1311 places. —The CLERK: What the Education Department said was that they did not understand why the Board should propose to build for anything like 1,800 children. —Mr. Peerceasin was aware of that, but in the previous portion of the letter the Department attempted to prove that the Board hail an excess of accommodatioa. The In- spector must have reporte4 adversely to the Board's pro- posals. According to the Education Act where tle:re was a sufficiency of accommodation any school or building should be declared unnecessery, but since that strange communica- tion from the Department came to hand the Board actually found that the Inspector had passed, and the Department had scheduled, an increased accommodation of 427 places, principally by the denominational schools, which, e: the Department believed in the surplus of 138 places, it was their duty to declare unnecessary, areil refuse the grant eareed by this increase. It was very good of the managers ef these gchools to provide the entire cost of this enlarge- ment, and in supp'ying this accommodation they had re- lieved the ratepayers to that extent which in these times of depression was a matter of importance. But notwithstand- ing this it was obvious that if that strange communication was to set the school Board on one side while the increased accommodation was being provided by others it would have been all right, but it would have been more fair and honest for the Inspector and the Education Department to have
said so rather than to have acted in a -manner 80 incon-

sistent. What the Board bad a right to complain of was this, that the Inspector should report that the Board found the existing accommodation was sufficient when they had maintained that there was a deficiency of 616 places, as proved by last census, and that the Education Department hould be induced by that representation to say there was a surplus of 138 places, while in & few months they should schedule and aceept an increase of 427 plac,s. Such a proceeding, was, be thought, eimply trilii4 with the Board,

and insulting to its dignity and its common sense. Such a perversion of facts and inconsistency in high places was greatly to be deplored. They saw the result that morning, tot notwithstanding the increas?,d accommodation of 427 places, they. had parents coming there by the dozen ansl actually saying they could not get accommodation for their children. Yet for some reu.-3on or other the department, in 1881, tried to prove to the Board that they had an excess of accommodation of 138.—Father FENSELLY thought Mr. Pritchard misunclerstod the Inspector. He thought the In- spector never meant there was sufficient accommodation for children of school age; but rather that there was sufficient accommodation for children who went to school.—The CLERK pointed out that when the Board asked for increased accommodation the Education Department calculated the ciiildren.of school age as between seven and thirteen, while nine years previously they reckoned between the ages of three and thirteen. Had the former standard been taken nine years previously, no School Board would have been formed.— Toe CHAIRMAN remarked that the question had better be deferred to their successors on the new Board. Some accommodation would have to be made for boat chil- dren soon. As long as there were 50 places at the Wesleyan school, the Boaid must refer parents to that school.—fhe CLERIC said once the Board opened a new school, it became an opposition to the denominational schools, which could not maintain their present position. Mr. SIMPSON: If it were possible to provide a school for the boat children and the very ignorant children, and they could be kept in that school, it would be a very good thing, but I cannot see how , . ilt sto be accomplished. We must hope that the new Board will find a way out of the dilliculty.—The discussion ceased on the understanding that the matter be left for the consideration of the new Board.
