div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC IN WIDNES.
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC IN WIDNES.

At the end of last week there was every sign that small- pox would quickly be eradicated from be neighbourhood, but on Monday there were several fresh outbreaks, and en Thursday another case was reported to the Health Com- mittee. The hospital tents were ready for use on Tuesday evening, and the patients were removed there on the follow- ing day. There are now seven patients, two suffering from the disease in an acute form, and five being in the convalescent stags. The authorities now, however, find themselves placed in an unforeseen predicament. The medicil men in the town decline to attend at the hospital on the ground that by so doing they would injure their private practice. Drs. MacLennan, McDonnell, McCambridge, and Brannazan (Dr. Cooper's locum knew.) were invited to meet the Health Committee on Thursday evening to discuss She situation. It was agreed that the wisest course to ad ,pt would be to appoint a doctor to solely superintend the hospital, and we understand that on Tuesday next the Board will be recom- mended to act in that manner. In the meantime Dr. Bran- magma will attend to the hospital patients exclusively. It is stated that Dr. O'Keeffe, the chairman of the Health Com- mittee, was so annoyed at the action of the local medical men, that he declared he would undertake to attend the hos- pital free of cost sooner than that they should be deserted.
WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS AT
RUNCORN.

The annual sermons of the Runcorn branch of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society were preached at St. -Paul's Church on Sunday, by the Rev. C. W. L. Christien, of Burslem.—On Monday evening the annual meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. W. Ou'tram, J.P., Liver- pool, and there was a very large audience. There were on the platform :—The Revs. E. J. Robinson, S. Mees, C. W. L. Christien, Silvester Whitehead, and E. Williams ; Messrs J. Simpson, T. Norman, R. Shaw, E. Taylor, H. Randle, P. Speakman, B. Kniveton, and T. Simister (local secretary.)— Mr. SIMISTER said the following amounts had been re- ceived from the Runcorn branch during 1883: Collected by Mrs. George Hazlehurst, £9 19s, ; Miss Harrison, £8 Os 6d; Miss Norman and Miss Peacock, £l2 2s; Miss Simister, £8 Os 61; public collection on Sunday, £l5 21 3d; public collection at Camden School Chapel, .£1 4s ; collected in the girls' classes in Brunswick school, £3 14s lid; col- lected by the girls with boxes, £5 17s 4d; collected by girls with books, £26 9s 21: increase, £3 16s 71 ; collected in the boys' classes, £9 2s 8d : increase, £2 Os 5d ; collected by the boys with books, £lB Os 4d: increase, £6 is 101; collections in Brunswick school, £l2 Is 21; total amount from Brunswick School, £75 5s id: increase, £ll 17s Bd. Camden Sunday School: From boys' classes, £4 14s 4d; girls' classes, £5 is; collected with books, £8 13s id; in the Sunday School on Sunday, £1 15s 101: total amount from Camden scheol, £33 4s 3d, being an increase on the previous year of £3 8s 101. The amount received up to that evening was £l6O 4s id, being a total increase, r..,0 far, of £l5 8s id. Half of the £33 received from Camden school went to the Home Mis.ion Fund.—The CHAIRM? then delivered an apprapriate address.—The Rev. E. J. ROBINSON read a letter addressed to Mr. John Hazlehurst, from a person who stated that he had worked for Messrs. , Hazlehurst many years ago, when a youth, and had done many things which were not allowable. He had on a pre- vious occasion forwarded, anonymously, a sovereign as restitution, and he now enclosed a similar sum. The letter was signed J. Ff. Mr. Robinson said the sovereign would be devoted to the Missions. The Rev. C. W. L. CHRISTIEN delivered an excellent address on India ; while the Rev. SILVESTEII WHITEHEAD, missionary from China, dealt with the missionary question of that country.—On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by the Rev. S. SIEEs, a vote of thanks was accorded to the deputation ; and a similar com- pliment was pail to the committee and officials on the motion of Mr. B. KNIVETON, seconded by Rev. E. WIL- LIAMS.—The committee was re-appointed.—Mr. R. SHAW moved, and Mr. P. Sp E S.KMata seconded, a vote of thanks to the chair,nan, which was carried. —The Ray. E. J. ROBIN- SON announced that the collection that evening amounted to £54 13s lid, being an increase of £l5 lis 11d.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL WARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL WARD.

A special meeting was held on Thursday afternoon for the purpose of appointing chairman, vice-chairman, and com- mittees for the next three years, There were present the Revs. T. Finegan, J. Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. T. S. Timmis, R. Bradshaw, IL NY. Deacon, R. Shaw, J. B. Imison, P. Glover, and G. H. Danby (clerk.) The Clerk took the chair, and read the returning officers official notice of the result of the election. APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.

Dr. O.KEEFFE remarked upon the excellent manner in which the business of the Board had been conducted during the past three years, and said Mr. Timmis deserved the special thanks not only of the Board but the public at large, for the admirable way in which he had conducted the recent arrangements by which a contested election was avoided. Mr. Timmis, as chairman, had shown courtesy to every mcru- ber of the Board, and they could not do better than re-elect him to the position. It was well-known that he 11 id done an enormous amount of good in the education of the rising generation. (Hear, hear.) He was also equally well-known for his philanthropy, and althought be did not live in the township, he was deeply interested in its welfare. Mr. Tim- mis was the author of the Widnes Council of Education, and although it was but an ex- periment, it was an experiment which would be conducive to the accomplishment of much good, and he hoped to see other School Boards in the country following a similar course. He, therefore, proposed the nomination of Mr. Timmis as chairm in of the Board for the ensuing three years. Mr. Saaw seconded the prop ssition. He observed that the business-like way in which the business of the Bard had been conducted had not only gave satisfaction to the pnblic, but to. every member of the Board. They had received

every kindness and consideration at the hands of Mr. Tim- tuba. Whilst they considered that the Board had in their schools something like 2,400 children, he thought it said something for the excellent way in which the work of the Board had been done, that they had not at all interfered with the denominational schools. (Hear, hear.) They knew ho.' very easy it wonld have been to reverse this if the Board had attampted to put their schools in competition to schools supported by voluntary subscriptions. This would have been a great calamity for the town ; but they had the satisfaction of knowing that not only were the Bard schools full, but that every school in the district was better than when the Beard was formed. (Hoar, hear.) Taking these circumstances into consideration, he did not think they could de _better than appoint .Mr. Timmis
ehairwan:because by his high busines; qualities and kind- liness of disposition he was able to fill the position with honour to himself and honour to the town.

Mr. BRADSHAW cordially supported the appointment, which was unanimously agreed to. Mr. Timms on taking the chair was greeted with ap- plause. He thanked them for having again elected him to the position of chairman. He was not at all sure that they had made [he best selection, because he was conscious that he had a great many defects. He knew that he did not de-

vot?, that energy and that time to the werk of the Board which it required, partly on account of his health not being so good as it was, and partly on account of business exigencies, and to the fact that he was getting older. ("No," and laughter.) At any rate he did not feel the same inclination to work as formerly, but if they were willing to accept him he was willing to till the position. (Ap- plause.) Dr. O'KEEFFE : For better, for worse.

The CHAIRMAN in eulogistic terms spoke to the past services of Mr. Bradshaw, and proposed the appointment of that gentleman as vice-chairman. Mr. GLOVES seconded the motion, which was carried. APPOINTMENT Or COMMITTEES. The following committees we:e appointed :—District Education: Father Clarke, and Messrs. Deacon and Glover. General Purposes: To consist of the chairmen of the various committees; School Management: Father Finegan, and Messrs. Davies and Itnison. Sites and Buildieg : Mr. Brock, Father Finegan, and-Mr. rimmis. Finance: Messrs. Shaw, Bradshaw, and Dr. O'Keeffi. The OJAI/MAN paid a tribute to Mr. Shaw's ability as a financier, to which he ascribed the present admirable posi- tion of the 13oanl's finances. Mr. Shaw had been chairman of the Film:cis Committee since the formation of the Board.

OPENING Of THE WARRINGTON NUIV SCHOOL OF All. The new School of Art, the hietory of which together with a description of the new building, we published last. week, was formally opened by his Worship the Mayor (John Crosfield, Esq. Yon Thursday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of the principal inhabitants of Warringteu and the neighbourhood. The weather, happily, was beauti- fully tine, and the arrangements for the opening ceremony were iciest successfully carried out. The opening was fixed for three o'clock, prior to which hour the council of the School of Art and the members of the Town awned who were invited as the ceremony asseinWed in the Mayor's par- lour at the Town Hall, whence they walked in procession to the new building. Meanwhile many ladies and gentian!" who bad assembled to witness the opening ceremony met in the lecture room of the Museam and patiently awaited the arrival of the procession. The procession, which Was headed by a posse of police under the direction f the Chief-Constable (Mr. Hunt), left the Town Hall shortly before three o'clock. Immediately following the slicers were the members of the Council of the School of Art, including the chairman (Mr. John Rylands), Messrs. E. Brewtnall, C. Chorley, William Fell, John Ellison, H. A. Houghton, James Marshall, John Dun, ! William Owen (hon. sec.), and J. C. Thompson (master of the Institution). These gentlemen were succeeded by the members of the Corporation, at whose head was his Worship the Mayor wearing . his chain of office, the other members present being Alder- men Pickinere (the ex-Mayor), Burgess, Kean, Webver, and Chandley; Councillors Monks, Caldwell, Bolton, Wal- lington, Litton, Greening, Brown, Francomb, Dixon, and Woolfall ; and Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (Deputy Town Clerk). On arriving et the School of Art, Mr. John Rvlands pre- sented to the Mayer a beautiful silver key, with which his Worship at once unlocked the front door of the building, amid applause. The Institution then quickly filled, and a short time was spent in inspecting the werks of art with which the walls of the school are adorned. Subsequently, whilst the major portion of the company were asse:nbled in one of the lower motile of the building, The M A.YOU ascended a chair and said: Ladies and gen- tlemeu,—l hope in the first place you will excuse me being in this awkward position of having to stand on a chair. (Laughter.) Ido not believe I ever had to do it in my life before, and I feel in rather a precarious situation. I hope, 'therefore, you will make allowance for me. (Hear, hear.) It W 33 Wended that I should address a few rem irks from the balcony upstairs, but seeing that you have all as- ssinbled here we thought it better that I should just say a few words to you in this room. (Hear, hear.) First, let ins tell you that it is a great pleasure to me to be here on the last day of my in iyoralty to perform the most pleasing ceremony which has ever fallen to my lot (Atipleuse.) Any one who has ever visitor' the old School of Art must have seen those dim, dismal. dusty rooms, which were most I unsuitable for the accsinmodation of the students in that p!re.e. (Hear, hear.) I have been there myself al:my times, and I have often felt sorry to see the studen:s AO badly eccommodated, and I Also felt sorry that such an ,xclieat maeter tike Mr. iheeepahn—(aeplaase)—

should not have a suitable building in which to instruct his pupils. I was travelling in the railway train with Mr. Thompson ceining from Hertford one day—l can't say how long, but perhaps three years ago—and I rein irked to him that I thought it high time we should have a new School of Art. " Why," he said, "that is what I have been longing for for the last ten years." I said, " Well, if you will try I will help you to make a start." And so I did—(loud ap- plause)—and I was delighted to find that my fellow-towns- men took up this idea of a new School of Art with such spirit and such generosity. (Hear, hear.) I must nt ake a paint in thanking, especially the ladies, for the exertions they rnade—( applaus .t)—collecting, I believe, nearly £l,OOO towards the expense of this building. (Applause.) I tnink that a master like Mr. Thomps who has turned out p uPils who have made world-wide fame such as Fildes and War- rington Wood—a master like that richly deserves to have the best building that can be built for the instruction of his pupils, and I believe this building in which we are now assembled is as well constructed as any building cm be fur the instruction in art. (Applause) I must congratulate the architect on the manner he has done his work. (Applause.) There are a great many architects who sacrifice the internal arrangements of a buildina for the external appearance. Architects have faults like everybody else, and they are fond of making a building a kind of advertisement of their skill in design. (Hear, hear.) lam very glad to say that Mr. Owen has not erred in this respect. (Applause.) Mr. Owen has wisely taken counsel with Mr. Thompson. They have put their hands together and have constructed this building internally as good as it can be, amid left the outside to take care of it- , self, and even the outside, I must say, is far from being a I disgrace to the town. (Hear, hear.) I call it a handsome building. (Applause.) lam only sorry it does not happen to be in a pasition in the town wnere it could be more easily seen. That is to he regretted, but it could not be helped, whilst at the same time there is an advantage of being in a quiet street, because it will nut interfere with the students in their work. Then I think I must congratulate ,he builder also on the way he has done his work. (Hear, hear.) The building is as well built as it can possibly be. I hope that this building which we open this day will prove to be a great blessing to the town and to the students. We are all proud of our public build- ings in Warrington. We are proud of our Town Hall, of our new Hospital, our new Infirmary, of our new Post Office, our Museum, and last, but not least, we are proud of our new School of Art. (Applause.) I have great pleasure, ladies and gentlemen, in declaring that the School of Art is now open. (Loud applause.)

Mr. JOHN RYLANDS said that as they expected a large company in the evening, it was well that the speeches should be restricted et present, and that they should take the opportunity later on of thanking the Mayor for the put he had taken in the proceedings of that day. They ware all very much obliged to the Mayor, not only for per- forming that ceremony, but for the fact that it was through his munificent subscription to commence tha School of Art that they were enabled to proceed with the building, ad therefore to do fair justice to the subject they would be right in postponing it until the evening. (Hear, hear.) This concluded the ceremony. Mr. Rylands mentioned the arrangements which had been made for the evening con• versazione, and the company then inspected the building and the 55ecimens of art which were exhibited.

much merit; and the member for the borough, Mr. Melilla- nits, and Mr. Beastont have contributed a number of land- scapes and seascapes by M. Liuton, all of which will bear a close inspection. Other notable works on view are one attributed to Rubens, another to Guido, and minor works by Teniers, Liversedge, Hoist, Hulk, kc. The portrait of Mr. Alderman Davies, painted some years ago by the borough treasurer, Mr. Cherley, is yet a striking likeness, and evi- dences much technical skill. We need only add that many other local artistes, several of them students at the School of Art, aro well and creditably represented in the loan collec- tion.

div.head: CONVERSAZIONE.
div.p: THE CONVERSAZIONE.

In the evening the Mayor gave a conversazione, when the compeoy which assembled at the schoel may be suitably de- scribed as influential, fashionable, and representative ; indeed, seldom hae the inaugury of a building of the kind seen a gayer or more interesting throng than that which met to do it honour on Thursday evening. It was a pleasure to observe, too, the cordial feeling which seemed to prevail, and gratification was expressed on every hind that Warring- ton had seen its way to erect a building suitable and worthy of a study in which so many residents of the "old town ." have shone forth prominently and will doubtles do so again. Tne ladies aud gentlemen began to arrive shortly before eight o'clock. Amongst those who attended were the Mayor (John Crosfield, Esq.), J. G. Mc Winnies, Esq., M.P., Peter Rylands, Esq., M.P., and Mrs. Rylands, Mr. John Rylands (chairman of the Council of the School of Art), Alderman and Mrs. Pickinere, Alderman and Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Mr. H. N. Houghton, Mr. W. J. Horton, Mr. J. Connor, Alderman, Mrs., and the Misses Burgess, Mr. Wm. Owen, Councillor and Miss Greem, Mr. Kirkconnel, Alder- man Chandlev, Councillor and Mrs. Platt, Councillor, Mrs., and the Misses Brown, Councillor W. Pierpoinc, Rev. E. St. A. Duke' Mrs. Wilkinson and Miss Wilkinson, Mr. W. Mortimer, Dr. Sherratt, Mrs. Quekett, Mr. W. D., Mrs., aud Miss Joins, Alderman Webster and Mrs. Webster, Mr. John Dun, Mr. and Mrs. James Fairclougla, Mr. John Fair- dough, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Fletcher, Mr. John White, Councillor R. W. and Mrs. Francomb, Mr. Edward and Miss Milner, Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Williamson, Rev. R. Pitcher, Councillor and Miss Taylor' Mr. Edward Brewtnall, Mr. J. C. and Miss Thompson, Mr., Mrs., and the Misses T. Robinson, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Mesrris Miss Jenny Morris, Mr. Charles, Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) and Mn. Hunt, air. J. L. Tunstall, Mr. Paterson, itc. A band composed of embers of the Warrington Musical Society, =ducted by Mr. J. P. Reynolds, aud under the leadership of Mr. R. H. Pearson, was present, and played several selections. The performances of this band reflected much credit on Mr. Reynolds' skill in conducting. The company having passed a pleasant hour in the school, an adjourn. ment was made to the Art Gallery of the Museum, where the distribution of prizes took place. The Mayor presided, and was supported by the Council of the School. Mr. McMinnies, M.P., and Mr. Rylareds, M.P., were obliged to leave before the ceremony. Mr. JOHN RYLANDS said that he was requested to move a vote of thanks to the Mayor for opening the School of Art, as it was suggested in the afternoon that as the School of Art was not a convenient place to speak in that the speeches should be deferred until the evening. He had also to ask the Meyor to present the prizes to the successful students, and he would take the opportunity in doing so of makimg a very few remarks. They had seen lately in the public prints an account of the early days of the School of Art. Those accounts were not complete—so far as they went, they were tolerably accurate; but the real origin of the School of Art, which occurred a little before the date they saw outside the panels of the new building, occurred in this way: Mr. Brewtnall, in 1849, came to Warrington as mister of the Newton-road School, afterwards called the People's College, and being anxious to do what he could to teach art, he commenced such a course of instrection in that school. Soon after he became secretary of the Mechanics' Institution, and almost immediately began to institute the study of art there. He started a class, and Mr. Fletcher, who was at that time in Parr's Bank, became teacher of the class. He mentioned that circumstance, because really that was the origin of the Warrington School of Art. Mr. Fletcher, however, grew delicate, and subsequently died, and Mr. Charles, father of the gentleman who painted the portrait of the ex-Mayor, took that class, but Mr. Brewtnall found there was a great desire among those who took advantage of the teaching that was to be obtained, to extend the study, and saw Mr. Hemmersley, then master of the School of Design in Man- chester. He might mention that at that time there were only about half a dozen of such schools existing. Mr. Hammersley through this came over and delivered a lecture. He (Mr. Rylands) could take no credit himself for the foundation of the school, because he lived near Manchester at the time. From that which he had stated came the formation of the School of Art, which up to then had been in the Mechanics' Institution. Lord Winmarleigh hearing what was going on, called at the Newton-street school, and asked what was contemplated. Mr. Brewtnall explained everything to Lord Winmerleigh, who was so pleased that beat once gave £5. Then they talked the matter over for about an hour, when Lord Winne arleigh said, " I will give you £50." (Ap- plause.) That was practically the first outside help the School of Art received. Then was the school removed into the building at present occupied. He referred to this matter so that Mr. Brewtnall should have the credit which was due to him. (Applause.) With regard to the future of the School of Art they had to tender their sincere thanks to the _ _

Mayor for his starting the subscription list with £l,OOO)— (applause)—without which they would never have had that new building. They had got a School of Art that would probably answer the requirements of Warrington for twenty years to come at least, perhaps more than that. (Hear, hear.) Of course the institution mist be maintained and carried on in a proper manner, and the question had arisen "Who is to do it ?" Lord Winmarleigh, to begin with, con- sidered it was the duty of the Town Council to do it. He for one had no strong feeling either in favour of one mode of action or another, but it appeared to him that somebody must have the responsibility of the building, and they would have to see it was carried out in a proper manner. it was a question how far a building intended for the good of the public of Warrington should be left in the hands of a few

Individuals, and to what extent it was fair to expect them to take the responsibility of it. (Hear, hear.) He spoke. that because the subject had excited a good deal of talk, and he dare say there would be considerable more talking about it before it was settled. Hitherto the &hoe! of A,t had been self-supporting, and he did not see why, in a larger building and with better means of popularising the thing, that it should not be sslf-supporting in the future. (clear, hear.) Eventually it must be so, and, therefore, he had no strong feeling as to the responsibility resting on the Corperation. I Still it was felt by some that it was the duty of the Corpor- ation to take up this matter and become responsible for tbe school. He believed a rate of a farthing in the pound would be cmsiderably more than the school would tequire. (Hear, hear.) It was quite clear that they would have to raise a little more money. As far as the School itself went they had raised sufficient to be out of debt. They would have to obtain a !ale more money for the fittings; of course that would be left to the committee, but the sum required under this head would probably be £l5O, and if the Corpor- ation did not take it in hand they would have to deal with the qaestion on a larger scale. He spoke thus to those present simply that they might understand that the committee would look to them to assist them at the proper time, because he was geite sure that having got that beautiful S.elsool War- rington people would not let it become as a white elephant in their midst. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Hylands then asked the Mayor to distribute the prizes. (Applause.) The prizes were then distributed to the successful students, who were warmly greeted on receiving their awards from the hands of the Mayor. His Worship was assisted in the distribution by Mr. Owen. The certificate is awarded to Hilda Thompson for success in third grade.

The distribution of prizes having been concluded, Mr. Alderman WESTER rose and said be was en- trusted with a proposition with which he sure they would all cordially agree. It was that they tender their warmest thanks to the Mayor for presiding on that occasion, and for th 6 manner in which he had distributed the prizes that evening. (Applause.) Had it not been for the valuable and great munificence of his worship, the School of Art would not have been built for some time to come, or at any rate at present. It was not to be supposed that during the the thirty years the school had been in existence that the question of the erection of a new school had not been a burning one on many occasions. Over and over again it had been debated, and over and over again it had been set aside, owing to the difficulty of raising the necessary funds, which could not be overcome, but when they had received the munificent assistance they had from the Mayer they were imbued wall new spirit, and they set their shoulders to the wheel. The result was what they saw that day. (Applause.) There was no doubt it would be a difficult matter to continue, and to work the new School of Art unless there were increased means for its support, but he was sanguine himself that the same spirit and energy which had carried the :school forward to its present position would carry it forward now that it had assumed a much loftier condition than it had before. (Applause.) He was certain that such would be the case, and that the Cor- poration would he pleased to assist them if they were called upon by the School Council. (Hear, hear.) As the poet had said, "there was a tide in the affairs of man which, if taken at the flood, led on to success," and so he (Alderman Webster) believed there were tides in the progress of insti- tutions which would carry them forward to greater successes in the future. Everyone would, he was sure feel gratified if the school went forward prosperously in the future, and became a self-supporting institution. (Hear, hear.) Alder- man Webster, in conclusion, said he had great pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks to the Mayor for his greet muni- ficence in assisting them to erect that building and for dis- tributing the prizes' and he believed being the last official act his Worship would perform during his year of mayoralty. (Applause.) Mr. Alderman CHANDLEY said he could have no hesitation in seconding a vote of thanks to the Mayor for his goodness in coming amongst them to distribute the prizes that even- ing. He was quite sure his Worship must almost feel a nausea of praise for the way in which be had received the thanks of his friends during the last few days. It must have been very gratifying indeed to him. He (Alderman Chandley) believed that those thanks lead been sincere and well earned, and he be- lieved the Mayor was appreciated in his official capacity as a mayor, and that be was appreciated as a patron of art and as a townsman. (Hear, hear.) He (Alderman Chandley) had been associated with the School of Art from its earliest days. He had been a member of the School of Art Com- mittee for 30 or 40 years—certainly from its early forma- tion ; and he was sure it must be gratifying to the old members of the institution that it had had such a long ex- istence, and that it had grown and flourished as it had done. (Hear, hear.) But the new School pf Art owed its present position entirely to the Mayor, without whose munificence the new school would net have been built. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure indeed in seconding the vote of thanks to the Mayor, and he hoped he might live long to have a very pleasing reminiecence of his graceful act. (Applause.) He was quite sure the Mayor would look hack and dwell with pleasure on having round him that night so so many representatives of the institution and so many of the people of Warrington, and long might he have those reflections. He was also sure the Mayor's liberality would long be remembered by the inhabitants of Warrington. I ( Applause.)

• The resolution having been carried with acclamation, The MAYOR, who, in rising, was received with applause, said he was extremely obliged to the aldermen who had pro- posed and seconded that vote Qf thanks to him, and for the manner in which the company had received it. As Alder- man Cfiandley very truly said the votes of thanks showered upon him during the last fortnight had been something enormous. (laughter.) He did not think himself that he deserved them, but at the same time he could not help feel- ing a gratification in knowing that he had the sympathy and goodwill of all his fellow townsmen. (Applause.) It was a very pleasant feeling for a man occupying a public position when he had the sympathy of those over whom he reigned. (Hear, hear.) It would be a very disagreeable thing, he should think, to any one holding the position he did, who had not that sympathy. (Hear, hear.) He was pleased to attend there that night to distribute the prizes, and to do anything he could to assist art. (Applause.) He thought they could not over-estimate the education which was imparted by Mr. Thompson in the School of Art. (Hear, hear.) He felt and he was sure they all felt proud that they had in Warrington a gentleman so well calculated to occupy the office of teacher. He must say that the pupils Mr. Thompson had turned out, and the works of art which had been produced, reflected on him the very greatest credit. (Applause.) He was reading the other day the life of Naysmyth, the man who invented the steam hammer. His father was a man of great genius, and the sons enjoyed the same inventive faculty. Naysmith considered that the education of the eye was the most important education anyone could receive, and placed it first. There was a happy illustration im his life. When he was travelling from Norway he came to a farmhouse. There were no hotels in those days, and people had to put up at farmhouses. This old farmer nor his wife did not know a word of English,and Naysmyth was equally ignorant of their own language, and he could not make them under- stand what he wanted. So what did he do but he pulled out his pocket book and pencil and sketched a little table with a fowl, tea cup, a salt-cellar, and a loaf of bread. The old farmer's wife was delighted, as she knew at once what he wanted, and carried out his (directions. Then when he was going to bed he wanted to be called at six o'clock the following morning, and he did not know how to describe his wish. Being a man of idea and ready application he drew out his book again and sketched a little pony-cart with the sun rising just over the pony, and the farmer understood at once that he wanted that when the sun rose. (Laughter.) He (the Mayor) gave that little illustration to show how useful it was to have the faculty of drawing, or speaking by pencil as it really was. (Applause,) In conclusion, the Mayor expressed the plea- sure that it gave him to be there that evening, and the hope that wherever the future responsibility of the school rested that it would always be maintained efficiently and in a manner creditable to Warrington. (Loud applause.) The company shortly afterwards separated, a most plea- sant evening having been spent.

div.head: EXHIBITION OF PICTURES.
div.p: THE EXHIBITION OF PICTURES.

Considering the limited time at the disposal of the com- mittee who have had the management of this department of the opening arrangements, tbe exhibition of pictures and studies must be pronounced a success, and it is to be hoped it will result as it ought to do in a substantial gain to the building fund. It is not yet a month since the day of opening was fixed by the Council of the School, but hums- diately it was made known some of the past and present pupils originated the idea of holding an exhibition of their works, and with that object a mixed committee of ladies and gentlemen was speedily formed. Of this committee Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle and E. J. Hall were appointed secretaries, and the energetic manner in which each and all of the members of the committee have worked is worthy of all praise. Communications were sent out to many gentlemen of the town and neighbourhood, inviting them to lend pic- tures for exhibition, and to these invitations there has been a ready response. At first it WAS intended that the exhibition should be split up into four divisions—viz., one confined to works by present students, another to the works of past students, a third comprising the works of local artists or artists having a local connection, a fourth open to eminent artists not toed. In cons,laence, however, of the lack of time at the disposal of the committee, some of whom—notably the energetic Master, Mr. Thompson—have had to work almost night and day, it was found impossible to adhere to this arrangement, but there has nevertheless been an honest endeavour to classify the works as much as possible. One room on the ground floor is set apart to pictures sent on loan ; in another room. also on the ground floor, are col- lected all the works of the students past and present in chalk; the vestibule and staircase are filled with the archi- tectural and decorative works of Mr. Thompson's pupils : while on the upper floor one room is set apart for the works of the students, also past and present, in oil and sepiA, and another for works in water colours. There is also a small room on the upper floor containing a few pictures sent on loan. for which there was no space in the room below. Many of the pictures of the students, we should here also state, are for sale for the benefit of the new institution. It is, we think, to be re- gretted that no catalogue of the various works has ben compiled, for without this necessary adjunct to such an exhi- bition the visitor is unquestionably placed at a disadvantage. The pictures, however, in most cises, if not all, have a small ticlio: at the corner showing whose works they are and to whom they belong. We also n3te the absence of any collection of works of art from South Kensington, usually a feature of exhibitions of this character, but, we presume, no attempt has been made to obtain such a loan, doubtless for want of time.

It would be impessible in the spice at our disposal to comment on all the works of art exhibited, nor shill we at- tempt any such task. We shall content ourselves with simply noting the results of a cursory sur- vey of the contents of the different rooms. Commencing, then, with the students' work, we would mention that in one of the upper rooms, en the stair- case, and in the vestibule, there are displayed many archi- tectural and decorative original designs. That they are of a high order of merit is attested by the fact that many of them have been succeseful in carrying off national medals and other important prize., the names of the holders of which we published last week. What will strike the visitor most will, we think, be the variety of these designs, which are adapted chiefly for carpets, wall-papers, table-cloths, borders, dec. It is interesting to note how, in almost all Cases, these de- signs have been worked from the basis of some simple element. A natural flower or plant has been selected—say a passion flower or a sprig of mistletoe. The conven- tionalised form is worked up into designs for the various purposes we have mentioned, all the resources of petal, bud, and full-blown flower being utilised in the process, thus securing a consistent and harmonious whole. In a room on the ground floor, as we have alrea4 stated, are exhibited a number of chalk drawings by the Students, and amongst these are a few time studies. The object of these exhibits is to show the class-work done by the pupils of the School, and it must be admitted that some of the drawings evince considerable ability. The exhibits are composed chiefly of drawings from the nude, and various other objects from plaster casts. There are also scattered through- out the building some outline drawings of claisic scrolls and foliage from the solid, as well as outlines of flowers from nature. The work of the etudenrs, however, which deserves most attention is that which has been executed in oil and water colours, and of these there are a large number exhibited. In the room to the right on the upper floor are collected many examples of the students' painting in oil from still life, as well as 'sepia drawings from the casts. The latter have, as a whole, been exceedingly well done; whilst as regards the former the subjects selected have been chiefly combinations of birds, fruit, game, vege- tables, and miscellaneous domestic utensils, the colouring of most of which has been faithfully executed, and the details of the pictares carefully and artistically elaborated. The same remarks apply to the students water-colour drawings which are exhibited in another room. The fact that nearly all of them secured medals and prizes is an evidence that they possess considerable merit. Conspicuous amongst the loan collection in the lower room are the examples from the brush and pencil of Mr. G. Sheffield. A screen is devoted almost entirely to works in black and white by this prolific artist,wbose forte undoubtedly lies in this branch of art. There is about Mr. Sheffield's style a dash and vigour peculiarly appropriate to the stir- ring matine subject or the bold landscape. The habit of treating subjects in a broad and suggestive war so essential and appropriate in charcoal drawings has, however, a ten- dency to result in sketchiness where the more delicate mediam of water colour is concerned. This is the only fault noticeable in the colossal drawing of the locality of Wilmslow (Cheshire), lent by Mr. J. lunstall. 'the figures in the foreground, of the horses more especially, suffer for want of more finished drawing. Otherwise this' is a power- ful and telling picture. The seascape water colour by the same artist sheves much greater regard for detail, and is full of rich undertones. There are several examples amongst the oil paintings from the easel of Mr. J. Charles, the artist who recently, it will be remembered, so successfully painted the portrait of the ex- Mayor. The "Study of a Masculine Head," lent by Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, is the a:LOA striking exhibit, though perhaps the kindred subjects of "Playmates" and "Portrait of a Girl" represent the artist in his happiest vein, both being remarkable for delicate and tefined colouring. Mr Harry Wood's "Lancashire Roses" is a clever picture, in which the colours are handled in a way betokening considerable self-confidence and a subtle sense of harmony on the part of the artist. Amongst exhibits in water colour deserving of mention are a pastoral scene by David Cox; half-a-dozen charming landscapes by Hull; "Chicks," an interesting painting by Robert Barnes, lent by Mr. Alderman Pick- mere; and four excellent pictures illustrative of incidents in domestic life, by C. Paterson, these being lent by Mr. Councillor Monks. In the same class we must not omit to mention a picture belonging to Mr. Beamont illustrating a "Scene in Warrington Friary," which is noteworthy chiefly from its local interest. Among the oil paintings we noticed a study from the life by Mist- reedy, the property of Mr.' Thompson; and near to it a kindred picture, "The Bathers." by Herbert, R.A., lent Ly Mr. R. Davies. "The Pet Bud" is the subject of a choice piiuting by J. Rogers, R. 4 ; two studies ef heads by 31. Luc 13, OJth lent by Dr. Fox, are composi.ions of

THE PRINCE or WALES'S BlRTHDAY.—Yesterday b?ing the forty-second birthday of the Prince of Wales, it was celebrated in Londen, at Windsor, and at Sandringham in the usual way. Writing to King Leopold two months after the Prince was born, the Queen set down the follswing words:—" I wonder very much whom our little boy will be like. You will understand hour fervent are my prayers, and I am sure everybody's must be, to see him resemble his father in eve-y, every respect, bola in body and mind!" THE GREAT COLLIERY EXPLOSION: LATER DETAILS.— Althomgh the explorers, 17 in 'number, were at work all night, only three bodies have been recovered sincelhursday afternoon, and three since six o'clock yesterday morning. The bodies near the bottom of the pit shaft were got to with- out much difficulty, hat there were many impediments in the way of rinick progress. As they proceed farther in the mine the searchers are better able to realise the extent of the explosion. The greater portion of the walls forming the sides to the roadway has been demolished, and the ruins will have to be removed before some of the corpses can be recovered, which will mean considerable delay. In all 45 bodies have been brought up to the surface, and it is feared there are still about 10 or 12 in the pit. When the terrible calamity occurred there were 111 workpeople in the mine, and about a dozen escaped without injuries. During Thurs- day night two more of the injured miners died, bringing the total number of lives sacrificed to about 66 or 68.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH-EAST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—We beg to return you our sincere thanks for your kindness in again returning us as your repre- sentatives to the Town Council. Though a contest, under the circumstaßces, ought not to have been forced upon us, it has, in many respects, been productive of good, as it has given you the fullest opportunity of pronoun& g judgment upon our past conduct, and to us it has given the satisfaction of kn )wing that we still possess your confidence. To the many good friends that voluntarily took up our came with a zeal and energy be- yond praise, and whose labours we can never forget, we return our sincere thanks. We have the honour to be, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servants, R. W. FRANCOMB. J. CAVE WHITTLE. Warrington, Nov. sth, 1883.
